title: 5 - Representation Learning
text:
The Vastness of Image Space

Illustrated are the set of all possible images and the subset of natural images
Total possible \(256\times256\) RGB images: \(256^{256 \times 256 \times 3}\) ≈ infinite


Natural images: (relatively) tiny subset of this space


Implication: Pixel space is extremely inefficient for representing real images!

title: 5 - Representation Learning
text:
Definition

A representation is the output \(\mathbf{z} = f(\mathbf{x})\) produced by an encoder \(f\) applied to input \(\mathbf{x}\)



Semantic Coordinate System where distances \(\|\mathbf{z}_i - \mathbf{z}_j\|_2\) reflect meaningful relationships.


We focus on vector-valued (distributed) representations, not symbolic descriptions

title: 5 - Representation Learning
text:
What Makes Good Representations?
Invariance & Selectivity Balance

Invariance: \(\|f(\mathbf{x}) - f(g(\mathbf{x}))\|_2 < \epsilon\) for nuisance transform \(g\) (lighting, pose)
Selectivity: \(\|f(\mathbf{x}_i) - f(\mathbf{x}_j)\|_2 > \delta\) for semantically different \(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j\)
Trade-off: Too much invariance → loss of discriminative details
Sweet spot: Preserve task-relevant variations, discard irrelevant ones

Properties of Good Representations

Similar images should be close
Different images should be separated
Task-relevant details should be preserved
Nuisance variation should be ignored
Embeddings should be compact and reusable

title: 5 - Representation Learning
text:
Three Learning Paradigms

Supervised Learning: Learn from human labels (ImageNet)
Weakly Supervised: Learn from noisy/partial labels (image-text pairs)
Self-Supervised: Learn from data structure (no labels needed)

title: 5 - Representation Learning
text:
Supervised Learning



Encoder + classifier trained on labeled data (e.g., ImageNet, 1000 classes)
Cross-entropy loss on human-provided labels
Penultimate layer embeddings = transferable features

title: 5 - Representation Learning
text:
Weakly Supervised: CLIP

From Radford et al. (2021)

Dual encoders align images with text captions
Uses image-text pairs (web-scale data)
Contrastive loss: maximize diagonal, minimize off-diagonal

title: 5 - Representation Learning
text:
Self-Supervised Learning: Masked Autoencoding (MAE)

From He et al. (2021)

Mask 75% of image patches at random
Encode only visible patches (efficient!)
Decode with mask tokens inserted and reconstruct original pixels



Key insight: To fill in gaps, model must learn global structure

title: 5 - Representation Learning
text:
Self-Supervised Learning: Contrastive Learning






From Chen et al. (2020)







From Chen et al. (2020)







Pull positive pairs close together in embedding space
Push negative pairs apart
Form tight clusters of semantically similar samples

title: 5 - Representation Learning
text:
Self-Supervised Learning: Self-Distillation

From Caron et al. (2021)

A student sees different crops of an image and must match the teacher (a slow average of the student)
Different views of the same image → same output: nuisance changes are ignored
Centering and sharpening keep outputs from becoming identical for all images

title: 5 - Representation Learning
section: What Can We Do With Embeddings?
text:
What Can We Do With Embeddings?

Image search: find visually similar images
Classification: train a small classifier on frozen embeddings
Clustering: group images without labels
Outlier detection: find unusual or duplicate images
Dense tasks: use patch tokens for segmentation, detection, correspondence


Core idea: once images become vectors, many problems become geometry problems.

title: 5 - Representation Learning
text:
Image Search with Embeddings


Encode every database image: \[
\mathbf{z}_i = f(\mathbf{x}_i)
\]




Encode the query image: \[
\mathbf{z}_q = f(\mathbf{x}_q)
\]




Retrieve nearest neighbours: \[
\operatorname{topk}_i \; \text{sim}_{\cos}(\mathbf{z}_q, \mathbf{z}_i)
\]



No classifier. No labels. No fine-tuning.

text:

DINOv3 embeddings of furniture photos (ABO) in 2D; query in black, neighbours in red.

title: 2 - Images as Data
text:
Why It Matters
Many classification failures aren’t model failures, they’re data failures.

Imbalance, noisy labels, hidden shortcuts, leakage, wrong tensor assumptions.

title: 2 - Images as Data
text:
Images as Tensors (1/2)


Figure 1: An image as a tensor of shape H × W × C.

title: 2 - Images as Data
text:
Images as Tensors (2/2)


Figure 2: An image as a tensor of shape H × W × C.

Pixel values: uint8 [0, 255] → float [0, 1] → standardized (zero mean, unit variance)


Shape conventions:

NumPy / PIL: (H, W, C) — channels last
PyTorch: (C, H, W) — channels first

Mismatched conventions → silent bugs.

title: 2 - Images as Data
text:
Channels: What Does C Mean?


Figure 3: RGB (3 channels) vs. grayscale (1 channel).

1: grayscale, depth, IR/thermal, X-ray, ultrasound
3: RGB (or HSV, same info, different axes)
4: RGBA (alpha) or RGB + near-IR
N (10s–100s): multispectral / hyperspectral (remote sensing, agriculture, astronomy)


For ordinary 2-D images, only C changes; the tensor structure stays H × W × C. For volumes or time series, we add additional axes.

title: 2 - Images as Data
text:
Thermal Imaging


Figure 4: Thermal images are often single-channel sensor measurements: each pixel represents heat / infrared intensity. For display, they may be mapped to false-color RGB.

title: 2 - Images as Data
text:
Quiz: Batch Shape
A batch of 32 RGB images, each 224 × 224, in PyTorch.
What is the tensor shape?

Answer: (32, 3, 224, 224) — batch × channels × height × width


The batch dimension is always first in PyTorch; it enables parallel GPU computation.

title: 2 - Images as Data
text:
Resolution


Figure 5: Same image at 224 × 224, 64 × 64, 16 × 16. Detail is progressively lost.

Higher → detail, more memory + compute
Lower → faster, but discards information
Aspect-ratio distortion → squashing deforms objects


Common: resize shortest edge + center-crop, or resize with padding.

title: 2 - Images as Data

Label Noise


Figure 10: Wolf or large dog? Empty, or a tail at the edge of the frame?

Inter-annotator disagreement on borderline cases
Systematic errors: annotators consistently confuse two classes
Ambiguous category boundaries: class definitions overlap


Deep networks can eventually memorize noisy labels (Arpit et al. 2017), so validation monitoring and data inspection matter.

title: 2 - Images as Data
text:
Hidden Bias


Figure 11: Same animal, different background: different prediction. The background, not the cow, drives the prediction. Adapted from Beery et al. (2018).

Geographic: limited regional diversity (architecture, vegetation, clothing)
Selection: internet-sourced images overrepresent certain demographics/styles
Watermark / source artifacts: visual quirks correlate with labels

title: 2 - Images as Data
text:
Dataset Splits

Train: used to fit model parameters
Validation: used for model selection and tuning
Test: used once for final evaluation


Splitting strategy must match the data-generating process.


Random: not always appropriate
Stratified: preserve class distribution across splits
Grouped: keep related images (same event, patient, location) in the same split

title: 2 - Images as Data
text:
Data Leakage
The model sees information during training that it will not have at deployment.


Figure 13: Same images and model, different splits: the score drops as the split gets stricter.

Causes: near-duplicates, same site in train and test, statistics computed on all data.

title: 2 - Images as Data
text:
Quiz: Skin Cancer Detection Dataset
500 patients, multiple visits each. Images randomly shuffled and split 80/10/10.
What goes wrong?

The same patient can appear in both train and test. The model may learn patient-specific cues instead of lesion-specific cues.


Fix: split at the patient level.

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Sequential Generation


Predict one element at a time, conditioned on all previous elements (Torralba et al. (2024)).

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Factorization

\[p(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = p(x_1)\, p(x_2|x_1)\, p(x_3|x_1, x_2) \cdots p(x_n|x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1})\]


Each conditional \(p(x_i \mid x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1})\) is modeled by a neural network (masked CNN or Transformer).



Image generation becomes a sequence prediction problem.

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Sampling Step by Step

Sample \(x_1 \sim p(x_1)\)
Sample \(x_2 \sim p(x_2 \mid x_1)\)
Sample \(x_3 \sim p(x_3 \mid x_1, x_2)\)
… continue until all pixels are generated

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Pros & Cons

Pros

Exact likelihood computation
Natural fit for language / discrete tokens



Cons

Sequential generation is slow
Pixel-level image generation is expensive
Errors can accumulate during sampling

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
The Adversarial Game


Generator \(g(\mathbf{z})\) fakes — Discriminator \(d(\mathbf{x})\) judges (Goodfellow et al. (2014)).

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Minimax Objective

\[\min_{g} \max_{d} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\text{data}}}[\log d(\mathbf{x})] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_z}[\log(1 - d(g(\mathbf{z})))]\]


\(d\): maximize correct real/fake classification
\(g\): minimize \(d\)’s success — fool the discriminator
Training alternates between the two

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
GAN Learning Process


Generator distribution tries to fool discriminator, while discriminator must distinguish real from fake (Foster (2023)).

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Pros & Cons

Pros

Fast sampling, one forward pass
Can produce sharp images
Historically pivotal for image generation



Cons

Training can be unstable
Mode collapse, limited variety
No direct likelihood
Modern text-to-image systems are rarely pure GANs

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
VAE Architecture


Encoder \(q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{x})\) — Decoder \(p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{z})\)

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Probabilistic Twist

Unlike standard autoencoders, the latent space is structured probabilistically, so random samples decode to meaningful outputs.

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Reparameterization Trick


\[\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{\mu} + \mathbf{\epsilon} \cdot \mathbf{\sigma}, \qquad \mathbf{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\]


Lets gradients flow through stochastic sampling.

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
ELBO Objective

\[\text{ELBO} = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})}[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{z})]}_{\text{Reconstruction}} - \underbrace{\text{KL}(q_{\psi}(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x}) \,\|\, p(\mathbf{z}))}_{\text{Regularization}}\]


Reconstruction — decoder must recover the input
KL regularization — pull posterior toward prior \(p(\mathbf{z}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\)
Result: a smooth, continuous latent space

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
VAE Latent Space


Traversing the latent space → smooth interpolation between faces (Prince (2023)).

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Pros & Cons

Pros

Principled probabilistic foundation
Structured, interpretable latent space (interpolation, factor analysis)
Stable training
Useful for representation learning



Cons

Tend to produce blurry outputs (improvable with more complex variants)

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Forward Diffusion


Gradually add Gaussian noise over \(T\) steps (Torralba et al. (2024)). Fixed, no neural network.

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Forward Process

\[\mathbf{x}_t = \sqrt{1 - \beta_t}\, \mathbf{x}_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t}\, \mathbf{\epsilon}_t, \qquad \mathbf{\epsilon}_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\]


\(\beta_t\) — noise schedule (linear, cosine, …)
\(\mathbf{x}_0\) (clean) → \(\mathbf{x}_T \approx \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\)
Can sample \(\mathbf{x}_t\) directly from \(\mathbf{x}_0\) → efficient training over many noise levels

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Reverse Diffusion


A neural network learns to gradually remove noise, step by step (Torralba et al. (2024)).

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Reverse Process

Start from pure noise: \[\mathbf{x}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\]


Iteratively denoise to a realistic sample \(\mathbf{x}_0\).


The network is conditioned on the timestep \(t\) — noise level varies dramatically across steps.

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Training Objective

\[\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{t, \mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{\epsilon}}\left[\,\|\, \mathbf{\epsilon} - f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)\,\|^2\,\right]\]


The model predicts the noise \(\mathbf{\epsilon}\) that was added to \(\mathbf{x}_0\) to produce \(\mathbf{x}_t\).

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Training & Sampling


Training: random \(t\), random \(\mathbf{\epsilon}\). Sampling: iterate from \(T\) down to \(0\).

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
U-Net Denoiser


Encoder–decoder with skip connections; timestep \(t\) embedded throughout (Prince (2023)).

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Pros & Cons

Pros

High-quality, diverse outputs (currently SOTA)
Stable, reliable training



Cons

Slow inference — iterative sampling
High compute cost (training and inference)

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Aside: Cold Diffusion


Gaussian noise isn’t fundamental — any invertible degradation works (blur, masking, pixelation) (Bansal et al. (2022)).


Success comes from the gradual, multi-step inversion, not the noise itself.

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
From Noise to Data, Continuously

Noise turns into an image as a continuous process over time \(t \in [0, 1]\) (frames interpolated from a photo, not model outputs).
A network \(v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)\) predicts a velocity: where should \(\mathbf{x}_t\) move? \(\quad \frac{d\mathbf{x}_t}{dt} = v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)\)


Note: here \(t = 0\) is noise and \(t = 1\) is data (opposite to diffusion).

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Training: Straight Lines

Pair a training image \(\mathbf{x}_1\) with noise \(\mathbf{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\), connect them with a line:
\[\mathbf{x}_t = (1 - t)\, \mathbf{\epsilon} + t\, \mathbf{x}_1\]


Predict the constant velocity along the line (Lipman et al. 2023; Liu et al. 2022):
\[\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{t, \mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{\epsilon}}\left[\, \| (\mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{\epsilon}) - v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t) \|^2 \,\right]\]


Like diffusion: mix image and noise, simple regression loss. But the target is the direction from noise to data.

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Flow Matching in 1D


Training lines cross; the network learns their average direction. The learned trajectories never cross.

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Sampling

Start from noise \(\mathbf{x}_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\) and follow the velocity (Euler steps):
\[\mathbf{x}_{t + \Delta t} = \mathbf{x}_t + \Delta t \, v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)\]


No fresh noise is injected: given the initial noise, sampling is deterministic.

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
In Practice

Stable Diffusion 3 (Esser et al. 2024): transformer trained with a flow matching objective in latent space
FLUX.1 Kontext (Labs et al. 2025): flow matching for generation and instruction-based editing

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
Pros & Cons

Pros

High-quality, diverse outputs
Simple, stable training (regression loss, no simulation)
Deterministic sampling, often with fewer steps than diffusion



Cons

Sampling still needs multiple network evaluations
High compute cost (training and inference)
Likelihood possible, but expensive

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
From \(p(\mathbf{x})\) to \(p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{c})\)

So far: model \(p(\mathbf{x})\) unconditionally.


In practice: model \[p_\theta(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{c})\]


\(\mathbf{c}\) — class label, text prompt, source image, mask, layout, depth, reference…

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
section: Conditioning Is Not a Separate Family
text:
Conditioning Is Not a Separate Family



Family
How conditioning enters




Autoregressive
condition each prediction step on \(\mathbf{c}\)


VAEs
condition encoder and/or decoder on \(\mathbf{c}\)


GANs
condition generator (and often discriminator) on \(\mathbf{c}\)


Diffusion
condition the denoising network on \(\mathbf{c}\)


Flow matching
condition the velocity network on \(\mathbf{c}\)




Modern text-to-image and image-editing systems use these mechanisms extensively.

title: 6 - Adapting Models
text:
The Question

You have a pretrained encoder.


You have a task with limited labeled data.


How much of the model should you train?

title: 6 - Adapting Models
text:
What Decides?

Representation: what does the pretrained encoder already contain?
Task: what does the downstream task require (vector, spatial features, similarity)?
Data: what can the target data support (labels, domain shift)?


A larger training set helps, but it is not the only deciding factor.

At a Glance








Strategy
What is learned?
Key property




k-NN
Nothing; uses labeled reference images
Fast test of feature quality


Linear probe
A small prediction head
Frozen encoder; features can be cached


Partial fine-tuning
Selected encoder layers + head
Encoder becomes task-specific


Full fine-tuning
Entire encoder + head
Maximum flexibility; higher training cost


LoRA
Low-rank updates to selected weights + head
Few trainable parameters, but backprop still passes through the encoder

title: 6 - Adapting Models
text:
k-NN — No Gradient-Based Training

Embed labeled reference images with a frozen encoder
For a new image, retrieve the \(k\) closest reference embeddings
Predict from their labels (majority or similarity-weighted vote)
Hyperparameters: \(k\), distance metric, weighting rule


What it tells you: whether the pretrained representation already separates your target data.

title: 6 - Adapting Models
section: Linear Probe — Freeze Encoder, Train Head
text:
Linear Probe — Freeze Encoder, Train Head

Keep the pretrained encoder frozen
Train only a linear classifier on the embeddings: \(\text{Linear}(d, K)\)
Embeddings can be cached: the encoder does not run every epoch


Good performance: the labels are linearly accessible from the representation.


A poor result does not prove the features are useless: the information may be nonlinear, or the feature extraction unsuitable.

title: 6 - Adapting Models
text:
Partial Fine-Tuning

Freeze most of the backbone
Unfreeze selected blocks (e.g. the last two) and the task head
The representation can change, with fewer trainable parameters


Which layers to tune depends on architecture, pretraining objective and task: an experimental choice.

title: 6 - Adapting Models
text:
Full Fine-Tuning

Update the encoder and the new head jointly
Most flexible strategy
More training memory, higher risk of overfitting or losing pretrained behavior
Use a smaller learning rate for the encoder than for the head


Not inherently a last resort: fine-tuning a small model can work with modest data. Measure on held-out data.

title: 6 - Adapting Models
text:
LoRA — Low-Rank Updates
\[
W' = W + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA, \qquad
B \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\quad
A \in \mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}}
\]

\(W\) stays frozen; only \(A\), \(B\) and the head are trained
\(r(d_{in}+d_{out})\) instead of \(d_{out}d_{in}\) parameters; rank \(r\) controls capacity
Unlike adapters, LoRA inserts no new layer: it changes existing weights
Backprop still passes through the whole encoder

title: 6 - Adapting Models
text:
What Limits Your Baseline?







Question
What to try or check




Are the features already useful?
Compare k-NN and linear probe


Is the encoder right for this domain?
Compare general, vision-language and domain-specific encoders


Does the task need spatial predictions?
Patch / feature-map outputs and a decoder or detection head


Does the probe underfit?
More capable head, partial FT, LoRA or full FT


Is the model overfitting?
Validation design, regularization, augmentation, less capacity


Is training expensive?
Cache frozen features, smaller backbone, parameter-efficient methods


Is inference expensive?
Backbone, input size, precision; freezing alone does not help




Establish a reliable baseline, then investigate what limits it.

title: 6 - Adapting Models
text:
Three Questions Before Fine-Tuning

Are the pretrained features already useful for the target task?
Does the task require an image-level vector, spatial features, or a similarity embedding?
Does updating the encoder improve held-out performance enough to justify the cost?


There is no universal dataset-size threshold that determines the best strategy.

title: 6 - Adapting Models
text:
Scenario 1: Camera-Trap Species
Scenario

500 labeled camera-trap images
Task: species classification


Recommended start: global embeddings + k-NN or linear probe, with a split that separates cameras or sites.


Compare fine-tuning if the baseline is insufficient. In the lecture’s experiment on unseen sites, frozen features reach 0.57 macro-F1, adapted backbones 0.85–0.87.

title: 6 - Adapting Models
text:
Scenario 2: Medical Domain Shift
Scenario

800 labeled chest X-rays
Two encoders: a general-purpose DINO model and a medical-image model


Recommended start: linear probe (optionally k-NN) on both encoders, with a patient-level split.


Evaluate AUROC and sensitivity. If both frozen baselines are inadequate, compare fine-tuning starting from the better encoder.


The number of images alone does not decide the method.

title: 6 - Adapting Models
text:
Scenario 3: Land-Cover Segmentation
Scenario

Satellite images with pixel-level annotations
Strong domain shift from ground-level photos


Recommended start: spatial features + a trainable segmentation decoder on a frozen encoder.


Then evaluate encoder fine-tuning. A global embedding loses the spatial detail this task needs.

title: 4 - Image Classification

Classification Variants


Figure 2: Different variants of classification.

title: 4 - Image Classification
text:
From Image to Logits
A classifier maps an input image to one score per class:
\[
\mathbf{z} = f_\theta(\mathbf{x})
\]


\(\mathbf{x}\): input image tensor
\(f_\theta\): neural network with learnable parameters
\(\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^K\): logits, one score for each class



Logits are not probabilities, they can be negative, positive, small, or large.

title: 4 - Image Classification
text:
Softmax Classifier
Softmax converts logits into class probabilities:
\[
P(Y = k \mid X = \mathbf{x}^{(i)}) = \sigma(\mathbf{z})_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j}}
\]


\(\mathbf{z}\) logits: unbounded class scores
\(\sigma(\mathbf{z})\) probabilities: positive and sum to 1
Larger logits receive larger probabilities

title: 4 - Image Classification
text:
Logits → Probabilities








Figure 3: Logits are arbitrary real-valued scores. Softmax converts them into probabilities.






Logits can be any real number — softmax always produces a valid probability distribution.

title: 4 - Image Classification
text:
Demo: Softmax




Raise one logit by 1, then by 5: how do the probabilities change? Open in new tab

title: 4 - Image Classification
text:
Cross-Entropy: The Idea
A good classifier assigns high probability to the correct class.

For an image whose true class is deer:


\(P(\text{deer}) = 0.95\) → small loss
\(P(\text{deer}) = 0.40\) → moderate loss
\(P(\text{deer}) = 0.02\) → very large loss


Cross-entropy only cares about the probability assigned to the true class.

title: 4 - Image Classification
text:
Cross-Entropy Formula
For one sample with one-hot label \(\mathbf{y}\) and predicted probabilities \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\):
\[
CE(\mathbf{y}, \hat{\mathbf{y}})
= -\sum_{j=1}^K y_j \log \hat{y}_j
\]

Because \(\mathbf{y}\) is one-hot, only the true class \(c\) contributes:

\[
CE = -\log \hat{y}_c
\]

So training minimizes the negative log-probability of the correct class.

title: 4 - Image Classification
text:
Quiz: Which Loss is Higher?
A model predicts:

\(P(\text{deer}) = 0.4\) for an image that is a deer
\(P(\text{deer}) = 0.6\) for an image that is a fox

Which prediction gives the higher cross-entropy?

The first prediction.
For the deer image:
\[
CE = -\log(0.4) \approx 0.92
\]


For the fox image, \(P(\text{deer})\) is irrelevant. Cross-entropy depends only on the probability assigned to the true class, here \(P(\text{fox})\).

title: 4 - Image Classification
text:
The Classification Pipeline
A classification model usually has two parts:

Backbone: extracts visual features from the image
Classification head: maps features to \(K\) logits


Conceptually:
\[
\text{image} \rightarrow \text{features} \rightarrow \text{logits} \rightarrow \text{probabilities}
\]


Training uses logits + labels to compute cross-entropy loss.

title: 4 - Image Classification
text:
Architecture Progression

AlexNet (2012): 8 layers, made deep CNNs dominant on ImageNet
VGG (2014): 16–19 layers, simple repeated \(3 \times 3\) convolution blocks
ResNet (2015): 50–152+ layers, residual connections enabled much deeper networks
ConvNeXt (2022): modernized CNN design, competitive with Vision Transformers


The common pattern: better feature extractors → better classification backbones.

title: 4 - Image Classification
text:
AlexNet (2012)


Figure 4: 5 conv + 3 FC layers, 1000-way softmax. Trained on two GTX 580 GPUs (3 GB each). Source: Prince (2023)

The network had to be split across GPUs due to memory limits.

title: 4 - Image Classification
text:
Which Architecture?

Don’t be a hero.


Start with a proven pretrained backbone:


ResNet-50 / ResNet-101: reliable baseline
EfficientNet: good when size or speed matters
ConvNeXt: strong modern CNN backbone
Vision Transformer / Swin / DINO-style features: strong when data and compute allow


Choose based on accuracy, speed, memory, available data, and deployment constraints.

title: 4 - Image Classification
text:
Why Augment?
A classifier should give the same label under nuisance transformations: position, size, orientation, lighting, occlusion.

Convolutions are only translation equivariant. Robustness to rotation, zoom or brightness must be learned from data.

title: 4 - Image Classification
text:
Data Augmentation

One training image, many augmented variants.
Random, label-preserving transformations, applied on the fly during training.

title: 4 - Image Classification
text:
Augmentation Families

Geometric: random crops and rescaling, horizontal flips, small rotations
Photometric: brightness, contrast, saturation, grayscale
Occlusion and mixing: Cutout, Mixup, CutMix


An augmentation must not change the label: a flip is harmless for animals, but not for text or a sign pointing left.

title: 4 - Image Classification
text:
Demo: Augmentation Stability




Rotate, crop or darken the image: when does the prediction of the pretrained CNN change? Open in new tab

title: 4 - Image Classification
text:
Quiz: Camera-Trap Augmentations
Classes: empty, deer, fox, badger, bird. Which augmentations would you use, which avoid?

Useful: horizontal flips, moderate crops, brightness/contrast, grayscale (night IR images)


Avoid: vertical flips and large rotations: camera traps are mounted upright


Careful: aggressive crops can cut the animal out, an “empty” image labelled “deer”

title: 4 - Image Classification
text:
Key Takeaways

Image classification maps an image to class logits.
Softmax converts logits into class probabilities.
Cross-entropy penalizes low probability assigned to the true class.
Most classifiers use a backbone plus a small classification head.
Architecture evolution: AlexNet → VGG → ResNet → ConvNeXt / ViT.
Start with a proven pretrained backbone; only customize when needed.
Data augmentation teaches invariances the architecture does not provide; it must preserve the label.

title: Project Ideas
text:
2 Classification Projects

2.1 Image Classification: EuroSAT Land Use and Land Cover Classification
Goal: Develop a model to classify satellite images. You should consider RGB images and images with 13 spectral bands (see wiki) in modeling. There are 10 classes and 27,000 images.
Approach: Investigate various model architectures and decide what works best. Compare pre-trained models with those you train from scratch. Use appropriate data augmentation techniques. Since the dataset is relatively small, you should be careful of overfitting and robustly compare different models. Use RGB-only models for simplicity.
Focus: Compare different pre-trained models (foundation models) and a model trained from scratch.
Dataset: The two datasets can be found here: https://github.com/phelber/eurosat. There is a dataset in RGB format and a dataset with 13 spectral bands.






Figure 1: Source: Link



Difficulty/Effort: Medium


2.2 Image Classification: Food Images
Goal: Develop a model to classify images of food. Pick 10 food classes (≈10k imgs)
Approach: Use pre-trained (foundation) models.
Focus: Compare different models, including CLIP zero-shot learning, and a DINO variant. Investigate how DINO improves with more labels.
Dataset: The dataset can be found here: https://data.vision.ee.ethz.ch/cvl/datasets_extra/food-101/, see Bossard et al. (2014). It is 5 GB.






Figure 2: Source: Link



Difficulty/Effort: Medium


2.3 Age Estimation from Faces
Goal: Predict apparent age from images of faces.
Approach: Train a CNN as a 101-class classifier (ages 0 to 100) and convert class probabilities to a numeric prediction via the softmax expected value (see paper, Rothe et al. (2015)). Compare against direct regression (single output).
Focus: Compare at least two variants: a CNN defined and trained from scratch and a pre-trained model with fine-tuning / as feature-extractor. Analyse the errors.
Dataset: The dataset can be found here Link. Use a small dataset with cropped faces, e.g. Link.






Figure 3: Source: Link



Difficulty/Effort: Medium - High


2.4 Wildlife Camera Trap Classification
Goal: Build a classifier for camera-trap images of wildlife. Choose either CCT20 (8 classes, 1,600 images in the course subset) or Snapshot Serengeti (48 species, ~2.6M images — use a curated subset).
Approach: Start with a pretrained backbone as a feature extractor. Address class imbalance using weighted loss or oversampling strategies. Compare at least two pretrained model families and evaluate the effect of fine-tuning vs. feature extraction.
Focus: Effect of class imbalance on standard metrics — accuracy can be misleading when one class dominates. Report F1 per class and analyse the confusion matrix: which species are most often confused, and why?
Dataset: CCT20 course subset (8 classes, 1,600 images); the full Caltech Camera Traps dataset is available at LILA BC. Snapshot Serengeti (48 classes, ~2.6M images) is available at LILA BC — the full dataset is large; selecting a balanced subset of 10–15 species is recommended. Additional camera trap datasets can be found at LILA BC.






Figure 4: Bobcat from the Caltech Camera Traps dataset. Source: LILA BC



Difficulty/Effort: Medium


2.5 Industrial Surface Defect Detection
Goal: Train a binary classifier to distinguish intact from cracked concrete surfaces, and reason carefully about the precision–recall trade-off in a safety-critical setting.
Approach: Use the Concrete Cracks dataset (~40k images). Fine-tune a pretrained model and evaluate performance across different decision thresholds. In safety-critical applications, false negatives (missed cracks) carry higher cost than false positives — make this trade-off explicit in your analysis.
Focus: Threshold selection and the precision–recall curve. Qualitative failure analysis: what does the model get wrong, and does it fail systematically?
Dataset: Concrete Cracks dataset (Mendeley Data, CC BY 4.0), see Özgenel (2019).






Figure 5: Source: Mendeley / Özgenel et al.



Difficulty/Effort: Medium


2.6 Product Image Retrieval
Goal: Build an image retrieval system that, given a query product image, returns the top-k most visually similar items from a gallery using learned embeddings.
Approach: Extract embeddings from a pretrained CNN or ViT backbone. Build a nearest-neighbour index with cosine similarity. Evaluate with precision@k and recall@k. Compare at least two backbone architectures to assess how embedding quality affects retrieval.
Focus: How does the choice of backbone — and whether it is fine-tuned or used frozen — affect retrieval quality? Qualitative inspection of failure cases is particularly informative here.
Dataset: Amazon Berkeley Objects (ABO) Furniture (~25k images, 6 categories) or DeepFashion In-Shop Retrieval (~3,300 images, 5 classes). The multi-view structure of ABO makes retrieval evaluation especially natural; DeepFashion provides item-level train/test splits.






Figure 6: Source: Amazon Berkeley Objects



Difficulty/Effort: Medium


2.7 Histopathology Fine-Tuning with LoRA
Goal: Apply parameter-efficient fine-tuning to adapt a pretrained Vision Transformer to a medical imaging task — specifically, classifying normal vs. atypical mitotic figures in histopathology patches.
Approach: Use a HuggingFace ViT backbone and apply LoRA adapters (rank 4–16). Compare three settings: frozen backbone (feature extractor), LoRA fine-tuning, and full fine-tuning. Discuss the domain shift from natural images (ImageNet pretraining) to H&E-stained histopathology patches.
Focus: Parameter count vs. performance trade-off; convergence speed across settings; domain shift as a factor in choosing fine-tuning strategy. Because the dataset is small, report results across multiple random seeds.
Dataset: AMI-Br (128×128 histopathology patches, binary labels). The dataset is intentionally small — robustness to seed variation is part of the analysis.






Figure 7: Source: AMI-Br / TUPAC16 + MIDOG21



Difficulty/Effort: High

title: Project Ideas
text:
3 Research Projects
These projects test a recent claim from the literature rather than solve an application problem. The outcome is open: a carefully executed negative result is as valuable as a positive one.

3.1 Does MatryoshkaLoRA Transfer to Vision Transformers?
Goal: MatryoshkaLoRA (arXiv:2605.07850) is a recent variant of LoRA that learns a nested hierarchy of low-rank adapters: after training, the adapter can be truncated to any rank \(k \leq R\) without retraining. On LLM benchmarks (Llama 3, GSM-8K, ARC-C, HellaSwag) the authors report not only good accuracy at truncated ranks, but also gains of 1–4 percentage points over standard LoRA at full rank. The method has not been evaluated on vision models. Your task is to find out whether these claims hold when fine-tuning a vision transformer for image classification.
Background: Standard LoRA computes \(\mathbf{W}_0 + \mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\) with a fixed rank \(R\). MatryoshkaLoRA inserts a fixed diagonal scaling between the adapters, \(\mathbf{W}_0 + \mathbf{A}\,\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{p})\,\mathbf{B}\), where \(\mathbf{p}\) up-weights the leading rank components (e.g. \(\mathbf{p} = [4,3,2,2,1,1,1,1]\) for \(R=8\) and nested ranks \(\{1,2,4,8\}\)). This way every sub-rank receives a training signal in each step. At inference, \(\mathbf{p}\) is dropped and the first \(k\) components are used. Official code: IST-DASLab/MatryoshkaLoRA.
Approach: Use a DINOv3 backbone (ViT-S/16 or ViT-B/16, available on HuggingFace after accepting the license) with a linear classification head. Establish a frozen-backbone (linear probe) baseline first. Then compare standard LoRA and MatryoshkaLoRA (and optionally DyLoRA) at a maximum rank of e.g. \(R=32\). Evaluate MatryoshkaLoRA truncated to ranks \(\{1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32\}\) and compare against standard LoRA models trained separately at a subset of these ranks.
Focus:

Fair comparison: the scaling vector \(\mathbf{p}\) changes the effective learning rate. Tune the learning rate separately for each method (a small grid suffices), otherwise you may measure a learning-rate effect rather than a method effect.
Headroom: if the linear probe is already close to the ceiling, there is nothing to gain from fine-tuning. Choose a dataset with domain shift (e.g. AMI-Br) or reduce the training set (e.g. 10–50 images per class) to create headroom.
Statistical robustness: the reported gains are small. Use at least 3 seeds and report mean ± standard deviation.
Rank–accuracy curve: plot accuracy over rank for both methods. Does a single MatryoshkaLoRA run match separately trained LoRA models at each rank?

Dataset: At least two datasets from the table above. AMI-Br (domain shift, small) combined with a natural-image dataset (Food-101 subset, Snapshot Serengeti subset, or CCT20) is a good pairing.






TipAI Assistants



AI coding assistants may be used for the implementation — this keeps the project manageable and shifts the focus to experimental design and analysis. You must, however, be able to explain how the scaling vector \(\mathbf{p}\) is constructed and why it produces a nested rank hierarchy. Keep the experimental grid small and fixed in advance (ranks × methods × seeds × learning rates) to avoid an explosion of runs.


Difficulty/Effort: High

title: AI Coding Agents
text:
TipTLDR Recap





Central message

AI can greatly increase what you can accomplish — but accomplishing more does not automatically mean learning more.
What matters is which cognitive activities are delegated and which remain with you.

AI for Learning

Whether effort is “productive” depends on the learning objective, not on the task itself
Three roles: AI as tutor (you reason, AI asks and hints), AI as collaborator (you decide, AI proposes), AI as agent (AI executes, you specify and verify)
Risks: cognitive offloading, “cognitive surrender”, illusion of learning, fewer discussions with peers and instructors
Self-check after AI-assisted work: Explain → Predict → Modify → Diagnose

AI for Applied Projects

Benefits: speed, prototyping, exploring libraries, investigating data, review
Risks: plausible-but-wrong results, self-confirming tests, silent changes to experimental conditions, supply chain, prompt injection
Productivity evidence is mixed and setting-dependent

Deep learning code fails silently — in three ways

Code runs but implements the wrong operation
Code is correct but the experiment measures the wrong quantity
The experiment is correct but the conclusion is not justified

Verification

Four levels: implementation → experimental → scientific → operational
Expected behavior must be derived independently of the implementation
Define acceptance criteria before the agent writes code; track provenance

Takeaways

Use AI deliberately · Stay cognitively engaged · Take responsibility for results

title: AI Coding Agents
text:
1 Motivation
AI coding assistants have evolved rapidly: from autocompleting a single line, to generating whole functions from a comment, to agents that work autonomously on an entire codebase. An agent might receive a complex task in natural language (“fine-tune a DINOv3 model on my camera trap images”), inspects the repository and the data, writes code, runs it, reads error messages and outputs, and iterates.
Using AI tools in education obviously has benefits and risks. AI tools can help learn faster, explore more, and build far more ambitious projects than would otherwise be possible given the available time. At the same time, an agent can produce a complete, working project without any understanding. Accomplishing more does not automatically mean learning more. Effective use depends on which cognitive activities you delegate and which you keep.
In practice AI tools also change where expertise is needed. Writing a data loader from scratch becomes less important; problem formulation, experimental design, evaluation, and critical interpretation however remain cruicial. Implementation skills do not become obsolete: understanding software and model internals is essential to diagnose subtle failures. As discussed in the Training Guide, training neural networks fails silently — and recognizing such failures requires exactly the knowledge this course aims to teach.
This page first focuses on how to use AI for learning, then on how to use coding agents in applied projects, and finally on how to verify results — your own and the agent’s.

title: AI Coding Agents
section: 2 What is an AI Coding Agent?
text:
2 What is an AI Coding Agent?
A coding agent combines a large language model (LLM) with tools and a loop. In contrast to a chat interface that only returns text, an agent can act on its environment:

Read: inspect files, search the codebase, read documentation and dataset metadata
Write: create and edit files
Execute: run scripts, tests, experiments, shell commands, install packages
Iterate: observe outputs (a stack trace, a metric, a plot) and decide on the next step

An agent can support three different activities:

Code generation: producing code that implements a requested operation (“write a function computing IoU”).
Agentic software engineering: navigating a repository, making changes, running checks, and iterating toward a goal (“add mixed-precision training and make sure all tests pass”).
Agent-assisted scientific work: helping to formulate hypotheses, design experiments, identify methodological risks, and interpret results (“investigate whether the dataset contains correlated observations and recommend a split”).

The same tool can also act as a tutor that explains, asks questions, and gives hints. This leads to the central question: what role should AI play when the goal is learning?

title: AI Coding Agents
text:
3 AI for Learning

3.1 Learning vs. Productivity
Consider two ways of spending 40 minutes:

Debugging a tensor shape mismatch in a PyTorch training loop.
Investigating why a model trained on camera trap images fails at a new camera location.

It is tempting to call the first a waste of time and the second a “productive” effort. But debugging a shape mismatch can be a good learning experience: it reveals how convolutional layers transform spatial dimensions, how batches are represented, or how broadcasting works. Personally, I used to write comments in the code to document input and output shapes which helped me understand and debug the flow of data through a neural network.
Whether effort is productive is not a property of the task, but of the learning objective:








Task
If the learning goal is…
Appropriate AI assistance




Fix a tensor shape mismatch
Understand tensor shapes
Hints and diagnostic questions


Fix a tensor shape mismatch
Compare model architectures
Let AI fix it, then inspect the change


Implement a CNN
Learn CNN mechanics
Attempt the implementation yourself


Implement a CNN
Explore generalization
Delegate routine implementation


Evaluate a classifier
Understand evaluation metrics
Compute examples by hand


Evaluate a classifier
Compare pretrained backbones
Delegate metric computation, validate the protocol yourself



A consequence that is particularly relevant in continuing education: participants with different backgrounds may appropriately use different levels of assistance on the same exercise. A software engineer may delegate the training loop and focus on evaluation design; someone new to Python may learn most by writing the training loop with AI as a tutor.


3.2 What Do We Know?
Empirical evidence on AI and learning is still limited and mixed. In a randomized controlled trial with 120 university students at a single institution, those who used ChatGPT as a study aid scored lower on a surprise retention test 45 days later (57.5% vs. 68.5% correct) than those who used traditional study methods (Barcaui 2025). In contrast, a study with novice programmers found that access to an AI code generator improved code-authoring performance without a significant penalty on later post-tests (Kazemitabaar et al. 2023). Neither study evaluates autonomous coding agents, and both populations differ from this course — the results should not be generalized lightly.
Beyond experimental findings, educational institutions are formulating pedagogical recommendations. The MIT Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training (2026) proposes the principle of augmentation, not automation: AI should enhance curiosity, creativity, and learning rather than automate them. The report names several concerns:

Illusion of learning: obtaining a correct answer from a chatbot feels like having learned.
Cognitive surrender: falling back on AI at the first hint of struggle.
Displaced social learning: AI interaction replacing study groups, peer discussions, and contact with instructors.

These are best read as a framework for designing good learning practices — not as proof that AI inevitably reduces learning. At the same time, the report notes that “the potential of these technologies to augment work across campus is immense”.
Universities worldwide face this tension (The New York Times, 2026): AI proficiency is increasingly seen as a professional necessity, yet education aims to develop exactly the reasoning that can be delegated. The same reporting cites a study of 26,000 secondary-school students in which AI adoption raised homework scores by 18% but lowered scores on secure exams by 20% — performing well with AI is not the same as having learned. Ohio State’s president frames the central question as “What is OK to offload to A.I., and what is not? The answer to that depends on the field and depends on your stage of learning.” The University of Sydney’s “two-lane approach” responds by combining both: some assessments under secure conditions without AI, others that require AI use.
My recommendation is to strike a balance: learn both to solve selected problems on your own and to solve more ambitious problems effectively with AI.


3.3 Choosing the Level of AI Assistance
AI can take on different roles, which differ both in autonomy and in pedagogical purpose:






Level 1 — AI as Tutor
You do the reasoning and the implementation. The AI asks questions, explains, and gives incremental hints.
Best for: unfamiliar concepts and fundamental techniques.









Level 2 — AI as Collaborator
You and the AI develop the solution together. You make the technical decisions, review alternatives, and validate results.
Best for: applying concepts and developing practical competence.









Level 3 — AI as Agent
The AI executes multi-step tasks with substantial autonomy. You specify the objective and verify the important outcomes.
Best for: implementation-heavy work where the underlying concepts are already understood.



These are not stages that everybody must progress through. In the same project, you may use an autonomous agent for the data loading infrastructure while using AI as a tutor to understand contrastive learning.
Figure 1 illustrates that the amount of AI assistance and the amount of your own cognitive engagement are two separate dimensions. More assistance does not have to mean less thinking — if you stay actively involved in reasoning, predicting, and evaluating.






Figure 1: AI assistance and cognitive engagement are not necessarily inversely related. Conceptual model, not empirical measurements. Own illustration; the terms augmentation and automation follow the MIT report.





3.4 Effective Learning Workflows
How AI is prompted largely determines in which quadrant of Figure 1 one ends up. The following prompts illustrate interactions that keep the reasoning with you.
Socratic tutoring — when struggling with an unfamiliar concept:
Help me understand why self-attention uses separate query and key vectors.
Ask me questions, give hints progressively, and correct my misconceptions.
Do not immediately provide the full explanation.
Guided debugging — when the debugging process is part of the learning objective:
My CNN produces an unexpected tensor shape. Do not change the code yet.
Help me trace the dimensions layer by layer, ask me to predict the output
shape of each layer, and point out where my predictions are inconsistent.
Critical collaboration — for experiments and project work:
Review my experimental design for comparing two pretrained vision models.
Challenge my assumptions about splits, preprocessing, metrics, and confounders.
Prioritize threats to validity and suggest tests that could reveal them.
Do not modify the implementation.
In contrast, prompts such as “fix this error”, “write the training script for my project”, or “explain what this code does” are not wrong — but when the objective is learning, they delegate exactly the part that builds understanding.
A ready-to-use system prompt implementing the three levels for ChatGPT/Claude projects and coding agents is available on the AI Tutor Prompt page.


3.5 Illusion of Competence and Self-Assessment
The main risks for learners are:

Cognitive offloading of productive effort: delegating exactly the struggle that builds understanding.
Illusion of competence: a working notebook, or a fluent AI explanation one can repeat, feels like understanding.
Missing judgment: detecting the subtle errors further below requires the knowledge the course aims to build.

It helps to distinguish three kinds of understanding, which overlap but are not interchangeable: understanding a concept, being able to apply it independently, and being able to critically evaluate an AI-generated solution. A simple routine after AI-assisted work tests all three:

Explain: describe the key concepts and implementation decisions without consulting AI.
Predict: what happens if a parameter, the architecture, or a preprocessing step changes?
Modify: make one meaningful change independently.
Diagnose: when a failure or unexpected result occurs, explain its cause before asking for a fix.

This is a suggested learning strategy, not a formal assessment instrument. Being able to modify and troubleshoot a system is particularly telling: reproducing an AI explanation is possible without the understanding needed to apply it.
In particular, be able to explain the design decisions of your work — what was split how and why, which preprocessing the backbone requires, which metric answers which question — and defend them with evidence. Do not delegate this reasoning to the agent: having the agent explain its choices is cognitive offloading of exactly the understanding the project should demonstrate.
Finally, learning is also social. AI is an additional resource, not a replacement for discussing with peers, asking instructors, or explaining a concept to someone else. For example, formulate and compare your hypotheses about an experiment in a group first, then ask an agent to challenge them.






NoteExercise: Can You Explain What Your Agent Built?





Duration: 10–15 minutes. Goal: experience the difference between completing a task and understanding it.

Ask an AI agent to implement a simple image classifier with a training and evaluation pipeline.
Before running it: identify the key design decisions and predict the expected behavior (e.g. approximate accuracy, training time, which classes will be confused).
Inspect the implementation. Explain the training objective, the data flow, and the evaluation procedure.
Without AI assistance, modify one important aspect (e.g. the split, the augmentation, or the metric) and predict its effect before running it.
Ask the AI to critique the original solution and compare its findings with your own.

Discussion: Did the agent help you understand the system, or primarily help you obtain a working implementation? What would you do differently next time?

title: AI Coding Agents
text:
4 AI for Applied Projects
In industry and research — and in your course project — coding agents are increasingly part of the daily workflow. The question is how to organize work so that agents can be highly productive while their results remain verifiable.

4.1 Benefits

Speed for routine work: data loaders, configs, logging, plotting, and other boilerplate.
Rapid prototyping and experimentation: baselines, ablations, and backbone comparisons in a fraction of the time — supporting the “build a baseline pipeline” step of the training recipe.
Navigating unfamiliar code and libraries: large APIs (timm, transformers, torchvision.transforms.v2), reference implementations of papers.
Investigating data: summarizing metadata, finding duplicates, plotting class distributions, inspecting misclassified samples.
Review and critique: an agent instructed to challenge a pipeline can find leakage, metric bugs, or unjustified conclusions.
Tackling previously infeasible tasks: work that would not have been attempted at all due to time constraints.



4.2 Risks

Plausible but wrong results: code runs and produces numbers, but contains methodological errors (see examples).
Optimizing for the wrong goal: asked to make a failing script or test pass, an agent may weaken checks, catch and ignore exceptions, or modify the evaluation instead of fixing the underlying problem.
Self-confirming verification: generating tests is easy; generating meaningful, independent tests is much harder (see Independent Verification).
Silent changes to experimental conditions: updating a dependency, changing a seed, modifying a dataset filter, or switching a checkpoint — each reasonable on its own, yet invalidating a comparison between experiments.
Outdated or hallucinated APIs: deprecated arguments (pretrained=True instead of weights=...), non-existent model identifiers, and — worst — a silent fallback to random initialization when the pretrained weights cannot be loaded.
Supply chain: hallucinated package names can be registered by attackers (“slopsquatting”, see Spracklen et al. (2025)).
Prompt injection and data exposure: agents read untrusted content — READMEs, documentation, dependencies, issues — that may contain instructions attempting to influence what the agent executes or discloses. Repository content or data may also be transmitted to external services. For confidential datasets (e.g. medical images), this deserves explicit attention.
Review burden and ownership: large agent-generated changes are hard to review; if nobody understands the pipeline, diagnosing failures becomes difficult.



4.3 Collaboration Modes
How much autonomy to grant depends on the task. In contrast to the learning levels above, these modes describe workflows, and they require different degrees of supervision:








Mode
Human responsibility
Agent responsibility




Direct implementation
Specify change, review output
Implement and test


Plan and execute
Review approach and milestones
Investigate, plan, implement


Exploratory research
Evaluate hypotheses and evidence
Investigate alternatives, run analyses


Adversarial review
Decide which findings matter
Challenge assumptions, identify weaknesses



Implementing a known function can be verified by a test. Determining the right evaluation protocol for an unfamiliar dataset requires judgment about the deployment scenario — which the human must own.






🤔 Think About It
What is the stopping criterion of a coding agent? How does it decide that a task such as “train a classifier with good performance” is finished?


Key considerations

It depends on the task description, the agent’s configuration, and the available checks. With a vague task, a plausible stopping point is “the script runs and prints a reasonable validation accuracy”. With explicit acceptance criteria — “no location appears in both train and test”, “the model overfits 32 images”, “macro-F1 is reported per class”, “results are compared to a linear probe baseline” — the agent can execute a substantial validation workflow before stopping. Vague success criteria invite superficially successful solutions.






4.4 What About Productivity?
Evidence on productivity is mixed and setting-dependent. A randomized study with 16 experienced open-source developers working on their own, familiar repositories found that early-2025 AI tools made them 19% slower, while they believed they were faster (Becker et al. 2025). A follow-up study (Joel Becker 2026) estimated an 18% speedup for returning developers and 4% for newly recruited ones. These estimates are statistically inconclusive (confidence intervals include zero) and, according to the authors, an unreliable signal due to selection effects: developers increasingly declined to participate or withheld tasks because they did not want to work without AI.
Productivity is also multidimensional: implementation time is only one part, next to correctness, review effort, maintainability, and the ability to tackle tasks that were previously out of reach. An experienced developer in a familiar repository and a student building an exploratory ML prototype are very different settings.

title: AI Coding Agents
text:
5 When Code Fails Silently
The statement “deep learning code fails silently” can be made more precise. There are three distinct propositions:

Code can execute correctly while implementing the wrong operation — e.g. an IoU function with a wrong union, or an augmentation that does not transform the bounding boxes.
An experiment can be implemented correctly while measuring the wrong quantity — e.g. a correct training loop evaluated on a split that leaks near-duplicates.
An experiment can be conducted correctly while its conclusions remain unjustified — e.g. claiming backbone A beats backbone B based on a single seed and a 0.5% difference.

These apply equally to human- and agent-written code. Agents add speed, scale, and autonomy — and the possibility that nobody developed a mental model of the system. The following examples are typical of computer vision projects. In every case, the code runs without error, and recognizing the problem requires subject-matter expertise.

5.1 Example 1: The Split Encodes a Deployment Assumption
Task: “Train a species classifier on my camera trap images and report test accuracy.”
A typical default is a random split:
train_ds, val_ds, test_ds = random_split(dataset, [0.7, 0.15, 0.15])
Camera traps record sequences (several near-identical frames per trigger) at fixed locations. A random split places near-duplicates into training and test set, and the model can exploit the background rather than the animal. Whether this is a problem depends on the question being asked:







Generalization objective
Appropriate split




New frames from already observed sequences
Frame-level split (rarely a meaningful objective)


New sequences at known camera locations
Sequence-level split


New dates or seasons at known locations
Temporal split


Completely unseen camera locations
Location-level split



from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit

splitter = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
train_idx, test_idx = next(splitter.split(df, groups=df["location_id"]))
Note that GroupShuffleSplit creates a single holdout split that keeps groups separate; it does not guarantee class balance or representativeness. Check the class distribution of the resulting splits, or use StratifiedGroupKFold.
The same structure appears with multiple images per patient, per product, or overlapping tiles of a satellite scene. The general principle: a train/test split encodes an assumption about the deployment distribution. An agent can be tasked to investigate what constitutes an independent observation — but deciding which deployment scenario matters is your responsibility.


5.2 Example 2: Augmentations Encode Assumptions
Task: “Add data augmentation to reduce overfitting.”
A generic pipeline is easy to generate:
T.Compose([T.RandomResizedCrop(224), T.RandomHorizontalFlip(), T.RandomRotation(30)])
Several distinct failure modes can hide in such a pipeline:

The transformation changes the label: rotating a 6 produces a 9; flipping an image labelled “left lung lesion” invalidates a laterality-sensitive label.
The transformation removes the relevant object: RandomResizedCrop with its default scale (0.08, 1.0) can crop away a small, distant animal in a camera trap image, leaving an empty background labelled “zebra”. How often this happens depends on object size and position. For detection with correctly updated annotations, cropping can be perfectly valid.
The transformation creates unrealistic samples: a flipped chest X-ray shows the heart on the wrong side. For a binary pneumonia classifier this may not change the label, but it trains on anatomically implausible data.
Image and target are desynchronized: transforming the image but not the bounding boxes or masks (e.g. using torchvision.transforms v1 on images only) silently corrupts the targets.

Augmentations impose invariance and distributional assumptions. Choosing them is a modeling decision, not boilerplate.


5.3 Example 3: Flawed Evaluation
Task: “Evaluate the model on the validation set and report the results.”
val_ds = ImageFolder("data/val", transform=train_transform)
for x, y in val_loader:
    preds = model(x).argmax(1)
    correct += (preds == y).sum()
print(f"Accuracy: {correct / len(val_ds):.3f}")
The snippet contains several issues with very different implications:







Issue
Implication




Random (training) transforms on validation data
Increases measurement variability and changes which distribution is evaluated; not necessarily a bias in a fixed direction


Missing model.eval()
For models with mode-dependent layers (Dropout, BatchNorm), predictions differ from inference behavior — invalidates the evaluation


Missing torch.no_grad()
Wastes memory and compute; does not make predictions incorrect


Accuracy on imbalanced data
Can hide poor minority-class performance; with 65% “deer”, predicting only “deer” yields 65% accuracy



A further, process-level issue: an agent asked to “improve the test score” will tune against the test set, effectively turning it into a validation set. And the agent’s summary (“the model achieves 94% accuracy”) is a claim, not a verified result.


5.4 Further Examples






NotePreprocessing Mismatch with the Pretrained Backbone





Task: “Use a pretrained SigLIP model as a feature extractor.”
A common default is the ImageNet normalization (mean=[0.485, 0.456, 0.406], std=[0.229, 0.224, 0.225]). Many foundation models were trained with different statistics (SigLIP uses mean and std of \(0.5\), mapping pixels to \([-1, 1]\)), resolutions, or cropping. A related classic is loading images with OpenCV (BGR) and feeding them to an RGB model. The impact is model- and task-dependent — sometimes negligible, sometimes substantial — and nothing in the code indicates the problem.
Preprocessing is specific to the checkpoint and implementation, not to the architecture family. Resolve it from the model and verify it with a pinned library version:
import timm

model = timm.create_model("hf-hub:timm/vit_base_patch16_siglip_224.webli", pretrained=True)
config = timm.data.resolve_model_data_config(model)
print(config)  # inspect mean, std, input_size, interpolation, crop_pct
transform = timm.data.create_transform(**config, is_training=False)









Note“Fixing” a Crash by Hiding It





Task: “The training script crashes, please fix it.” Some images are corrupted. A quick fix that makes the script run:
def __getitem__(self, idx):
    try:
        img = Image.open(self.paths[idx])
        return self.transform(img), self.labels[idx]
    except Exception:
        return self[(idx + 1) % len(self)]  # silently skip
The crash disappears, but except Exception also swallows unrelated bugs; replacing a failing sample with its neighbor changes the sampling distribution (neighbors often share class or sequence); and if all samples fail (e.g. a wrong root directory), the recursion ends in a RecursionError far from the actual cause. The immediate objective (prevent a crash) conflicts with the methodological one (preserve correct sampling). Better: scan and log problematic files once, decide explicitly how to handle them, and fail loudly otherwise.









NoteA Detection Metric that Passes its Tests





Task: “Compute precision and recall for my object detector at IoU 0.5.”
tp = 0
for pred in preds:
    ious = [iou(pred.box, gt.box) for gt in gts]
    if max(ious, default=0) >= 0.5:
        tp += 1
precision = tp / len(preds)
recall = tp / len(gts)
A simple test with one prediction per object passes. But one ground-truth object can be matched by multiple predictions: duplicates all count as true positives, precision is inflated, and recall can exceed 1. A common protocol processes predictions in order of decreasing confidence and matches each ground-truth box at most once. Benchmark protocols differ in details — COCO evaluation, for example, also handles categories, crowd/ignore flags, and area ranges — so prefer established tools such as pycocotools or torchmetrics.









NoteExercise: What Would You Investigate First?





An agent has trained a camera trap classifier and reports:




Accuracy




Training
98%


Validation
96%


New site (deployment)
72%



The dataset contains multiple images per camera location. What would you investigate first?

Whether the validation split shares locations with training
Whether a larger backbone improves performance
Whether stronger augmentation improves robustness
All three, without prioritizing an explanation



Click for discussion

Good first investigation: 1
The small train/validation gap combined with a large drop at the new site suggests that the validation set does not measure the relevant generalization — likely a shortcut based on location-specific features (background, camera angle). Before changing the model, establish exactly how the validation and new-site datasets were constructed. Options 2 and 3 may help later, but without a trustworthy validation protocol, their effect cannot be measured.
Extension: given the agent’s training code, formulate three tests that would detect potential problems — then run them.

title: AI Coding Agents
text:
6 Verification
The examples share a pattern: the code runs, and the error lies in an assumption about the data, the model, or the evaluation. Checking that code works is not the same as checking that a result is valid. It is useful to distinguish four levels of verification — for your own work as much as for an agent’s:








Level
Question
Typical evidence




1. Implementation correctness
Does the program implement the intended operations?
Unit tests, shape assertions, reference implementations, inspecting transformed inputs


2. Experimental correctness
Does the evaluation measure what it claims to measure?
Split validation, leakage checks, baselines, metric checks, reproducibility


3. Scientific validity
Does the evidence support the conclusion?
Ablations, multiple seeds and uncertainty estimates, confounders, alternative explanations


4. Operational validity
Does it work under realistic deployment conditions?
Distribution shift, latency, memory, failure handling, security, monitoring



Agents can assist at every level, but evidence at one level does not establish correctness at another. A perfectly tested pipeline (level 1) can still evaluate on a leaky split (level 2).

6.1 Independent Verification
Agents can generate both the implementation and the tests that confirm it. If both share the same misunderstanding, all tests pass. Consider an IoU function with a wrong union:
def iou(a, b):  # boxes in xyxy format
    inter = intersection_area(a, b)
    union = area(a) + area(b)          # bug: should subtract inter
    return inter / union

def test_iou():
    # expected value computed with the same (wrong) formula
    assert iou([0, 0, 2, 2], [1, 1, 3, 3]) == 1 / 8
The test passes; the correct value is \(1/7\). “Independent” refers to how the expected behavior is derived — not necessarily to who writes the test (a different agent may well share the same misconception). Independent sources of expectations include:

Analytically derived properties: identical boxes must give IoU \(= 1\) (the buggy version returns \(0.5\)); disjoint boxes must give \(0\).
Reference implementations: compare against torchvision.ops.box_iou or pycocotools.
Constructed counterexamples: duplicate predictions for the detection metric, a split with a known shared location.
Acceptance criteria defined before implementation.



6.2 Acceptance Criteria before Implementation
Verification criteria can be specified before an agent writes a single line of code, which makes the task much harder to satisfy superficially. For a camera trap training pipeline, for example:

Dataset integrity: no location_id appears in both training and test set.
Preprocessing: generated inputs match the pretrained model’s reference transform.
Learning sanity check: the model can overfit a tiny subset (e.g. 32 images).
Metric implementation: metrics on a hand-constructed example match expected values.
Generalization: sequence-level and location-level test performance are both reported.
Traceability: dataset version, model weights, configuration, and random seeds are recorded.



6.3 Reproducibility and Provenance
Agents iterate quickly, and every iteration may change something. To keep experiments comparable, track:

Data: dataset version, filters, split definition (ideally the split indices themselves)
Model: exact checkpoint identifier and source
Configuration: all hyperparameters in a versioned config file
Environment: pinned library versions (a lock file)
Results: metrics with the commit, config, and seed that produced them







🤔 Think About It
Which of the examples above would be caught by a unit test? Which by visualizing a batch of inputs after preprocessing? And which only by reasoning about the data and the deployment scenario?


Key considerations


Unit tests (with independently derived expectations): the detection metric (duplicate predictions as counterexample), unsynchronized box transforms, silently skipped samples (count loaded samples per class), missing model.eval() (assert model.training is False in the evaluation function).
Visualizing inputs after preprocessing: wrong normalization or channel order, label-breaking augmentations, crops that remove the object.
Reasoning about data and deployment: split design, which invariances hold, which metric answers the question.

The last category is the hardest to automate — and the one this course aims to build.

title: AI Coding Agents
text:
7 Takeaways
AI tools will keep improving, and many of the specific failure modes on this page may become less frequent. Three principles are more durable than guidance tied to any particular tool or model generation:

Use AI deliberately: choose its role based on what you are trying to learn, not merely on what can be automated.
Stay cognitively engaged: ask questions, make predictions, challenge explanations, and regularly work independently.
Take responsibility for results: understand the assumptions, validate important claims, and be able to explain what the system does and why.

text:
TipLearning Objectives





After this lecture you should be able to:

Describe why activation functions enable non-linear function approximation.
Interpret the role of depth vs width (efficiency of representation, hierarchical features).
