title: 1 - Introduction
text:
1 Motivation
Deep Learning models have played a transformative role in Computer Vision over the last decade, significantly enhancing and expanding the capabilities to process and generate visual data.
The integration of deep learning in computer vision has massively improved the accuracy and efficiency of visual recognition, classification, analysis, and generation. This has opened up new possibilities in applications such as autonomous driving, facial recognition, medical image analysis, and content creation. These models are now embedded in a wide variety of products and services.
Let’s take a look at several applications of deep learning assisted computer vision applications.

1.1 Applications
To monitor wildlife populations biologists can deploy camera traps to capture images from passing animals (see Figure 1). These images need to be analysed, for example, biologists need to know which species can be seen in each image. Deep learning can speed up that process significantly, as shown in Willi et al. (2019), and more recently in Beery et al. (2019) and Gadot et al. (2024).






Source: Breitenmoser-Würsten et al. (2024)




Figure 1: Image from a camera trap.



Recent advances in generative deep learning enable anyone to create photorealistic synthetic images (see Figure 2 for examples). While these technologies have many positive applications (art, design, prototyping), they also raise concerns about misinformation and deepfakes, motivating research into synthetic media detection (Mathys, Willi, and Meier (2024) and Willi et al. (2026)).


















Figure 2: Examples of synthetic images: left from Mathys, Willi, Graber, et al. (2024), right from Source.




Apple’s photo library uses deep learning to automatically classify and search through your photos. The system can recognize scenes (beach, mountain), objects (dog, car), and even activities (birthday, wedding). Additionally, sophisticated safety systems scan for problematic content while preserving privacy through on-device processing (Figure 3).






Figure 3: Apple’s on-device safety features detect sensitive content while maintaining user privacy. Source



Deep learning can be used to identify objects, to find similar images (image search / retrieval), or to find (near-)duplicates (perceptual hashing), see Figure 4 (left). Models can cross modalities and, for example, process visual data and produce textual outputs. An interesting example is image captioning or the detection and translation of text in images (optical character recognition - OCR), see Figure 4 (right).






Identification & Search







Translation



Figure 4: Google Lens

One area with high commercial interest and competition is self-driving capabilities. Figure 5 shows a demonstration of the perception system required for autonomous driving, including detecting vehicles, pedestrians, cyclists, and understanding lane markings and traffic signs in real-time.






Figure 5: Example from Waymo. Observe how the system simultaneously tracks multiple objects.



Figure 6 shows how these vehicles operate in real-world scenarios.






Figure 6: Example from Waymo. Waymo self-driving cars use three steps to solve self-driving: sense, solve, and go.



Face recognition technology, such as Apple’s Face ID (Figure 7), has become ubiquitous in consumer devices. The system uses infrared depth sensing to create a 3D map of facial features, making it more secure than 2D image-based recognition and robust to different lighting conditions.






Figure 7: Example from Apple Face ID. Watch how the infrared dot projector creates a depth map of the face.



Computer vision has also been very useful in agricultur. Figure 8 shows an application where apples can be counted from image data. Furthermore, drones might be used to estimate crop yield, type and health.






Figure 8: Example from Häni et al. (2020)



Deep learning has also been applied extensively in the medical area. In particular, many imaging technologies, such as MRI or CT, can be analysed with computer vision techniques. Figure 9 illustrates a generic segmentation model which can be used to identify organs and other anatomical structures on pixel-level.






Figure 9: Example from Ma et al. (2024).



Photo-editing has been brought to new levels of sophistication with AI-based capabilities. Figure 10 shows an impressive example from the Google Magic Editor. Maybe even a bit too good?






Figure 10: Example from Google Magic Editor









🤔 Think About It
What computer vision tasks do you think the model in Figure 10 must perform to enable this editing capability?


Possible tasks involved


Object detection and segmentation (identifying what to remove/move)
Inpainting (filling in removed areas)
Style transfer (matching lighting/texture)
Scene understanding (maintaining realistic perspective)





The increasingly better models and the ability to run them quickly and resource-efficiently on mobile devices have enabled such applications. Figure 11 shows that special chips have been developed to process images with Deep Learning models quickly.






Figure 11: From Link.

title: 1 - Introduction
text:
2 Computer Vision Tasks
The following sections introduce some fundamental computer vision tasks, which may be combined into more complex tasks and applications.

2.1 Image Classification
In image classification, an image is assigned to a predefined set of classes. In multi-class classification, there are \(\gt 2\) classes; in binary classification, there are exactly 2 classes; and in multi-label classification, there are multiple sets of classes. Figure 12 shows an example of multi-class classification.






Figure 12: Multi-Class Image Classification example: a model predicts the most likely class for an image along with confidence scores (Krizhevsky et al. (2012)).





2.2 Object Detection
Object detection involves locating and recognizing multiple objects in an image. Figure 13 shows an example Redmon et al. (2016). Each object is localized with a bounding box and assigned an object class with a confidence score.






Figure 13: Object Detection example (from Redmon et al. (2016)). Bounding boxes localize the objects, showing the predicted class and confidence for each detection.





2.3 Segmentation
In segmentation, individual pixels are assigned to specific objects (instance segmentation) or classes (semantic segmentation). Figure 14 shows an example of instance segmentation from He et al. (2018), where individual objects are detected and precisely localized at the pixel level.






Figure 14: Instance Segmentation example (from He et al. (2018)). Each person is individually segmented with pixel-level masks.



The following video shows an example of semantic segmentation:






Figure 15: Semantic segmentation applied to aerial imagery of agricultural fields. Each pixel is classified into crop types, field boundaries, and other land categories.





2.4 Keypoint Detection
In keypoint detection, specific points on objects — typically human body joints — are localized. Figure 16 shows an example from the paper by He et al. (2018). This can be used to transfer movements from a person to an avatar or to recognize human activities (action recognition).






Figure 16: Keypoint Detection example (from He et al. (2018)).





2.5 Image Generation
There are various applications where models transform input images into specific output images (image-to-image translation) or generate completely new images from scratch (unconditional generation). Below are example applications.

2.5.1 Image Manipulation
Interactive manipulation allows users to modify images by dragging points to reshape objects while maintaining realistic appearance.






Figure 17: DragGAN by Pan et al. (2023)





2.5.2 Image Translation
Figure 18 shows an example of image generation from the paper by Isola et al. (2018), where images are generated conditioned on image inputs (translated). This can be used, for example, to convert a sketch of an object into a photorealistic depiction of it.






Figure 18: Image Generation example (from Isola et al. (2018)).





2.5.3 Image Super Resolution
In the gaming industry, Deep Learning is used to upscale low-resolution images to high-resolution in real-time (image super resolution), as shown in Figure 19. This enables higher frame rates while maintaining visual quality.






Figure 19: Nvidia DLSS (Deep Learning Super Sampling) improves gaming performance. Source





2.5.4 Image Colorization
Image colorization can be learned with Deep Learning. This involves transforming a black-and-white image into an RGB image. Figure 20 shows an example.






Figure 20: Norwegian Bride (est late 1890s) from DeOldify: Link





2.5.5 View Synthesis
In view synthesis, new camera viewpoints of a scene are generated from a model. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) are models that can generate novel views from a set of input images taken from known viewpoints. Figure 21 shows training data (input images from different angles) and the synthesized novel views the model can generate.






Figure 21: Neural Radiance Fields - example (from Mildenhall et al. (2020)).



Modern variants can produce impressive quality, as shown in Figure 22.






Figure 22: 3D Gaussian Splatting for real-time novel view synthesis Kerbl et al. (2023).





2.5.6 Unconditional Generation
In unconditional image generation, images are generated that resemble the training data distribution without specific input guidance. While you have no direct control over what specific image is generated, you can often manipulate latent variables to modify generated images or interpolate between samples. Figure 23 shows photorealistic portraits generated by a model trained on human faces.






Figure 23: StyleGan3 (from Karras et al. (2021)).





2.5.7 Text to Image
Figure 24 shows an example of image generation from the paper by Rombach et al. (2022), where images are generated conditioned on text inputs.






Figure 24: Image Generation example (from Rombach et al. (2022).)



On civitai, there are numerous examples and models to admire or download.



2.6 Further tasks
There are many more computer vision tasks. The following list is not exhaustive:



Image Classification
Object Detection (and Tracking)
Image Segmentation

Semantic Segmentation
Instance Segmentation

Optical Character Recognition (OCR)
Pose Estimation
Facial Recognition
Action Recognition



Image Generation

Style Transfer
Image Inpainting
Super-Resolution
Text-to-Image (and more)

Image Captioning
3D Reconstruction
Image Retrieval





2.7 What about videos?
Many of the image-level tasks can be extended to videos. After all, videos are nothing but a sequence of images.
The most recent impressive examples are from video generative models:






Figure 25: OpenAI Sora 2 - Prompt: a man rides a horse which is on another horse



But also object / keypoint tracking:






Figure 26: CoTracker - Tracking points across video frames for motion analysis (Karaev et al. (2024))









NoteQuiz: Which Application belongs to which task?





Match each application to the most appropriate computer vision task:
Applications:

Analyzing camera trap images - Identifying which animals appear in wildlife monitoring photos
Apple’s on-device image categorization and safety filters - Classifying photos into categories or detecting inappropriate content
Image search - Finding visually similar images in a large database
Finding tumors in medical images - Precisely localizing and delineating abnormal tissue in CT or MRI scans
Counting apples in an orchard - Detecting and tallying individual fruits on trees

Available Tasks:

Image Classification
Object Detection
Image Segmentation
Image Retrieval/Embedding



Click for result


Analyzing camera trap images → Image Classification or Object Detection

Image Classification if you only need to know which species are present (one or more labels per image)
Object Detection if you need to count individuals or localize where each animal appears in the frame
The choice depends on the specific analysis requirements and label availability

Apple’s on-device image categorization and safety filters → Image Classification

This involves assigning images to predefined categories (e.g., “food”, “people”, “landscape”) or detecting inappropriate content
Multi-label classification is used when an image can belong to multiple categories

Image search → Tricky - Not directly a standard task

This doesn’t fit neatly into classification, detection, or segmentation
Closest to Image Classification conceptually, as it relies on learned image representations/embeddings
In practice, uses feature extraction (embedding) to compute similarity between images
Often leverages classification networks trained on large datasets, but applied for retrieval rather than classification

Finding tumors in medical images → Image Segmentation

Requires pixel-level precision to delineate tumor boundaries
Semantic Segmentation if identifying tumor vs. non-tumor tissue
Instance Segmentation if distinguishing between multiple separate tumors

Counting apples in an orchard → Object Detection

Need to localize and count individual apples
Each apple gets a bounding box, and counting is straightforward from detection results
Could also use instance segmentation for more precise boundaries, but detection is typically sufficient

title: 1 - Introduction
text:
3 Challenges
A number of fundamental challenges must be overcome when analyzing images with machine learning models.

3.1 Semantic Gap
The semantic gap refers to the discrepancy between the low-level pixel information that can be directly extracted from an image and the high-level semantic interpretation understood by humans. An image consists of millions of pixel values, but deriving semantically meaningful concepts like “cat” or “sitting” from these raw numbers is extremely challenging.






Figure 27: Illustration of the semantic gap: computers see numbers, humans see meaning.





3.2 Viewpoint
The semantic meaning of an image remains constant regardless of camera viewpoint, but the pixel values change dramatically. A model must learn to recognize the same object from different angles.






Figure 28: The same cat from different viewpoints looks completely different at the pixel level.





3.3 Deformation
Objects, especially living beings, are often flexible and can appear in vastly different shapes and poses. Models must recognize a cat whether it’s curled up sleeping or stretched out running.






Figure 29: Cats exhibit significant shape variation due to pose changes. Source





3.4 Illumination
Changes in lighting conditions dramatically affect pixel values and can obscure object features. The same object under different lighting can produce vastly different images.






Figure 30: The same scene under different lighting conditions. Source





3.5 Background Clutter
Background pixels can visually resemble the object of interest, making precise object localization and segmentation difficult. The model must learn to distinguish foreground from background.






Figure 31: Cat camouflaged against a similarly-textured background. Source





3.6 Occlusion
Objects are often partially hidden by other objects in the scene. Models must learn to recognize objects even when only part of them is visible.






Figure 32: Partially occluded cat - only part of the object is visible. Source





3.7 Intra-Class Variation
Objects belonging to the same class can exhibit enormous variability in appearance, color, size, and texture. All cats are cats, but they can look very different from each other.






Figure 33: High intra-class variation: all are cats but with vastly different appearances. Source





3.8 Context Dependence
Figure 34 shows that contextual information can be crucial for correct object classification. The surrounding scene provides important cues about what objects are likely to be present.






Figure 34: Is this a tiger? Context clues help determine the answer. Source



Figure 35 represents an interesting example where context is important: Shown are four images with severe quality degradation (blur) and oval objects indicated with dashed black lines. Notably, each marked object is exactly identical on pixel level (apart from a rotation) — yet we can form clear hypotheses what each of the objects represents.






Figure 35: In the presence of image degradation a visual system (e.g. humans) heavily uses context information. Even though the circled blobs are identical, we interpret them as either: plate, bottle, cell phone, car, pedestrian or shoe. Source Torralba et al. (2010)

title: 1 - Introduction
section: 4 From Classical Computer Vision to Deep Learning
text:
4 From Classical Computer Vision to Deep Learning

4.1 The Limitations of Hand-Crafted Features
Images typically have very high dimensionality. For example, an RGB image with a resolution of \(800 \times 600\) has a dimensionality of \(800 \times 600 \times 3 = 1,440,000\). Classical machine learning algorithms often struggle with such high dimensionalities:

They are very slow or require a lot of memory.
They cannot exploit the 2-D structure of images.
They are very sensitive to slight changes in images (e.g., rotations).
They can easily overfit, as the number of features is close to the number of observations (training set).

When modeling images with (classical) machine learning algorithms, methods from (classical) computer vision are often used. With the help of such methods, features can be extracted from images, and the algorithms can learn on these features. This avoids modeling high-dimensional raw data. Figure 36, Figure 37, and Figure 38 show various feature extraction methods.
Figure 36 shows that, for example, the distribution over the color spectrum can be extracted from an image. This could be an important feature.






Figure 36: Color Histograms as Features (Source: Johnson (2022))



Figure 37 shows that techniques like Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) Dalal and Triggs (2005) can be used to extract structures from images. Such features were successfully used for pedestrian detection Dalal and Triggs (2005).






Figure 37: HOG as Features (Source: Johnson (2022))



Figure 38 shows another feature variant. Visual patches can be extracted from a dataset, clustered, and then used as descriptors.






Figure 38: Bag of (visual) words Features (Source: Johnson (2022))



Finally, all features can be combined, often more is better, as shown in Figure 39.






Figure 39: Image Features (Source: Johnson (2022))



Depending on the parameterization, HOG descriptors, for example, can be very large for images. The resulting feature vector from Figure 39 can still be reduced in dimensionality, e.g., with Principal Component Analysis.
Figure 40 shows the CIFAR10 dataset. A well-known dataset for testing models, consisting of 10 classes with 6,000 images each.






Figure 40: CIFAR10 Dataset Source





4.2 The ImageNet Breakthrough (2012)
To accelerate research in computer vision and make progress more measurable, the PASCAL VOC Challenges were introduced Everingham et al. (2007). These involved various tasks, such as detecting objects in photographs (Figure 41).






Figure 41: Images/illustrations from Link and Johnson (2022). On the left, you see object annotations in images, and on the right, you see the development of Mean Average Precision over the years.



The easy availability of images on the internet has made it possible to collect increasingly larger datasets. ImageNet is such a very large, hierarchically annotated image dataset Deng et al. (2009) with over 1.4 million images, categorized into 1,000 object classes. Figure 42 illustrates the dataset.






Figure 42: ImageNet, Image Source, details in Deng et al. (2009)



Since 2010, challenges have been regularly conducted on the ImageNet dataset Russakovsky et al. (2015), such as image classification and object detection. Figure 43 shows the development of the error rate over time.






Figure 43: Source: Johnson (2022)





4.3 End-to-End Learning
The key conceptual shift is from hand-designed feature pipelines to end-to-end learning. Rather than designing features manually, the model learns to extract relevant features directly from raw pixels. Figure 44 illustrates this paradigm.






Figure 44: Illustration from Johnson (2022)



Deep learning-based approaches have several key advantages over classical methods:

Automatic feature extraction: No need for hand-crafted features like SIFT or HOG.
Hierarchical representations: Learn features at multiple levels of abstraction (edges → textures → parts → objects).
Better scaling: Performance improves with more training data and compute.
End-to-end optimization: Unified optimization from raw inputs to task outputs.
Transfer learning: Pre-trained models can be adapted to new tasks with limited data.



4.4 Deep Learning History
We will now explore the most important milestones in deep learning for image analysis.

4.4.1 Hubel and Wiesel
Hubel and Wiesel (1959) showed in experiments on cats that there are complex cells/neurons in the visual cortex that only respond to certain patterns. In addition to these complex cells, there are also simple cells that only respond to lines at a certain angle.






Figure 45: Illustration Source





4.4.2 Neocognitron
Fukushima (1980) defined a model of a neural network that can recognize visual patterns. It already has the hierarchical structure of a modern convolutional neural network and is inspired by biological neural networks, particularly from the insights of Hubel and Wiesel (1959).






Figure 46: The Neocognitron Fukushima (1980).





4.4.3 Backpropagation
Rumelhart et al. (1986) introduced the backpropagation algorithm in the context of neural networks. This algorithm is used to train modern neural networks: it finds the parameters of an artificial neural network (ANN) to solve a specific task. Backpropagation is based on the chain rule from calculus and is also important for other machine learning models.






Figure 47: Backpropagation in neural networks Rumelhart et al. (1986).









Tip



A good video on backpropagation: 3Blue1Brown Backpropagation Calculus




4.4.4 Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)
Lecun et al. (1998) implemented convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to recognize handwritten digits. The architecture is specialized for the 2-D structure of image data and trained a model very similar to modern CNNs, as shown in Figure 48.






Figure 48: LeNet-5 architecture Lecun et al. (1998): the first successful CNN for digit recognition.



After AlexNet’s breakthrough in 2012 (see previous section), CNNs rapidly evolved and were applied to increasingly complex tasks. Notable developments include:

VGGNet (2014): Showed that depth matters—16-19 layers with small 3×3 filters
ResNet (2015): Introduced skip connections, enabling networks with 50-152 layers
COCO Challenges: Expanded beyond ImageNet to multi-task benchmarks (detection, segmentation, keypoints)
Mobile architectures: Efficient CNNs for deployment on phones and embedded devices



4.4.5 Other Architectures in Computer Vision
CNNs are still in use today (2025). Meanwhile, there are alternative architectures, such as transformer-based models (Dosovitskiy et al. (2020)), which are extremely successful in language modeling, or multilayer perceptron-based architectures (Liu et al. (2021)).
The question of which architecture type will prevail is open. Currently, it seems that both CNNs and transformer-based models have their place, and often perform similarly (Smith et al. (2023)). Furthermore, hybrid-architectures, combining the strengths of CNNs and transformers have been proposed Vasu et al. (2023). Some works use both architecture types, depending on whether parameter efficiency (CNNs) or raw performance (transformers) are prioritized Siméoni et al. (2025).

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
TipLearning Objectives





After this lecture you should be able to:

Explain why pixel-space diffusion is computationally expensive and how latent diffusion addresses this
Describe the components of a Stable Diffusion-style system: text encoder, VAE encoder/decoder, and diffusion model
Understand the architectural shift from U-Net denoisers to Diffusion Transformers and why it matters
Distinguish the architecture of a generator (U-Net, diffusion transformer) from its generative objective (diffusion, flow matching)
Explain how multimodal conditioning extends image generation beyond simple text prompts, and compare modular and unified multimodal architectures
Describe the role of post-training — preference optimization and distillation — in modern image models
Choose appropriate adaptation strategies — prompting, reference images, LoRA, or fine-tuning — for different use cases
Compare practical deployment options: hosted APIs, enterprise platforms, and open-weight models
Recognize responsible use considerations: hallucination, bias, synthetic data risks, provenance, and copyright

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
1.1 The Pixel-Space Bottleneck
Diffusion models are iterative: they do not produce the final image in a single forward pass, but repeatedly apply a denoising network. If diffusion is performed directly in pixel space, this network operates on a very large representation, and the size grows quickly with the resolution.



Resolution
Number of RGB values




256 × 256
196,608


512 × 512
786,432


1024 × 1024
3,145,728



A rough intuition for the computational cost is:
\[
\text{cost per denoising step}
\times
\text{number of denoising steps}
\]
The cost per step depends on more than the number of RGB values: it also depends on the width and depth of the network and on its architecture. For transformers, which process an image as a sequence of patch tokens, the cost of self-attention grows quadratically with the number of tokens. Doubling the resolution quadruples the number of tokens and therefore increases the cost of attention by a factor of up to 16.
The number of steps is the second lever. Classical diffusion samplers use tens to hundreds of steps. Flow-based and distilled models can generate good images in a handful of steps (see How Modern Image Models Are Trained), but each step still has to process the full representation.
The core bottleneck is therefore that pixel-space diffusion asks the denoising network to operate directly on a large, high-dimensional representation. This creates three practical problems:

high memory usage
slow training and sampling
expensive high-resolution generation

This leads to the idea of latent diffusion:

Do not run diffusion directly on pixels if a smaller learned representation is sufficient.

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
section: 3.1 From U-Net Denoisers to Diffusion Transformers
text:
3.1 From U-Net Denoisers to Diffusion Transformers
Earlier diffusion systems commonly used U-Net denoisers. This is a natural choice for images because convolutions encode locality and the encoder-decoder structure captures both global context and spatial detail.
More recent systems increasingly use transformer-based denoisers (see Figure 3). The basic idea is to represent the noisy image or noisy latent as a sequence of tokens. These tokens may correspond to patches, latent patches, or learned visual tokens. The transformer then predicts how these tokens should be denoised.






Figure 3: Transformer-based architecture for diffusion models: Tokens (patches or latent representations) interact through self-attention, capturing long-range dependencies. Timestep embeddings condition the network on noise level. From Peebles and Xie (2023).



Conceptually, this is similar to the transition from convolutional networks to vision transformers in discriminative computer vision. Instead of processing the representation primarily as a spatial feature map, the model processes it as a sequence. Attention allows each token to interact with other tokens, which can be useful for modeling long-range relationships and global structure.
The comparison is summarized below.








Aspect
U-Net diffusion
Diffusion transformer




Representation
spatial feature maps
token sequence


Main operation
convolution + attention blocks
self-attention + MLP blocks


Inductive bias
strong image locality
more general sequence modeling


Conditioning
often cross-attention
cross-attention or joint attention over text and image tokens


Scaling behavior
strong, but architecture-specific
often attractive for large-scale training


Multimodal extension
possible, via added conditioning layers
architecturally simpler: additional tokens in the sequence



The important point is not that transformers are always better. U-Nets remain effective and efficient in many settings. The important point is that transformer-based denoisers fit naturally into a broader trend: text, image, video, and other modalities can all be represented as tokens or token-like latent representations. This makes it easier to build models that combine multiple modalities.

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
section: 3.2 Diffusion or Flow Matching? Objective vs. Architecture
text:
3.2 Diffusion or Flow Matching? Objective vs. Architecture
The terms U-Net and diffusion transformer describe the architecture of the network. They do not describe what the network is trained to predict. This is determined by the generative objective, and it is a separate design choice. Classical diffusion trains the network to reverse a stochastic noising process by predicting the added noise. Many modern systems instead use flow matching (see Flow Matching), which trains the network to predict a velocity that transports noise to data along a straight path:
\[
\mathbf{x}_t = (1 - t)\, \mathbf{\epsilon} + t\, \mathbf{x}_1,
\qquad
v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t) \approx \mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{\epsilon}
\]
where \(\mathbf{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\) is noise, \(\mathbf{x}_1\) is a training image (or its latent), and \(t \in [0, 1]\). In practice, both formulations start from Gaussian noise, apply the network iteratively, and can use either architecture. Flow matching, however, often requires fewer sampling steps, because its trajectories from noise to data are straighter.
Stable Diffusion 3 is a typical example that combines all three ideas: a VAE latent space, a transformer denoiser, and a rectified flow objective (Esser et al. 2024). The widely used FLUX models follow the same recipe and also use flow matching for instruction-based editing (Labs et al. 2025). Modern image generation is therefore not simply “classical denoising implemented with transformers”.








Design choice
Classical Stable Diffusion
Modern systems (e.g. SD3, FLUX)




Representation
VAE latent
VAE latent


Architecture
U-Net
diffusion transformer


Objective
diffusion (noise prediction)
flow matching (velocity prediction)

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
3.3 Why Token-Based Architectures Are Attractive
A token-based representation gives a more uniform interface between modalities. Text is already represented as a sequence of tokens. Images can be represented as patch tokens, latent tokens, or visual embeddings. Video can be represented as tokens across space and time. Reference images, masks, or editing instructions can also be converted into conditioning representations.
This is one reason diffusion transformers and multimodal transformers are attractive for modern systems. They provide a route toward architectures where text, image, and possibly video information can interact more directly. This does not mean that all modalities become identical. Text tokens and image tokens still have different origins and structure. But a transformer architecture provides a common computational mechanism: attention over sequences of representations.
Notably, tokenization alone does not make a model understand how a prompt relates to an image. Semantic alignment between text and image tokens is learned from large amounts of paired training data, and it depends on how the conditioning information enters the network. Two mechanisms are common (see Figure 4):

Cross-attention: image tokens attend to the output tokens of a separate text encoder, which is typically frozen. Information flows only from the text into the image. This is the mechanism of the original Stable Diffusion U-Net.
Joint attention: text and image tokens are concatenated into one sequence, and attention runs over both, so that information flows in both directions. The multimodal diffusion transformer (MM-DiT) of Stable Diffusion 3 uses separate weights for each modality, but a joint attention operation (Esser et al. 2024).







Figure 4: Cross-attention vs. joint attention, shown as attention matrices: rows are the tokens that read information (queries), columns the tokens that are read (keys). With cross-attention, only the image tokens read from fixed text tokens. With joint attention, all four blocks exist, and the text tokens are updated as well. The weights are illustrative.



That this alignment is learned can be made visible. With cross-attention, every spatial position of the latent attends to the tokens of the prompt. Averaging these attention weights over the sampling process yields one map per word, which shows where in the image the model has used that word (see Figure 5). The word “dog” attends to the dog and “cat” to the cat. Interestingly, the adjective “red” attends mainly to the sofa it describes. This binding of words to image regions is not built into the architecture. It emerges from training on image-text pairs, and it is the basis of editing methods that modify an image by manipulating these maps (Prompt-to-Prompt).






Figure 5: Cross-attention maps of Stable Diffusion 1.5 for selected words of the prompt, averaged over attention heads, the layers at 16x16 resolution, and 30 sampling steps. Brighter regions attend more strongly to the word.

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
3.4 Multimodal Diffusion Systems
A multimodal diffusion system extends the basic text-to-image setup by accepting more than one type of input. Instead of conditioning only on a text prompt, the model may also condition on an image, a mask, a reference subject, an editing instruction, or previous generated content.
This enables workflows that are difficult to achieve with text prompts alone. For example, a user may provide an image and ask the model to change only the background. Or the user may provide a reference image of a product and ask the model to generate advertising images while preserving the product identity. Or the user may iteratively refine a generated image in a conversational interface. See Figure 6 for an example of a multimodal interactive generation workflow (done with Nano Banana 2, Raisinghani (2026)).




Source

After: “Remove the book lying on the floor, replace it with clean floor”

After: “Recolor the sofa and ottoman to a vibrant turquoise color”



Figure 6: After: “Change the carpet color to match the turquoise sofa”



How are such systems built? There is more than one architectural answer. Figure 7 illustrates three simplified patterns, which differ mainly in how tightly understanding and generation are integrated.






Figure 7: Three architectural patterns of multimodal image generation. Blue: understanding of the inputs, green: generation. The patterns are deliberately simplified and are not exact diagrams of the named models.




Text-conditioned generator. A separate text encoder converts the prompt into conditioning, and a latent diffusion or flow model generates the image. This is the classical Stable Diffusion-style pipeline. Editing and reference images require additional conditioning mechanisms.
Multimodal encoder + multimodal diffusion transformer. A vision-language model encodes the prompt and the input images, and a multimodal diffusion transformer processes these conditioning tokens jointly with the image tokens being generated. Qwen-Image 2.0, for example, uses Qwen3-VL as condition encoder and unifies generation and editing in a single model (Zhao et al. 2026). Seedream 4.0 handles text-to-image synthesis, editing, and multi-image composition within one diffusion transformer (Seedream et al. 2025).
Unified multimodal model. A single LLM-style transformer processes text and images, and also generates both. HunyuanImage 3.0, for example, predicts text tokens autoregressively, but generates image latents with diffusion inside the same model (Team 2026).

Figure 8 shows a concrete example of the second pattern for an editing task: the user provides a photo of two palm trees and the instruction “Replace the two coconut trees with two phoenix trees”. The frozen vision-language model Qwen3-VL encodes the instruction together with the input image, which captures what should change. In addition, the input image is encoded by the VAE, which preserves how it looks: its exact layout, colors, and details. The target image enters as noisy VAE latents together with the timestep \(t\). All these token types are processed jointly by a stack of transformer blocks, which predict how to denoise the target tokens. For text-to-image generation, the input image is simply omitted.






Figure 8: Architecture of Qwen-Image 2.0 for an editing task. A frozen Qwen3-VL encodes the prompt and the input image (semantic conditioning), a VAE encodes the input image (appearance conditioning), and the noisy latents of the target image are denoised by a multimodal diffusion transformer that processes all tokens jointly. From Zhao et al. (2026).



Notably, in all three examples, the image itself is still generated by diffusion or flow matching in a VAE latent space, although fully autoregressive image generation exists as well (see Autoregressive Models). What changes between the patterns is how much of the system’s language and image understanding is available during generation.
The distinction between the underlying model and the user-facing system becomes important here. A user may experience the system as a single assistant, but internally it may involve several components: a multimodal language model, an image encoder, an image generation model, an editing model, safety filters, retrieval systems, or tool-calling infrastructure.

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
section: 3.5 How to Explain Systems Like ChatGPT or Gemini
text:
3.5 How to Explain Systems Like ChatGPT or Gemini
A modern multimodal assistant may combine several capabilities:

understanding text instructions
understanding uploaded images
maintaining conversational context
planning an edit or generation request
using a specialized image generation model
using a specialized image editing model
checking safety constraints
returning the result through a unified interface

The user experiences one coherent system. Internally, the system may be modular, unified, or somewhere in between. Two extremes are useful to distinguish:

Tool-orchestrated systems: a language model interprets the request and calls a separate image generation or editing model as a tool, for example by writing a detailed prompt for it.
Natively multimodal models: one model both understands and generates images, as in pattern 3 of Figure 7. OpenAI, for example, describes image generation in GPT-4o as native and autoregressive (Source).

From the user’s perspective, both can look identical. Technically, they differ substantially: a native model can use its full understanding of the conversation and of uploaded images during generation, while a tool-orchestrated system passes only what fits into the interface between the components. For most commercial assistants, the internal architecture is not disclosed, so statements about it should remain hypothetical.
This is the main conceptual takeaway:

Modern multimodal generation is not just a model that maps one prompt to one image. It is increasingly a system for understanding, planning, generating, editing, and iterating across modalities.

This perspective also helps explain why modern image generation is moving closer to general AI assistants. The image model is no longer only a standalone generator. It becomes one capability inside a broader multimodal system.

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
section: 3.6 How Modern Image Models Are Trained
text:
3.6 How Modern Image Models Are Trained
Architecture and objective explain how a model generates images. They do not fully explain why current models follow complex prompts, render legible text, and produce aesthetically pleasing images. Much of this results from the training pipeline. Recent technical reports describe pipelines with several stages, summarized in Table 1.



Table 1: A representative training pipeline of modern image generation models. Individual models deviate from it.










Stage
Goal
Typical training signal




Pretraining
learn visual concepts, composition, and text-image alignment
billions of image-text pairs, often with increasing resolution


Supervised fine-tuning
improve aesthetics, instruction following, and task-specific behavior
small, carefully curated datasets


Preference and reward optimization
improve aesthetics, prompt adherence, and editing quality
human preference pairs, learned reward models


Distillation
reduce the number of sampling steps and the cost
outputs of the model itself (teacher)






Pretraining is where most of the compute goes. To keep it affordable, resolution is typically increased progressively: Qwen-Image 2.0, for example, is first pretrained at 256 and 512 pixels, where training is cheap, and only later continues at 1024 and 2048 pixels (Zhao et al. 2026).
Preference and reward optimization is the image counterpart of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) for language models. Reward models, often fine-tuned vision-language models, score generated images, for example for prompt alignment, aesthetics, or identity preservation. The generator is then updated to produce images with higher rewards. Qwen-Image 2.0, for example, gains substantially in blind pairwise comparisons after this stage (Xu et al. 2026). Interestingly, the human preferences we used for evaluation in Evaluating Generative Models here become a training signal. The model therefore also inherits their limitations: it optimizes what the reward measures, which may be aesthetic appeal rather than faithfulness or diversity.
Distillation trains a student model to reproduce the outputs of a teacher model with far fewer sampling steps, and often without classifier-free guidance, which otherwise doubles the number of network evaluations per step. This directly addresses the cost problem from the Motivation. The distilled student of Qwen-Image 2.0, for example, generates an image with 4 network evaluations, compared to 40 sampling steps of its undistilled teacher (Zhao et al. 2026). Seedream 4.0 combines adversarial distillation and distribution matching to generate 2K images in a few seconds (Seedream et al. 2025). Distillation can also serve other purposes: Qwen-Image 2.0 uses it to merge separately optimized text-to-image and editing models into a single model (Xu et al. 2026).






🤔 Think About It
Open model families often publish both an undistilled base model and a fast distilled variant. Why might the distilled model be a poor starting point for fine-tuning or LoRA training?


Key considerations

A distilled model is trained to jump from noise to an image in a few large steps. It no longer learns the full velocity field that the standard flow matching objective describes, so fine-tuning it with that objective can destroy the few-step behavior. A common workflow is therefore to adapt the undistilled base model, and to rely on distillation, or on adapters that transfer to the distilled model, for fast inference.

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
4.1 The Adaptation Spectrum








Method
What changes?
Use when…




Prompting
only the input text
you need fast exploration or weak control


Reference images / image editing
input image context
you need one-off subject, style, or local edits


Masks / inpainting / control inputs
generation is constrained
you need spatial or structural control


Textual inversion
a learned token embedding
you need a lightweight concept token


LoRA / DreamBooth-LoRA
small trainable adapter weights
you need persistent style, subject, or domain adaptation


Full fine-tuning
many or all model parameters
you need a strongly specialized model and have enough data/compute



The practical rule is:

Do not fine-tune because the model is imperfect. Fine-tune when the same failure appears repeatedly and simpler controls are not enough.

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
4.2 Prompting and Reference Images First
Prompting is the lowest-cost form of adaptation. It can control subject matter, style, camera angle, lighting, composition, mood, and output format.
a studio product photo of a hiking backpack,
white background, softbox lighting,
high detail, commercial photography
For many applications, this is enough. Modern image models can also use reference images, masks, and multi-turn edits to preserve a product, character, or style without any training.
A typical first workflow is:
prompt
→ inspect result
→ add reference image or mask
→ edit locally
→ only then consider training
However, prompting and reference images may still fail when we need strong repeatability: the same product in hundreds of scenes, a fixed brand style, a recurring character, or a specialized visual domain.

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
4.3 When LoRA Still Makes Sense
LoRA is a lightweight fine-tuning method. Instead of updating all model weights, it freezes the base model and learns a small low-rank update:
\[
\Delta W = BA
\]
The result is a small adapter that can be loaded on top of the base model.
LoRA is useful when the goal is not just one good image, but a reusable image generator with a persistent bias toward a subject, style, or domain.
Good LoRA use cases include:

a recurring character or mascot
a specific product or object
a consistent brand or illustration style
a domain such as fashion, architecture, product photography, microscopy, or industrial imagery
local or private deployment with an open model
many lightweight variants of one base model

LoRA is less useful for:

one-off image generation
general image quality
factual reasoning
precise spatial layout
problems that can be solved with masks, reference images, or editing

In other words:

LoRA is no longer the default answer to “how do I control the model?” It is useful when we need persistent specialization.

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
4.4 Example Workflows







Situation
Preferred workflow




One-off image
prompt + reference image + editing


Product shown in a few scenes
reference image + image-to-image / inpainting


Product or character reused across many scenes
DreamBooth-LoRA or LoRA


Company-wide visual style
style reference images; style LoRA if consistency must hold across many generations


Specialized visual domain
LoRA first, full fine-tuning only if necessary



Several current tools make this accessible without large budgets. Hugging Face Diffusers provides LoRA and DreamBooth-LoRA training examples, including FLUX-based workflows. Replicate provides hosted FLUX fine-tuning via web interface or API, so users can train a subject or style adapter without managing GPU infrastructure.
Useful references:

Hugging Face Diffusers LoRA: https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/en/training/lora
Hugging Face FLUX QLoRA example: https://huggingface.co/blog/flux-qlora
Replicate FLUX fine-tuning: https://replicate.com/docs/get-started/fine-tune-with-flux
Replicate FLUX fine-tuning API: https://replicate.com/blog/fine-tune-flux-with-an-api

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
4.5 Full Fine-Tuning
Full fine-tuning updates many or all model parameters. This gives maximum flexibility, but it is expensive and risky. It requires more data, more compute, larger model artifacts, and careful evaluation.
It may be appropriate for highly specialized domains such as medical imaging, satellite imagery, industrial inspection, or proprietary product imagery. For most projects, it should not be the first choice.
A useful decision rule is:







Situation
Prefer




quick exploration
prompting


local edit
inpainting / image editing


preserve layout or pose
masks, depth, pose, edges, ControlNet-like conditioning


reuse a subject or product many times
DreamBooth-LoRA / LoRA


reproduce a visual style consistently
style reference images, then LoRA


adapt to a narrow visual domain
LoRA, possibly full fine-tuning later


build a fully specialized generator
full fine-tuning or custom training

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
4.6 Evaluating Adapted Models
Adaptation is only useful if it is evaluated. A few cherry-picked images are not enough.
For an adapted model, ask:

Does it preserve the subject, product, or style?
Does it still respond to different prompts?
Does it overfit to the training examples?
Does it reduce diversity?
Does it introduce artifacts?
Is the improvement large enough to justify maintaining the adapter?

A simple evaluation strategy is to define a fixed prompt suite before training and compare:
base model
vs.
prompt/reference-image workflow
vs.
LoRA-adapted model
Visual inspection should be complemented with simple quantitative measures, computed over the whole prompt suite and several seeds:







Question
Possible measure




Is the subject or style preserved?
image similarity to the reference images, e.g. cosine similarity of DINO or CLIP embeddings


Does it still follow the prompt?
text-image similarity (CLIP score) or a vision-language model as judge


Does it reduce diversity?
average pairwise similarity between images generated with different seeds


Do people prefer it?
blind pairwise comparison against the base model



These measures are imperfect, as discussed in Evaluating Generative Models, but they make the comparison reproducible and reveal overfitting that a few cherry-picked examples hide.
This keeps the central question clear:

Did adaptation solve a real, repeated failure mode?

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
5.1 Example: MRI to CT
MRI-to-CT synthesis is a typical image-to-image translation problem.
The goal is not simply to create a plausible CT-like image. The output should preserve anatomy and provide meaningful information for the downstream use case.
This suggests a workflow such as:

collect paired and registered MRI/CT data
train a supervised translation model
evaluate structural accuracy and downstream usefulness
use generative models only if they provide a clear benefit

This is a good example where physical validity matters more than photorealism.

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
section: 5.2 Example: Solar Activity With and Without Flares
text:
5.2 Example: Solar Activity With and Without Flares
Generating solar images with and without flares is a conditional scientific generation problem.
The model may be asked to:

generate images conditioned on flare class
predict future observations from previous frames
simulate possible flare-related changes
generate rare-event examples for augmentation

Here, temporal information, multi-channel sensor data, and event labels may all be important conditioning signals.
Again, the key question is not just whether the generated image looks realistic, but whether it is scientifically meaningful and useful for analysis or prediction.

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
6.1 Choosing an Access Pattern








Need
Prefer
Why




Fastest prototype
Hosted API
minimal setup, no GPU operations


Strong current model quality
Hosted API
access to frontier or near-frontier models


Internal demo or product experiment
Hosted API or Replicate/fal.ai
quick integration and iteration


Governance, IAM, logging, quotas
Enterprise platform
fits organizational cloud and security workflows


Regulated or sensitive company workflow
Enterprise platform
integrated auditing and access control


Private or sensitive images
Enterprise platform or private deployment
contractual and technical control over data handling


Reproducible experiments
Open-weight model
fixed model versions and controllable inference pipeline


Customization / LoRA
Open-weight model or hosted fine-tuning
access to weights or adapter workflows


Local/offline use
Open-weight model
no dependency on external API availability


Maximum control
Open-weight model
inspectable pipeline, custom schedulers, adapters, safety layers


Lowest operational burden
Hosted API
provider manages infrastructure


Lowest vendor lock-in
Open-weight model
easier to move across infrastructure providers



The categories are not perfectly separate. For example, Replicate can expose open-weight models through a hosted API, and enterprise platforms may provide access to both proprietary and open models. Still, the distinction is useful because each option makes a different tradeoff between convenience, control, governance, cost, and reproducibility.
Note that the category alone does not make a deployment secure. Whether sensitive data is adequately protected depends on the contractual terms, the data retention and training policies of the provider, the deployment configuration (for example the region), and the access controls. An enterprise platform makes these aspects easier to manage, but they still have to be checked and configured.

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
6.2 Three Access Patterns









Access pattern
Examples
Strengths
Limitations




Hosted API
OpenAI, Google, Replicate, fal.ai
fastest setup, strong models, no GPU management
opaque model changes, provider dependency, usage-based cost


Enterprise platform
Vertex AI, Azure, Bedrock
IAM, logging, monitoring, quotas, compliance integration

Open-weight model
Hugging Face Diffusers, ComfyUI, self-hosted pipelines

A practical rule of thumb:

Start with a hosted API for exploration, move to an enterprise platform when governance matters, and use open-weight models when control, reproducibility, privacy, or adaptation becomes central.







Figure 10: Replicate: a hosted API that provides access to both proprietary and open-weight models, allowing users to choose between convenience and control. Source.

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
6.3 Hallucination in Image Generation
Hallucination is often discussed for language models, but image models can hallucinate too.
They may invent:

objects
text
logos
identities
physical relationships
medical or technical details
impossible geometry
misleading context

The output may look visually convincing while being factually wrong. For example, a generated product image may include plausible but nonexistent features. A generated street scene may show signs or architecture that never existed. A generated scientific illustration may look authoritative while being anatomically or technically incorrect.
This is why visual plausibility should not be confused with correctness.






Figure 11: The new electric Ferrari Luce seen from the rear. This image is visually plausible but given the vehicle is electric, it is unlikely to have a visible exhaust pipe. This is an example of a plausible but factually incorrect generated image.

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
6.4 Synthetic Data: Useful but Risky
Synthetic data is an important application of generative models. It can be useful when real data is scarce, labels are expensive, rare cases are underrepresented, or privacy concerns limit data collection.
Examples include:

generating rare object poses
augmenting defect detection datasets
simulating unusual lighting conditions
creating training examples for early prototypes
generating privacy-preserving examples for demonstrations

However, synthetic data also creates risks. If models are trained on increasing amounts of synthetic data without careful filtering, artifacts can be amplified. Diversity can decrease. The generated distribution may drift away from the real data distribution. Models may start learning the mistakes of previous models.
This problem is sometimes discussed as synthetic data pollution or model collapse. Model collapse is, however, not inevitable. It occurs mainly when synthetic data replaces real data over successive model generations. If synthetic data is accumulated alongside the original real data, the degradation can be avoided, as shown for language models, diffusion models, and VAEs (Gerstgrasser et al. 2024). The exact outcome depends on the data mixture, filtering, training setup, and evaluation procedure, but the general warning is simple: synthetic data should be validated, not assumed to be beneficial.






Figure 12: Example: deterioration of generated image quality under pollution or domain shift. From Alemohammad et al. (2023).



The practical question is therefore not whether synthetic data is good or bad. The practical question is whether a specific synthetic dataset improves performance on the real target distribution.

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
6.5 Bias in Generated Images
Generative models learn from large-scale datasets, and large-scale datasets reflect the biases of the world and the biases of data collection. These biases can appear in generated outputs.
A model may associate certain occupations with certain genders. It may represent beauty, professionalism, wealth, poverty, or danger in stereotyped ways. It may overrepresent some cultures and underrepresent others. It may produce different levels of realism or dignity for different demographic groups.
This is not only a technical issue. It affects how generated images shape expectations, reinforce stereotypes, and influence communication.






Figure 13: AI bias example. Source: Washington Post.









Figure 14: Example outputs illustrating biased visual associations. Source: Washington Post.



For practical work, bias evaluation should be tied to the use case. A creative toy application has different risks than a hiring platform, educational tool, public communication campaign, or medical assistant. But in all cases, generated outputs should be inspected critically rather than treated as neutral.

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
6.6 Provenance, Watermarking, and Detection
As synthetic images become more realistic, provenance becomes increasingly important. Provenance asks where an image came from, who created it, whether it was edited, and whether the editing history can be verified.
Relevant questions include:

Was the image captured by a camera or generated by a model?
Was it edited after capture?
Which parts were modified?
Is there metadata describing the origin?
Is there a watermark or content credential?
Can the source be cryptographically verified?







Figure 15: “Real or Not?” Example of uncertainty around whether an event image is real or synthetic. Source: Spiegel.



There are several possible approaches:

visible watermarks
invisible watermarks
metadata-based provenance
cryptographic signatures
synthetic image detectors
content credentials

None of these is perfect. Metadata can be removed. Watermarks can sometimes be attacked. Detectors can fail under distribution shift or adversarial manipulation. Provenance is therefore best understood as a system-level problem rather than a single model-level solution.
A recent example illustrates these limits. In July 2026, Google introduced an AI feature in Google Earth that allowed users to generate images and superimpose them onto satellite views of the real world. Within hours, people used it to create realistic fake scenes of real places: a plane crashing into a Manhattan skyscraper, army tanks on the Golden Gate Bridge, or a bomb crater next to the Washington Monument (see Figure 16). Google paused the feature the next day, “while we work on implementing stronger guardrails”.






Figure 16: Fake bomb crater next to the Washington Monument, created by a Washington Post reporter with a short prompt in Google Earth’s AI image feature. The map labels and the familiar interface lend the fake credibility. Source: Washington Post.



Notably, the generated images did carry an invisible SynthID watermark. However, when a Washington Post reporter photographed one of the altered images with an iPhone, Google’s detector no longer identified it as AI-generated. Even an intact watermark only helps if someone actually checks it — while images are typically viewed and shared within seconds. The example also shows why the context of a generator matters: the fakes inherit the credibility of a source that journalists, governments, and open-source researchers have relied on for years to assess the impact of wars and disasters.

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
6.7 Copyright and Licensing
Generated images also raise copyright and licensing questions. These questions can concern the training data, the model weights, the generated outputs, and any adapters or fine-tuned checkpoints used in the workflow.
Important questions include:

What data was used to train the model?
Is the model license compatible with the intended use?
Can outputs be used commercially?
Could outputs resemble protected training examples?
Are there restrictions on generated content?
Are LoRA adapters or fine-tuned models licensed separately?
Are reference images owned or licensed by the user?

For professional use, these questions should be addressed explicitly. From an engineering perspective, licensing is part of the model selection process, not an afterthought.

title: 10 - GenAI: Modern Systems
text:
6.8 Practical Responsibility Checklist
Before using generated images in a project, it is useful to ask a few basic questions.
First, what is the risk level of the use case? A playful internal prototype is different from a medical, legal, political, or journalistic use case.
Second, could the image mislead people? If so, labeling, provenance, and review become more important.
Third, are there identity, privacy, or consent issues? This matters especially when generating or editing images of people.
Fourth, are there copyright or licensing constraints? This applies to the base model, reference images, generated outputs, and adapters.
Fifth, could the output reinforce stereotypes or biased visual associations? If the output will be public or influence decisions, this needs careful review.
