title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
TipLearning Objectives





After this lecture you should be able to:

Explain how generative modeling differs from classification: sampling from a distribution of plausible outputs instead of predicting a label (one-to-many vs. many-to-one mapping)
Describe the role of random inputs and latent variables in enabling diverse outputs from a single condition
Distinguish unconditional and conditional generation, and recognize common conditional generation tasks
Describe the common goal of generative models, \(p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \approx p_{\text{data}}(\mathbf{x})\), and explain maximum likelihood as one principle to reach it
Define fidelity and coverage, and explain the trade-offs between model properties: sampling efficiency, fidelity and coverage, latent-space structure, and likelihood computation
Select appropriate evaluation methods for generative models depending on the task and available ground truth, and explain why fidelity and coverage must be assessed separately (precision and recall vs. FID)

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
1 Motivation
Generative AI has had a profound effect on many aspects of our society. Particularly, the release of ChatGPT (see OpenAI 2022) kicked off a new era of AI applications, focused on generating natural language. Recently, the quality of image generative models has made significant leaps: Nowadays, it is difficult to distinguish between real and synthetic images (see Figure 1).






Figure 1: Source



Arguably, the most impressive generative models are multimodal: they understand text and images and allow precise control of the generation process using natural language. Models such as GPT Image 2 (Source), Nano Banana 2 (Source) and FLUX.2 (Source) edit existing images by following instructions (see Figure 2). Notably, the requested aspect is changed while the rest of the scene is preserved.
















Figure 2: Instruction-based image editing with Nano Banana 2. Left: original image (Source). Middle: prompt “Replace the elephant with a lion, keep background identical, only replace the animal, keep its pose.” Right: prompt “Keep the scene exactly as is, only change the lighting condition to dawn.”



Modern models can also use one or several reference images as a condition. They generate new scenes while preserving the identity of an object, a person, or a style (see Figure 3).













Figure 3: Reference-based generation. Left: reference image (Source). Right: generated with Nano Banana 2 using the prompt “The exact same wooden toy monkey from the reference image is dancing joyfully in a lush tropical jungle. It holds a yellow banana in one hand and a shampoo bottle in the other hand. Preserve every detail of the toy: the dark brown wooden body, light beige wooden face and belly, rope arms, and round wooden hands and feet. Photorealistic scene, vibrant jungle background with green leaves and sunlight filtering through the canopy.”



Commercial applications of generative AI include the virtual staging of rooms with objects (furniture). This helps realtors present their properties in a more appealing and “real” way (see Figure 4).













Figure 4: Virtual staging examples from Link



AI-generated images are prevalent in commercials and ads. Restuarants or fast food businesses increasingly use generative AI to promote their menus (Lieferando Examples), since it is cheaper and quicker than hiring a food photographer (Source). The results often look uncanny (see Figure 5). Humans are particularly sensitive to food that does not look real, and food images depend on texture, repetition, and the interfaces between materials, which older and free models handle poorly: they may, for example, spread the pattern of sesame seeds over an entire dish. Moreover, even a convincing image does not show the dish that is actually served: it is plausible, but not faithful. We will return to this distinction in Section 6.4. Image editing also works the other way around: Figure 5 (b) shows a real burger that was allegedly edited to look undercooked, presumably to claim a refund from a delivery service. The origin of this example is unconfirmed, but it shows how easily a photo used as evidence can be manipulated.











(a) AI-generated food image used in restaurant advertising. Source











(b) Original (left) and allegedly AI-edited, undercooked version (right) of a burger. Unconfirmed. Source







Figure 5: AI-generated and AI-edited food images.



Video generation has advanced rapidly as well. Models such as Google’s Veo 3.1 generate short clips including audio and can be conditioned on reference images (Source).
Not all generative models create images from scratch. Image super resolution is a task where generative models up-sample images spatially and enrich detail (see Figure 6). Again, the generated details are plausible, but they are not necessarily the details of the true high-resolution image.






Figure 6: From Ledig et al. (2017)



Similar ideas are used in real-time graphics. NVIDIA DLSS renders a game at a lower resolution and upscales each frame with a neural network, which is cheaper than rendering natively at high resolution (see Figure 7). Recent versions even synthesize entire additional frames between rendered ones (Source).






Figure 7: NVIDIA DLSS (Link).



Generative AI is used in many domains nowadays. Figure 8 shows an application where MRI images are converted to synthetic CT scans. CT scans expose the body to radiation and should thus be avoided if possible. However, CT scans show bone structure much better than MRIs. This application helps get the best of both worlds.






Figure 8: MRI to CT conversion example, from Schärer (2023)









NoteMore applications





Creating highly creative and diverse images has been enabled by recent advances of models trained on internet-scale datasets. Different companies, such as Midjourney have built businesses around this capability to make it easy for users to generate images (see Figure 9).






Figure 9: Source



Companies such as Canva have integrated generative models into their design tools, making it easy for users to generate images and use them in their designs (see Figure 10).






Figure 10: Source



Image editing through conversation became widely accessible in 2025. Figure 11 shows two images that were generated in turn with GPT-4o image generation, following user instructions about how to change the first image.













Figure 11: Examples from OpenAI image generation. The two images were generated in turn, following user instructions about how to change the first image. Source



AI-generated content in advertisements seems particularly prevalent. Suspected AI-generated content is shown in Figure 12.















Figure 12: AI generated? Top: Source, Bottom: Source









🤔 What do you think? Are these ads AI-generated?



Midjourney, a company known for its image generation service, also released a model that animates images into short videos (see Figure 13).







Figure 13: Source



NVIDIA DLSS combines several neural networks, each addressing a different part of the rendering pipeline:

Super Resolution: The game renders at a lower resolution, and a network upscales each frame using information from previous frames. Interestingly, up-scaling with a neural network is cheaper than rendering natively at high resolution (see Figure 7).
Frame Generation: A network synthesizes entire additional frames between rendered ones, using motion vectors and optical flow. Since DLSS 4.5, up to five frames can be generated per rendered frame (Source).
Ray Reconstruction: Ray tracing is expensive, so only a limited number of rays is computed, resulting in a noisy image. A network replaces hand-tuned denoisers and predicts the missing pixels (see Figure 14, Source).

All three produce pixels that were never rendered, but to different degrees: super resolution and ray reconstruction refine a rendered frame, while frame generation synthesizes entire frames for which no rendered counterpart exists.






Figure 14: NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction for improved graphics (Link).



Generative models are also used to create synthetic training data for predictive models, such as for solar flare prediction (see Figure 15).






Figure 15: Synthetic images of solar flares (from Ramunno et al. (2024)).






Generative AI has come a long way. Almost nothing illustrates that better than the quality of generated images of human faces (see Figure 16).






Figure 16: Evolution of generative AI. From left to right, top to bottom: Goodfellow et al. (2014), Liu and Tuzel (2016),Radford et al. (2016), Karras et al. (2018), Karras et al. (2019), Karras et al. (2020), Ho et al. (2020), Rombach et al. (2022), Saharia et al. (2022), Betker et al. (2023)



Over time, the dominant model families have shifted (see Table 1). We will discuss these families in more detail later.



Table 1: Milestones of image generation.










Period
Development
Examples




2014–2019
GANs: from blurry, low-resolution images to photorealistic faces
Goodfellow et al. (2014), Karras et al. (2019)


2020–2022
Diffusion models; latent diffusion makes high-resolution text-to-image generation widely accessible
Ho et al. (2020), Rombach et al. (2022), Saharia et al. (2022)


2023–2024
Better prompt following; transformer backbones trained with flow-based objectives (rectified flow)
Betker et al. (2023), Esser et al. (2024)


2025–2026
Native multimodal models; instruction-based editing with one or several reference images
GPT-4o image generation, FLUX.1 Kontext (Labs et al. 2025), Nano Banana 2, FLUX.2, GPT Image 2






Notably, no model family has completely replaced another. Image generation in GPT-4o, for example, is autoregressive (Source), and latent diffusion models train their autoencoder with an adversarial loss, a key idea of GANs (Rombach et al. 2022).
How do such models work, and what does it mean for a model to generate data? In the following, we develop the core ideas step by step, starting from a task we already know well: classification.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
2 What Is Generative Modelling?
Let’s contrast generative modelling with a classification task (see Figure 17). As a simplified mental picture, let’s denote \(f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{y}\) for a classifier, and \(g(\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}\) for a generative model.
In classification the model has as input an image \(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\) and models a probability distribution over all classes \(\mathbf{\hat{y}}^{(i)}\) which ideally assigns a high probability to the true label \(\mathbf{y}^{(i)}\).






Figure 17: Classification.



At first glance, generative modelling seems to reverse this process: The input can be a label \(\mathbf{y}\), such as a class label, and the output is an image \(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\), see Figure 18.






Figure 18: Generative modelling.









NoteWhat is the problem?





Looking at the input and the output of Figure 18. What could be a problem?


Click for result

If the input (in this case) to the generative model is a label, such as elephant, how can the model generate not just that one elephant?




An important distinction between a classifier and a generative model is:

\(f(\mathbf{x})\) is a many-to-one mapping. Many inputs (e.g. images of elephants) should be associated with the same label (e.g the elephant label).
\(g(\mathbf{y})\) is a one-to-many mapping. One label (e.g. elephant) should be associated with many outputs (e.g. images of elephants).

Generative modelling is therefore not simply the inverse of classification. More precisely, both tasks can be described by conditional probability distributions, but over different variables:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{classification:} \quad & p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x}) \\
\text{generation:} \quad & p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y})
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]
A classifier models a distribution over a handful of classes, and we are usually interested in its most probable class. A conditional generative model has to represent a distribution over all plausible images of an elephant, an extremely high-dimensional space. Moreover, we do not want the single most probable image: we want to sample from the distribution, such that each call produces a different, plausible elephant. Notably, simply inverting a trained classifier does not work: optimizing an input image to maximize a classifier’s confidence for a class typically yields unrecognizable patterns rather than realistic images (Nguyen et al. 2015). Figure 19 illustrates the classification side: one input image is mapped to one distribution over a few classes.






Figure 19: Classification. A classifier maps an image to a distribution over classes. The class probabilities are illustrative. Input photo: Source.



Since neural networks consist of deterministic operations (such as matrix multiplications and additions) we need a way to transform \(g()\) to a stochastic function. Only then is it possible to generate different elephants and not always the same image (see Figure 20).






Figure 20: Generative modelling with a diverse set of outputs.



One way to achieve this is to give the generative model an additional random input \(\mathbf{z} \sim p(\mathbf{z})\) and to generate samples using \(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{y})\). Typically, \(p(\mathbf{z})\) is a simple distribution that is easy to sample from, such as a standard Gaussian: \(\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\). Each new draw of \(\mathbf{z}\) yields a new output.
Figure 21 shows the resulting conditional generator: it combines the same condition \(\mathbf{c}\) with different random inputs \(\mathbf{z}^{(1)}, \mathbf{z}^{(2)}, \mathbf{z}^{(3)}\) and produces a different, plausible image for each of them. In contrast to the classifier in Figure 19, the output is not a distribution over a few classes but a sample from a distribution over images.






Figure 21: Conditional generation. The same condition (“elephant”) combined with different random inputs yields different, plausible images.



One way to think about \(\mathbf{z}\) is as a latent variable: it is not observed, but it captures variation in the data that is not specified by the input. In our elephant example, the condition \(\mathbf{y}\) specifies that the image should show an elephant, while \(\mathbf{z}\) might define aspects of the animal (pose, size, number of individuals) and of the scene (time of day, surroundings). This is an intuition rather than a guarantee: the model is free to use \(\mathbf{z}\) in whatever way helps it to produce diverse outputs.






NoteWhere does the randomness come from?



A single random vector that is mapped to an image is only one way to make a generator stochastic. Depending on the model family, randomness enters in different ways:

Single latent vector: GANs and VAE decoders map one sample \(\mathbf{z}\) to an output in a single forward pass.
Initial noise image: Diffusion and flow matching models start from a noise image of the same size as the output (or its compressed representation) and transform it gradually. Many diffusion samplers additionally inject fresh noise at every step.
Sequential sampling: Autoregressive models predict a probability distribution over the next pixel or token, sample from it, and repeat. There is no single explicit latent vector.

We will see these mechanisms in more detail in the next lecture.








NoteLatent Variables Intuition





Consider the dataset shown in Figure 22: What could be latent variables for this dataset?


Click for result

Each output is defined by its width and height. Therefore, we have two (unobserved) latent variables.










Figure 22: A dataset of cylinders. Reproduced from Foster (2023).



Figure 23 shows a plausible latent space and the mapping \(g\) from a point in that space to a sample.






Figure 23: A 2D latent space for the cylinder dataset: \(z_1\) controls the width, \(z_2\) the height. Filled cylinders are training examples, dashed ones do not occur in the training data. The generator \(g\) maps any latent point \(\mathbf{z}\), also one without a training example, to a cylinder. Reproduced from Foster (2023), with the notation adapted to this lecture.



This example is deliberately simple: the latent space is two-dimensional and each axis has a clear meaning. Latent spaces of real image generators are high-dimensional, and their individual dimensions usually do not correspond to human-interpretable properties such as pose or time of day.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
3 Controlling Generation
Generative models differ in what information is given to them. Sometimes we want the model to generate freely, for example any plausible face, room, or product image. This is called unconditional generation: the random input is the only input of the model, and different samples of \(\mathbf{z}\) produce different plausible outputs.
\[
\hat{\mathbf{x}} = g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})
\]
More often, especially in computer vision applications, we want the model to generate under constraints, such as a class label, a text prompt, an input image, a mask, or a reference image. In conditional generation, the model additionally receives this conditioning information \(\mathbf{c}\):
\[
\hat{\mathbf{x}} = g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{c})
\]
The class label \(\mathbf{y}\) of our elephant example is one such condition. In general, the condition \(\mathbf{c}\) specifies what should be generated, preserved, completed, enhanced, or changed. In probabilistic terms, an unconditional model learns to sample from \(p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\), while a conditional model learns to sample from \(p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{c})\).






NoteNotation



In the following, we use \(\mathbf{z}\) as a shorthand for all random inputs of the model, whichever of the mechanisms discussed above is used. We often write \(g()\) to simplify notation.





























Figure 24: Unconditional vs. conditional generation. The top row shows random samples of people, while the bottom row shows samples of people conditioned on the prompt “young person with glasses and curly hair.”









NoteDiscussion



Looking at Figure 24, what do you notice? The images were generated with ChatGPT’s image generation model.


As a result, generative computer vision is much broader than text-to-image generation: models can create, edit, complete, enhance, translate, or animate visual data (see Table 2).

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
4 How Generative Models Learn
How do we train a model to produce data that looks like real data? We assume that the training images \(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathbf{x}^{(N)}\) are samples from an unknown data distribution \(p_{\text{data}}(\mathbf{x})\). The goal of a generative model is to learn a model distribution \(p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\) that approximates it:
\[
p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \approx p_{\text{data}}(\mathbf{x})
\tag{2}\]
Some models define \(p_{\theta}\) explicitly as a formula that can be evaluated. Others define it only implicitly, through their sampling procedure.






NoteProbability densities



Images take (approximately) continuous values, so \(p_{\text{data}}\) and \(p_{\theta}\) are probability density functions over the image space \(\mathcal{X}\), for example \(\mathcal{X} = \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}\). A density \(p: \mathcal{X} \to [0, \infty)\) must integrate to one:
\[
\int_{\mathcal{X}} p(\mathbf{x}) \, d\mathbf{x} = 1
\]
In contrast to a probability mass (e.g. the class probabilities of a classifier), a density value is not a probability: it can be larger than 1, and the probability of observing one exact image is zero. Only regions of \(\mathcal{X}\) have a probability. Intuitively, a high density at \(\mathbf{x}\) means that images in the neighbourhood of \(\mathbf{x}\) are likely.


What does such a density look like for images? Since images are high-dimensional, we cannot plot \(p_{\text{data}}\) directly. Figure 25 illustrates the idea in 1D: the x axis is a path through image space, from a real 0 to a real 7. Near the two modes, the images are plausible digits. Between the modes, they are blends that are neither a 0 nor a 7: such images lie in a region of low density, and a good generative model should rarely produce them.






Figure 25: Illustration of a density along a path through image space. Each position corresponds to a pixel-wise blend of two MNIST digits. Real digits lie at the modes (green), mixtures of both digits between them (red). The density is illustrative and not computed from the images.



What does Equation 2 mean in practice? First, generated samples should be realistic: they should lie in regions where \(p_{\text{data}}\) has a high density. Figure 26 illustrates the principle with the path from Figure 25: Models should aim to synthesize samples which are probable under the true distribution.






Figure 26: Plausible and improbable generated samples. Shown is the true distribution (blue) along the path from Figure 25. Green dots are plausible samples near the modes. Red crosses are improbable samples in regions of low density: a blend of both digits between the modes, and noisy digits, which do not occur in the training data, in the tails.



Realistic samples alone, however, are not enough. A model that always produces the same, most typical image, generates only realistic samples, but it has not learned the distribution. Generated samples should also cover all regions where real data occurs, in the right proportions. A good generative model represents the full distribution, not merely individual high-density samples.






NoteKey concepts: fidelity and coverage




Fidelity: generated samples lie in regions where \(p_{\text{data}}\) has a high density, i.e. they look like real data.
Coverage: generated samples occur in all regions where \(p_{\text{data}}\) has a high density, in the right proportions, i.e. the model generates the full variety of the real data.

A good generative model needs both. In Section 6.3.2, we measure them with two metrics: precision (fidelity) and recall (coverage).


Figure 27 illustrates the two aspects with a simple 1D example.






Figure 27: Fidelity vs. coverage for a bimodal target distribution (blue). (a) The model concentrates on one mode: its samples are realistic, but the left mode is never generated. (b) A single Gaussian, fitted by maximum likelihood, covers both modes but generates many samples in between. (c) A model close to the target achieves both.




4.1 Maximum Likelihood
How can we make \(p_{\theta}\) similar to \(p_{\text{data}}\) if we only have samples from \(p_{\text{data}}\)? A classic approach is maximum likelihood estimation: we choose the parameters \(\theta\) such that the training data is as likely as possible under the model:
\[
\theta^{*} = \underset{\theta}{\arg\max} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})
\tag{3}\]
It can be shown that, for a large number of training samples, this is equivalent to minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\text{data}} \,\|\, p_{\theta})\), a measure of the difference between the two distributions. Maximum likelihood strongly penalizes a model that assigns a low density to any real training example, which encourages coverage. It requires, however, that \(p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\) can be evaluated (or at least bounded) for a given image.
Figure 28 illustrates how the modelled distribution improves by increasing the likelihood of observing the training data.






Figure 28: Maximum likelihood in 1D. A mixture of two Gaussians (orange) is fitted to training samples (blue). (a) The initial model assigns a low density to many training examples. (b) After fitting by maximum likelihood, the model places its density where the training data lies, and the average log-likelihood increases.



Note: Evaluating a density and sampling from it are different capabilities. A model that can evaluate \(p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\) is useful on its own, for example to detect outliers, but it still needs a mechanism to generate samples. Conversely, some models can generate samples but cannot evaluate \(p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\).


4.2 Interactive Demo: Learning a 1D Distribution
The following demo lets you play the role of a generative model. The target distribution (blue) is fixed. You choose the parameters of a generator, draw samples, and compare them with the target. The button Fit by maximum likelihood fits the generator to 1,000 training samples drawn from the target. The displayed fidelity and coverage are simple versions of precision and recall, two metrics we will meet again in Section 6.3.2.







NoteExplore the demo

With a single Gaussian, press Fit by maximum likelihood. Where does the fitted Gaussian lie, and why?
Choose the preset Mode collapse. Every generated sample looks realistic. Is this a good generative model?
Increase the number of samples to 10,000. What changes, and what does not?
Switch to the mixture of two Gaussians and fit it again. Compare its log-likelihood with that of the target itself.



Click for possible answers

Between the two modes, with a large standard deviation (mean ≈ 5, standard deviation ≈ 2.6). Maximum likelihood strongly penalizes training samples with a low density, so the fitted Gaussian must cover both modes. Coverage is high, fidelity is low.
No. Realistic individual samples do not make a good generative model: the left mode is never generated. The very low log-likelihood shows this, since the model assigns almost no density to a large part of the real data.
The histogram approaches the generator’s density, and fidelity fluctuates less between seeds. The generator itself does not change: more samples cannot compensate for a model that is too simple to represent the target.
The mixture recovers both modes: fidelity and coverage are close to the maximum of about 95%, and its log-likelihood is close to that of the target. Model capacity, not the number of samples, was the limitation.





The demo illustrates two typical failures. A model that is too simple cannot represent the target: it either misses a mode (low coverage) or generates many samples between the modes (low fidelity). A mode-collapsed model generates realistic samples, but only of part of the data (low coverage). In Section 6, we detect the same failures for images, whose distributions we cannot plot, with precision and recall.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
5 Properties and Trade-offs
Maximum likelihood is an important principle, but it is not the only one. Generative model families differ in how they are trained and in how they produce samples; we discuss them in the next lecture (Generative Model Families). These families make different trade-offs with respect to the following properties. Unfortunately, no single model family excels at all of them, although modern models narrow some of the gaps.

5.1 Efficient Sampling
Applications such as interactive tools, real-time graphics, or large-scale dataset creation require that new samples can be generated quickly. Figure 29 compares how many network evaluations the model families typically need for one sample. GANs and VAEs generate a sample in a single forward pass, diffusion and flow matching models typically need tens of steps, and autoregressive models one step per token. Modern variants reduce diffusion sampling to a few or even a single step through distillation (Salimans and Ho 2022; Song et al. 2023).






Figure 29: Typical number of network evaluations per generated sample (log scale). The numbers are orders of magnitude, not benchmarks: the cost of a single evaluation differs between architectures, and autoregressive models need one step per token (here for 16x16 to 64x64 tokens).





5.2 Fidelity and Coverage
A good generative model needs both fidelity and coverage, as introduced in Section 4. Figure 30 shows the two typical failures on a 2D toy dataset. A model with low fidelity covers all modes, but it also generates many samples between them, i.e. unrealistic samples. VAEs, for example, tend to cover all training data at the cost of sample quality (blurry images). A model with low coverage generates realistic samples, but only of a few modes of the data. This failure is called mode collapse and is a well-known problem of GANs. Likelihood-based models, in contrast, are encouraged by their objective to cover all training data. Diffusion models also tend to have good coverage.






Figure 30: Fidelity and coverage on a 2D toy dataset with 8 modes. (a) Training data. (b) A good model generates realistic samples of all modes. (c) A model with low fidelity covers all modes, but generates many samples between them. (d) A model with low coverage (mode collapse) generates realistic samples, but only of 2 modes.



Notably, the two properties are often in tension: techniques that increase fidelity tend to reduce coverage. A prominent example is guidance in diffusion models (Ho and Salimans 2022): it concentrates the samples on the most typical regions of a class. In terms of Figure 30, a strong guidance moves a model from (c) towards (d): the samples become more realistic, but less diverse.


5.3 Latent-Space Structure and Controllability
For models with an explicit latent space, such as VAEs and GANs, the structure of this space determines how well outputs can be explored and edited. Ideally, the latent space is smooth: similar latent vectors produce similar outputs, and interpolating between two latent vectors yields a gradual transition between the outputs1 (see Figure 31). VAEs explicitly encourage this through their training objective, and GANs such as StyleGAN also exhibit smooth latent spaces (Karras et al. 2019).






Figure 31: Decoded images of a regular grid of latent vectors of a VAE with a 2D latent space, trained on MNIST for this lecture (see demos/genai/genai_intro_figures.ipynb), following the visualization in Kingma and Welling (2014). Neighboring latent vectors produce similar digits, and moving through the latent space gradually morphs one digit into another.



Beyond smoothness, a latent space can be disentangled: each dimension controls one independent factor of variation, such as pose or lighting. Figure 32 illustrates this with the cylinder dataset from Figure 22. It has been shown, however, that unsupervised disentanglement is fundamentally impossible without inductive biases in the model or the data (Locatello et al. 2019).






Figure 32: Disentangled vs. entangled latent space, illustrated with a synthetic decoder that maps a 2D latent vector to a cylinder. (a) \(z_1\) only controls the width, \(z_2\) only the height. (b) \(z_1\) controls the overall size, \(z_2\) the aspect ratio: each latent dimension changes both width and height, the factors of variation are mixed. Both latent spaces can represent all cylinders.



Disentanglement is attractive for interpretability, but it is not required for controllable generation. Modern models achieve control primarily through conditioning, i.e. through text prompts, reference images, masks, or structural inputs such as edge or depth maps (see Section 3), rather than by manipulating individual latent dimensions.


5.4 Likelihood Computation
Some models can evaluate \(p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\) for any given input \(\mathbf{x}\) (see Figure 33). This enables training by maximum likelihood, the detection of outliers, and the comparison of models on test data. Autoregressive models and normalizing flows compute the likelihood exactly, VAEs, diffusion and flow matching models provide a lower bound or a computationally expensive estimate, and GANs provide none. Note that a high likelihood does not imply high-quality samples (see Section 6.1).





A model with an explicit density assigns a log-likelihood to any input: the typical point has a high, the outlier a very low value. (b) An implicit model such as a GAN only generates samples; it cannot tell how likely a given input is.



Figure 33

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
6 Evaluating Generative Models
Evaluating generative models is difficult because there is usually no single correct output. For a given prompt, label, mask, or input image, many different outputs may be valid.
A useful evaluation question is therefore not simply:

Is the generated image correct?

but rather:

Are the generated images realistic and varied, do they follow the condition, and are they useful?

Different evaluation methods answer different parts of this question. Table 3 maps typical evaluation questions to suitable methods, which we discuss in the following.



Table 3: Evaluation questions and suitable methods.









Evaluation question
Suitable methods




Do samples resemble real data? (fidelity)
precision, FID, KID, CMMD, human judgement


Does the model cover the variety of real data? (coverage)
recall, class or mode coverage, FID, KID, CMMD


Does the model assign a high density to real data?
test-set log-likelihood, if available


Does the output follow the prompt?
human judgement, CLIP-based alignment


Which model do people prefer?
blind pairwise comparison, preference leaderboards


Does an edit preserve the original content?
similarity of unchanged regions, human judgement


Are synthetic images useful for training?
downstream performance on real test data







6.1 Likelihood
For models with an explicit density, the average log-likelihood of \(N\) held-out test images measures how well the model covers real data:
\[
\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})
\]
Many models, such as GANs, do not provide it. Moreover, it has been shown that likelihood and sample quality are largely independent: a model can achieve a high likelihood while generating poor samples, and vice versa (Theis et al. 2016). Likelihood therefore does not tell us whether generated samples look good or follow a prompt.


6.2 Human Evaluation
A direct but expensive approach is to ask humans to compare generated images. Typical questions are:

Which image looks more realistic?
Which image better matches the prompt?
Which image has fewer artifacts?
Which image would you prefer to use?

Human studies are often the most meaningful evaluation for visual quality, but they are slow, subjective, and difficult to use during model development.

6.2.1 Human Preference Benchmarks
An increasingly popular form of human evaluation is blind pairwise comparison. Given the same text prompt, two models generate images that are shown side by side without revealing which model produced which. Human evaluators select the image they prefer. Aggregating many such judgements makes it possible to rank models with a statistical preference model, such as the Bradley–Terry model, often reported on an Elo-like scale. Examples of public leaderboards are the Arena text-to-image leaderboard and the Artificial Analysis image arena.
In contrast to distribution-level metrics such as FID, these benchmarks directly capture human preferences. However, preference is subjective: it can reflect aesthetic appeal rather than faithfulness, coverage, or usefulness for a downstream task.






NoteDiscussion



If humans consistently prefer images from model A over model B, does this imply that model A is the better generative model? In which applications might this conclusion be misleading?


Click for possible answer

Not necessarily. Preference benchmarks rate individual, mostly creative images for a given prompt. They reward aesthetic appeal and prompt following, but they do not measure coverage: a model that always generates the same polished style can win many comparisons. The conclusion can be misleading wherever faithfulness matters more than appeal, for example in super-resolution, medical image translation, or synthetic training data, where a less pleasing but faithful or diverse output is more useful.






6.3 Distribution-Level Metrics
Many automatic metrics compare the distribution of generated images with the distribution of real images. Since distances between raw pixels say little about image content, the images are first mapped to feature vectors with a pretrained network.

6.3.1 Fréchet Inception Distance (FID)
The most widely used metric is the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) (Heusel et al. 2018). It is computed in three steps (see Figure 34):

Real and generated images are mapped to 2048-dimensional feature vectors with a pretrained Inception network.
A Gaussian is fitted to each set of feature vectors: mean \(\mathbf{\mu}_r\) and covariance \(\mathbf{\Sigma}_r\) for the real, \(\mathbf{\mu}_g\) and \(\mathbf{\Sigma}_g\) for the generated images.
The Fréchet distance between the two Gaussians is computed:

\[
\text{FID} = \underbrace{\lVert \mathbf{\mu}_r - \mathbf{\mu}_g \rVert^2}_{\text{mean term}} + \underbrace{\operatorname{tr}\big(\mathbf{\Sigma}_r + \mathbf{\Sigma}_g - 2 (\mathbf{\Sigma}_r \mathbf{\Sigma}_g)^{1/2}\big)}_{\text{covariance term}}
\tag{4}\]
The mean term measures how far apart the centres of the two feature clouds are, the covariance term compares their spread and shape. FID is zero for identical Gaussians: the lower, the better.






Figure 34: FID. Top: computation pipeline. Bottom: real (blue) vs. generated (orange) features, shown in 2D instead of 2048-d.



Figure 34 demonstrates that FID reacts to a lack of fidelity (a, shifted features) as well as to a lack of coverage (b, only one cluster is generated). Notably, both failures result in a similar FID: a single number does not reveal which of the two is the problem. Further limitations:

it assumes that the features follow a Gaussian distribution (in Figure 34, three clusters are summarized by a single Gaussian)
its value depends on the number of samples, so FIDs are only comparable for a fixed sample size (Bińkowski et al. 2021)
the Inception features were trained on ImageNet and may be poorly suited to other domains, such as medical images, or to the rich content of modern text-to-image models (Jayasumana et al. 2024)







NoteAdditional metrics: KID and CMMD





Kernel Inception Distance (KID) (Bińkowski et al. 2021) compares the same features without the Gaussian assumption, using a kernel-based distance (maximum mean discrepancy, MMD). It is unbiased and thus more reliable for small sample sizes. CMMD (Jayasumana et al. 2024) follows the same idea but replaces the Inception features with CLIP embeddings (Radford et al. 2021). Its authors show that it agrees better with human judgement of modern text-to-image models than FID.









NoteHistorical note: Inception Score (IS)





Before FID, the Inception Score (IS) (Salimans et al. 2016) was the standard metric. The idea is that good generated images should be classified confidently by a pretrained Inception classifier, while the full set of generated images should cover many classes (see Figure 35).






Figure 35: Evaluating generative AI models using a classifier-based score.



Its main limitations:

it does not compare generated images to real images
it is most meaningful for class-balanced datasets such as ImageNet
it does not detect a lack of coverage within a class (e.g. always generating the same elephant)






6.3.2 Precision and Recall
To measure fidelity and coverage separately, Kynkäänniemi et al. (2019) define precision and recall for generative models. Both compare the real and the generated feature vectors. The region covered by each set (its manifold) is approximated by placing a ball around every feature vector, with a radius that reaches to its \(k\)-th nearest neighbour within the same set.



Table 4: Precision and recall for generative models.










Concept
Metric
Definition




fidelity
precision
fraction of generated samples that lie within the manifold of the real data


coverage
recall
fraction of real samples that lie within the manifold of the generated data






The fidelity and coverage values in the demo of Section 4 are simple versions of these two metrics. In Figure 27, model (a) achieves a high precision but a low recall, while model (b) achieves a high recall but a lower precision. Likewise, the mode-collapsed model in Figure 34 (b) achieves a high precision but a low recall, which FID alone cannot distinguish from a lack of fidelity.
The following demo lets you compare FID, precision and recall directly. The real features (blue) are fixed; you change the generator and observe which metric reacts.







NoteExplore the demo






Compare the presets Shifted and Mode collapse. Both have a high FID. How do precision and recall tell the two failures apart?
Choose Too narrow. What happens to FID, and what to recall? Why?
With Good model, reduce the number of samples to 50 and change the seed a few times. What happens to FID?
Show the balls around the real points and choose Too broad. Which generated points count against precision?



Click for possible answers


Shifted has a low precision: many generated points lie outside the real manifold (low fidelity). Mode collapse has a high precision but a low recall: every generated point is realistic, but two of three clusters are missing (low coverage).
FID stays close to zero, but recall drops clearly. FID summarizes each set by a single Gaussian, which is dominated by the distances between the three clusters, so narrower clusters hardly change it. Precision and recall compare the sets locally and detect the missing variation.
FID fluctuates and stays above zero, although the generator is perfect. FID is biased for small sample sizes, which is why FIDs are only comparable for a fixed number of samples.
The hollow orange points: they lie outside all balls around real points, i.e. in regions without real data.





Like all distribution-level metrics, precision and recall summarize a whole set of images. A model can achieve good average scores while still failing on rare classes, spatial relations, text rendering, or fine-grained details.



6.4 Conditional and Task-Specific Evaluation
For conditional generation, realism alone is not enough: the output also has to follow the condition and serve its purpose.






NoteDiscussion



Which of the tasks from Section 3 require the model to be creative, and which require the model to be faithful to a given input?


Click for possible answer

Unconditional image generation and text-to-image generation often emphasize creative variety, although they still need to produce plausible images.
Tasks such as inpainting, super-resolution, image translation, and image editing require the output to be faithful to the input. The model should generate new visual content, but it should also preserve important information from the condition, such as identity, geometry, anatomy, layout, or product appearance.



The evaluation should therefore match the intended use case (see Table 5).



Table 5: Evaluation of conditional and task-specific generation.










Task
What should be evaluated?
Possible methods




text-to-image
Does the image match the prompt?
CLIP-based scores, human judgement


image editing, inpainting
Was the requested change made plausibly, and is the rest preserved?
similarity of unchanged regions, human judgement


super-resolution
Are details realistic and faithful to the input?
perceptual quality, reconstruction metrics (e.g. PSNR, SSIM)


medical image translation
Is the target domain reached while preserving anatomy?
expert review, downstream diagnosis


reference-based generation
Is the identity of the product or person preserved?
preservation of identity and geometry


synthetic training data
Does it improve the downstream model?
performance on real validation/test data






For text-to-image models, prompt alignment is often measured using vision-language models such as CLIP, for example with CLIPScore: the cosine similarity between the CLIP embeddings of the image and the prompt (Hessel et al. 2022). CLIP-based scores capture the overall semantic agreement well, but they are unreliable for compositional details: CLIP often behaves like a bag of words and is largely insensitive to word order, attribute binding (“a red cube and a blue sphere”) and relations between objects (Yuksekgonul et al. 2023).






Figure 36: Evaluation of conditional generation.



Task-specific evaluation is particularly important for scientific, medical, and industrial applications. A generated image can look realistic but still be scientifically or semantically wrong.






WarningPlausible is not the same as faithful



In super-resolution, the information lost by downsampling cannot be recovered. A generative model fills in details that are plausible given the low-resolution input, but not necessarily the details that were actually there. Notably, there is a fundamental trade-off: beyond a certain point, improving perceptual quality necessarily increases the deviation from the true image (distortion), and vice versa (Blau and Michaeli 2018).
For creative applications, plausible details are often all we need. For medical or scientific images, such as synthetic CT scans generated from MRI (Figure 8), hallucinated structures can be harmful. Here, faithfulness to the ground truth and validation by domain experts are essential.


In summary, there is no single best metric for generative models. A good evaluation starts from the evaluation question (Table 3) and combines several perspectives: distribution-level metrics for benchmarking, precision and recall to separate fidelity from coverage, and task-specific checks of whether the output is faithful to the condition.

title: 3 - CNNs
text:
TipLearning Objectives





After this lecture you should be able to:

Explain why MLPs are a poor fit for image data.
Describe the three key CNN principles: local connectivity, parameter sharing, and translation equivariance.
Distinguish invariance from equivariance and relate each to specific vision tasks.
Explain how convolutions operate and how they can be parameterized (kernel size, stride, padding, dilation).

title: 3 - CNNs
text:
1 Why CNNs Work for Images
Images have unique properties that make them challenging for standard neural networks:

High-Dimensional: An RGB image of size \(224 \times 224\) has \(224 \times 224 \times 3 = 150{,}528\) values
Locality: Nearby pixels are statistically related (edges, textures, objects)
Stability under transformations: Interpretation of an image does not change under many geometric transformations. A cat should be recognized regardless of its position in the image.
Hierarchical Structure: Images contain features at multiple scales (pixels → edges → textures → objects)







Figure 1: A high-resolution photograph (left) with three regions (sky, cow, grass), each marked with boxes of \(12 \times 12\), \(48 \times 48\) and \(192 \times 192\) pixels. The crops (right) show the image content at these three scales: within the small boxes neighboring pixels have almost the same color, at the medium scale pixels form textures and parts (cloud edge, fur, flowers), and only the large boxes contain whole objects. Image Source









NoteQuestion: How are nearby pixels related?



Looking at Figure 1, can you explain how nearby pixels are related?
Think about it: What visual patterns or structures do you notice?


Click for answer

Nearby pixels in images are strongly correlated due to:

Object Coherence: Objects occupy contiguous regions. Pixels within an object (like a cow’s body) share similar colors and textures
Smooth Transitions: Natural images have gradual changes in color and intensity, not abrupt random variations
Texture Patterns: Repeating structures (like grass or fur) create local statistical patterns
Edges and Boundaries: Sharp transitions occur at object boundaries, but even edges span multiple neighboring pixels




Even though Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are much better suited to model images than Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), we start by investigating the properties and difficulties of modeling images with MLPs. This will help understand how properties embedded in the architecture of CNNs (inductive biases) make them much more suitable for computer vision tasks.

1.1 MLPs and Images
The input to an MLP is a vector \(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\), which is transformed through multiple hidden layers to the output layer. The fully connected layers can only process 1-D vectors. Therefore, images \(\in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}\) must be flattened into 1-D vectors \(\in \mathbb{R}^p\), where \(p= H \times W \times C\). This causes MLPs to become very large when applied to high-dimensional inputs such as images. See Figure 2 for an illustration.






Figure 2: Illustration of an MLP applied to an image.



In the CIFAR-10 dataset, which consists of very small images of \(\in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 32 \times 32}\), a single neuron in the first hidden layer already has \(3 \times 32 \times 32 = 3{,}072\) weights to learn (see Figure 3). For larger images, the number of weights is correspondingly much larger.






Figure 3: Source: Johnson (2019)



Since each neuron in the first hidden layer is connected to each input value and each connection has a specific weight, the weights of individual neurons (columns of \(\mathbf{W}\)) can be reshaped to the image dimensionality and thus be visualized. This reveals the patterns a specific neuron is reacting to. See Figure 4 for an illustration.






Figure 4: Illustration of weight matrix \(\mathbf{W}\) and how the weights of a single neuron can be reshaped into the input image dimensionality.



Often the patterns we want to learn are not stationary. Ideally we want to recognize them under translations of the inputs, e.g., \(g(\mathbf{x})\) where \(g()\) is a spatial translation. Figure 5 illustrates the problem, where the same pattern appears at different spatial positions.






Figure 5: Illustration of different inputs with the same pattern but shifted spatially. Illustrated are the weights of the first neuron. Green cells represent high weight values and yellow cells represent low values.









NoteQuestion: Patterns at different locations



Can an MLP learn to detect the same pattern at different spatial locations? If yes, how? See Figure 5.
Think about it: If an MLP learns to detect a cat in the center of an image, what happens when the same cat appears in the corner?


Click for answer

MLPs must learn separate detectors for each possible position! This is extremely inefficient because:

Parameter explosion: Need different weights for each spatial location
Data requirements: Must see target pattern in every possible position during training
Poor generalization: Fails on positions not seen during training

This is why MLPs with the same number of parameters perform much worse on image tasks compared to CNNs.



To summarize, MLPs have three fundamental limitations on images:

High-Dimensional: The size of an MLP scales with the input dimensionality, which may exceed memory and compute budgets.
No Locality: MLPs have no notion of locality and thus cannot exploit the inherent spatial structure of natural images.
No Stability under Translations: MLPs need to learn position-dependent patterns, which is very inefficient.







TipTry MLPs on images in your browser.



Try to draw the same digit at different positions and observe what happens!

MLP Demo

The demo at the end of this lecture (Section 3) compares an MLP and two CNNs on digits that are shifted away from their training position.




1.2 Invariance and Equivariance
For many tasks involving image data, small variations in the input (\(\mathbf{x}\)) should either not change the model output (\(f(\mathbf{x})\)), invariance, or should change the output in tandem with the input changes, equivariance.
A function \(f(\mathbf{x})\) is invariant to transformation \(g(\mathbf{x})\) if: \[f(g(\mathbf{x})) = f(\mathbf{x})\]
A function \(f(\mathbf{x})\) is equivariant to transformation \(g(\mathbf{x})\) if: \[f(g(\mathbf{x})) = g(f(\mathbf{x}))\]






ImportantIntuition




Invariant = “I don’t care about the transformation”
Equivariant = “I transform my output the same way the input was transformed”



Figure 6 shows an example of image classification. The scene is the same across all four panels, but each one applies a different type of perturbation: a spatial shift, a color change, or a rotation. The classifier should still produce the same label (“cow”) in every case — it should be invariant to these nuisance transformations.











(a) Original











(b) Translated













(c) Color-jittered











(d) Rotated







Figure 6: The same scene under four different input perturbations. A classifier that is invariant to these transformations produces the same label (“cow”) for all four panels. Invariance is not restricted to translation — we usually also want invariance to color/lighting changes and small rotations.



Figure 7 shows the analogous situation for object detection. The bounding boxes translate together with the cows — this is translation equivariance.











(a) Original











(b) Shifted right













(c) Shifted left











(d) Shifted up + right







Figure 7: Each panel shows the detector’s output on the same scene under a different translation. The bounding boxes move with the cows — the model \(f(\mathbf{x})\) is equivariant with respect to spatial translations.



We can summarize the required properties for different tasks:








Task Type
Property Needed
Why?




Classification
Translation Invariance
A cat is still a cat regardless of position


Object Detection
Translation Equivariance
If the object moves right, the bounding box moves right


Semantic Segmentation
Translation Equivariance
If the input shifts, pixel-wise labels shift





1.3 The CNN Idea
Now that we have seen the limitations of MLPs for images, let’s explore how Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) address these challenges.






TipThe Big Idea



Instead of connecting every neuron to every input, CNNs use three key principles:

Local Connectivity: Each neuron only looks at a small spatial region
Parameter Sharing: The same filter/detector is used across all spatial locations
Translation Equivariance: If the input shifts, the output shifts correspondingly

These are not just technical tricks: they encode our prior knowledge about how images work!


A single neuron in a CNN is only connected to a small portion of the image (local connectivity), as illustrated in Figure 8. As a result, CNNs have far fewer parameters than MLPs, preserve the spatial structure of images, and can detect the same feature anywhere in the image.






Figure 8: Source: Johnson (2019)





1.4 Inductive Bias
The concept of inductive bias refers to the assumptions a learning algorithm makes to generalize from training data to unseen data. MLPs have minimal inductive bias, they are very general, but require large amounts of training data. CNNs have strong inductive biases: they assume locality and translation equivariance, which makes learning on images vastly more efficient.
The right inductive bias for the data at hand is key to success. This is why CNNs excel at images (spatial locality matters), Transformers excel at sequences (long-range dependencies matter), and Graph Neural Networks excel at networks (graph structure matters). Choosing an architecture means choosing which assumptions to bake in.

title: 3 - CNNs
text:
2 How CNNs Work
CNNs consist of a sequence of different layers. Each layer transforms activations from the previous layer into new activations through a differentiable operation. Figure 9 shows an example architecture with the activation maps of the various layers.






Figure 9: The activations of a ConvNet architecture. The input image is on the left and the predictions on the right. Source: Li (2022).




2.1 Convolution Operation
Convolutional layers are the primary layers in CNNs, responsible for extracting visual features. Each filter is typically small along the spatial dimensions (height, width) relative to the input but extends across the entire input depth. During the forward pass, the filters are convolved along the height and width over the input. At each position, the dot product between the filter and input is calculated, producing a 2-D activation map that represents the filter’s response at each position. Intuitively, the CNN learns filters corresponding to typical visual patterns, such as edges and colors, in the first layer.






TipTrain a CNN for image classification in your browser!



CNN Explainer








ImportantFilters vs Kernels



Filter and kernel are sometimes used synonymously. Here, we differentiate by considering a filter as 3-dimensional (\(C \times H \times W\)) and a kernel as 2-dimensional (\(H \times W\)). A filter consists of \(C\) kernels.


The convolution operation is defined as:
\[
S(i, j) = (K * I)(i, j) =\sum_m\sum_n I(i + m, j + n)K(m, n)
\tag{1}\]
where \(I\) is the input, \(K\) is the kernel (typically smaller than \(I\)), and \(i\), \(j\) index the spatial positions.






Note



Convolution in deep learning is typically implemented as cross-correlation. Equation 1 actually defines cross-correlation.


Figure 10 illustrates convolution on an RGB image. The filter is multiplied element-wise with the corresponding values in the image, and the result is summed to produce one single value in the output.






Source: Prince (2023)




Figure 10: An RGB image with \(C_{in}=3\) channels. A filter with dimensionality \(3 \times 3 \times 3\) is multiplied elementwise with the corresponding input volume and then summed to produce one value in the output activation map. Source: Prince (2023)



Figure 11 illustrates how a single filter is applied: at each spatial position, the filter is placed over the corresponding input patch, the element-wise product is summed, the bias is added, and the result becomes one value in the output activation map. Sliding the filter across all positions fills in the full map.






Figure 11: A \(3 \times 3\) filter is applied at three successive positions of a \(5 \times 5\) input. Each position yields one value in the output activation map via \(\sum (\text{patch} \odot \text{kernel}) + b\).



The following demo illustrates this computation interactively. Draw an input image, choose one of the preset filters or edit the weights directly, and observe how the output activation map changes. Hovering over a cell in the output highlights the corresponding input patch and displays the calculation. Note that the filter weights are specified manually here, whereas a CNN learns them from data.






Tip🎮 Interactive Demo: Convolution with Manually Specified Filters




The demo applies a single \(3 \times 3\) kernel to a \(28 \times 28\) grayscale input with stride 1 and zero-padding (see Equation 1), without a bias term. Open the demo in a new tab or view the source code.


For RGB inputs (or any input with multiple channels), the filter has a matching depth: a \(3 \times 3\) filter on a 3-channel input is actually a \(3 \times 3 \times 3\) volume. Each slice is applied to the corresponding input channel, and the per-channel sums are added together with a single bias term, producing one scalar per spatial position. This is shown in Figure 12.






Figure 12: Multi-channel convolution at a single spatial position. Each channel’s \(3 \times 3\) filter slice is multiplied element-wise with its input channel; the three per-channel sums plus the bias collapse to one output value.



A convolutional layer typically contains several filters, each with its own weights and bias. Each filter produces one activation map, and stacking these maps along the channel axis yields an output volume with \(C_\text{out}\) channels — effectively a multi-channel image. Figure 13 illustrates this for four filters. In practice, data is processed in mini-batches of \(N\) images at once, so the convolution operates on a 4-D input tensor of shape \(N \times C_\text{in} \times H \times W\) and returns a 4-D output of shape \(N \times C_\text{out} \times H' \times W'\).






Figure 13: Four filters, each with its own weights and bias, are applied to the same input volume. The four resulting activation maps are stacked along the channel axis to form the output volume with \(C_\text{out}=4\) channels.





2.2 Translation Equivariance
Because the same filter is applied at every spatial position (parameter sharing), convolutions are naturally translation equivariant. The following video illustrates this property:






Figure 14: Illustration of translation equivariance in convolutional layers.



See Section 1.2 for the distinction between equivariance and invariance. Notably, CNNs need additional components (like pooling or global average pooling) to achieve translation invariance for classification tasks.
The demo in Section 3 at the end of this lecture tests this property on trained networks.
But what about other transformations, such as rotation, zoom, or brightness changes? Convolutions provide no guarantee for these: any robustness has to be learned from the training data, typically with data augmentation. The lecture on Image Classification discusses data augmentation and contains an interactive demo that tests how stable a pretrained CNN is under such transformations.


2.3 Padding, Stride, Kernel Size, Dilation
To define a convolution, various hyperparameters need to be set.
Stride determines the step size with which filters are moved over the input activations. If the stride is 1, the filter moves one pixel at a time (Figure 15). If the stride is greater, e.g., 2, it moves two pixels at a time, making the activation maps smaller (Figure 16).






Figure 15: Convolution with stride (1, 1). Left: input activations with the individual positions of the center pixel (red).









Figure 16: Convolution with stride (2, 2).









TipStride > 1 is commonly used



Convolutions with stride provide a way to reduce the spatial dimensionality within a CNN. The downsampling is learned, which can be advantageous over fixed operations like pooling.


Padding refers to adding values (often zeros) to the border of the input activations before performing the convolution. This can be useful to ensure that the spatial dimensions of the output match those of the input — essential for segmentation tasks. Figure 17 illustrates how padding helps maintain spatial resolution.






Figure 17: Left: Input (yellow) with zero-padding (white border), Middle: Filter, Right: Output.



Kernel size determines the spatial extent from which a value in the output activation map aggregates values. Figure 18 and Figure 19 show convolutions with different kernel sizes. Kernels usually have an odd number of pixels to ensure they have a center pixel. The number of parameters increases with kernel size.






Figure 18: Convolution with zero-padding and \(3 \times 3\) kernel that produces activation maps with unchanged spatial resolution.









Figure 19: Convolution with zero-padding and \(5 \times 5\) kernel that produces activation maps with unchanged spatial resolution.









TipBest Practice



Modern CNN Design: Use multiple 3×3 convolutions instead of larger kernels. This yields fewer parameters, more non-linearity (more activation functions between layers), and similar receptive field coverage.


Dilation specifies how much the kernel is spread out and thus directly influences the receptive field. Figure 20 illustrates how a dilated kernel is applied.






Figure 20: Illustration of how a kernel with dilation=2 (middle) is applied to the input activations (left) to produce activations (right).









Dumoulin and Visin (2016) has created animations for better understanding of convolutions: https://github.com/vdumoulin/conv_arithmetic.



Convolving a 3x3 kernel over a 5x5 input without padding and with stride 1x1. Source Dumoulin and Visin (2016)











NoteWhy Dilation?



Why would we use dilation \(d > 1\)?
Consider: What happens to the receptive field? What about computational cost?


Click for comprehensive answer

Dilation increases receptive field without adding parameters or computation!
Benefits of dilation:

Larger receptive field: See more context without more layers
Same parameter count: Filter size stays the same
Multi-scale features: Different dilation rates capture different scales

Use cases:

Semantic segmentation: Need large receptive fields while preserving spatial resolution
Dense prediction tasks: Want to see global context for local predictions
Efficient architectures: Alternative to deeper networks

Trade-offs:

✅ Larger receptive field with same parameters
❌ May miss fine-grained spatial relationships
❌ Can create “grid artifacts” if not used carefully

Example: A 3×3 kernel with dilation=2 has the receptive field of a 5×5 kernel but only 9 parameters instead of 25!
Atrous/Dilated Convolutions are especially popular in:

DeepLab (semantic segmentation)
WaveNet (audio generation)
Dilated ResNets (dense prediction)

The key insight: effectively expand the receptive field!



The following demo combines all four hyperparameters. Change kernel size, padding, stride, and dilation and observe how the size and the values of the output activation map change. Hovering over a cell in the output highlights the input cells from which it is computed, including the gaps caused by dilation, and displays the calculation.






Tip🎮 Interactive Demo: Convolution Parameters




The demo applies a single kernel to a \(9 \times 9\) grayscale input (one channel, no bias). The notation follows the formulas below: input size \(i\), output size \(o\), kernel size \(k\), padding \(p\), stride \(s\), dilation \(d\). The kernel weights are editable; changing the kernel size replaces them with the selected preset. The color scale of the output is kept fixed for comparison, press “Rescale” to adapt it to the current output. Open the demo in a new tab or view the source code.








NoteExercise: Convolution Parameters





Open the section “Exercises” below the demo and solve the tasks with the letter T as input. The demo checks your settings after every change and ticks the tasks that are solved.

Keep the size: use a \(5 \times 5\) kernel and get a \(9 \times 9\) output.
Reduce the resolution: use a \(3 \times 3\) kernel and get a \(5 \times 5\) output.
See the whole T with 9 weights: use a \(3 \times 3\) kernel such that a single output value is computed from an area covering the whole letter T (rows and columns 1 to 7).
Copy the input: make the output identical to the input.
Detect top edges only: with ReLU, get a \(9 \times 9\) output that is positive exactly at the top edge of the T and zero everywhere else.



Click for solutions


\(p = 2\), \(s = 1\), \(d = 1\): \(o = \lfloor (9 + 4 - 4 - 1)/1 + 1 \rfloor = 9\). In general, \(p = (k-1)/2\) preserves the size for \(s = d = 1\).
\(p = 1\), \(s = 2\): \(o = \lfloor (9 + 2 - 2 - 1)/2 + 1 \rfloor = 5\). Without padding, \(s = 2\) gives \(o = 4\).
Dilation \(d = 3\): the effective kernel size is \(d \cdot (k-1) + 1 = 7\), while the kernel still has only 9 weights. With \(p = 0\) and \(s = 1\) the output cell \((1, 1)\) reads rows and columns 1, 4 and 7, which span the whole T. Note that it reads only 9 of the 49 cells.
Preset “Identity” with \(p = (k-1)/2 \cdot d\), e.g. \(k = 3\), \(p = 1\) (or a \(1 \times 1\) kernel with weight 1 and \(p = 0\)).
A kernel that subtracts the cell above from the center cell, with \(p = 1\) and ReLU: \[
K = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\] The output is \(1\) where a bright cell lies below a dark one and \(\le 0\) everywhere else, which the ReLU sets to zero. The preset “Horizontal edges” does not solve the task: it compares the row above with the row below and is therefore positive in two rows: at the top edge of the T and in the dark row above it.







2.4 Calculations: Spatial Dimensionality of Activation Maps
You can calculate the dimensionality of the activation maps with the following formulas:

\(i\): Side length of the input activations (assumption: square inputs)
\(k\): Kernel size (assumption: square kernel)
\(o\): Side length of the output activation maps
\(s\): Stride (assumption: same stride along spatial dimensions)
\(p\): Number of paddings on each side (assumption: same number of paddings along spatial dimensions)
\(d\): Dilation rate.

\[\begin{equation}
o = \left\lfloor \frac{i + 2p - d\cdot(k-1) - 1}{s} + 1 \right\rfloor
\end{equation}\]







Note🧮 Quiz: Output Shape Calculation





Problem: You’re designing a CNN layer with the following parameters:

Input size: \(i = 32\) (height and width)
Kernel size: \(k = 3\)
Padding: \(p = 1\)
Stride: \(s = 2\)
Dilation: \(d = 1\)

Question: What is the output size \(o\)?


Click for step-by-step solution

Step-by-step solution:

Apply the formula: \(o = \lfloor \frac{i + 2p - d(k-1) - 1}{s} + 1 \rfloor\)
Substitute: \(o = \lfloor \frac{32 + 2(1) - 1(3-1) - 1}{2} + 1 \rfloor\)
Simplify: \(o = \lfloor \frac{32 + 2 - 2 - 1}{2} + 1 \rfloor\)
Calculate: \(o = \lfloor \frac{31}{2} + 1 \rfloor = \lfloor 15.5 + 1 \rfloor = 16\)

Answer: \(o = 16\)
Intuition: With stride 2, we’re roughly halving the spatial dimensions, but padding helps maintain some size.






2.5 Parameter Counting
The total number of parameters in a convolutional layer can be calculated as:
\[
\text{Total Weights} = (k \times k) \times C_{in} \times C_{out}
\]
Each filter has a size of \(k \times k \times C_{in}\), and there are \(C_{out}\) filters. If each output channel has a bias term, add an additional \(C_{out}\):
\[
\text{Total Parameters} = (k \times k \times C_{in} \times C_{out}) + C_{out}
\]






NoteQuiz: Parameter Counting





Scenario: A convolutional layer with:

Input: \(3 \times 32 \times 32\) (RGB image)
64 output channels
Kernel size: \(5 \times 5\)
Include bias terms

Questions:

How many weights in the filters?
How many bias parameters?
Total parameters?
If we used a fully connected layer instead, how many parameters would that require?



Click for solutions


Filter weights: \((5 \times 5) \times 3 \times 64 = 4{,}800\)
Bias parameters: \(64\) (one per output channel)
Total parameters: \(4{,}800 + 64 = 4{,}864\)
Fully connected alternative: \((32 \times 32 \times 3) \times 64 = 196{,}608\)

Insight: The CNN uses 40× fewer parameters while being more effective for images!






2.6 Stacking Convolutions and Hierarchical Features
Multiple convolutions can be executed in sequence (stacking). Each convolution is performed on the activation maps of the preceding convolution. Figure 21 illustrates the process.






Figure 21: Source: Johnson (2019)



The principle of stacking convolutional layers is important to understand. While the filters in the first convolutional layer, which directly operate on the input image, typically learn basic features such as lines in different orientations or colors, filters in subsequent layers learn more complex features by combining the features from preceding layers. This is similar to the hierarchical processing in our visual cortex. Zeiler and Fergus (2014) used a special technique to visualize patterns that filters in deeper layers are reacting to (see Figure 22).
Non-linear activation functions must be used between the convolutions. Otherwise, the stacked convolutions can be expressed as a single convolution (similar to how an MLP without activation functions reduces to a linear transformation).






Figure 22: Shown are patterns the learned filters are reacting to for several layers (in gray) and the corresponding image patches that achieve maximum activation values for these patterns. Source: Zeiler and Fergus (2014)





2.7 Receptive Field
The receptive field defines which inputs influence the activations of a neuron. If the receptive field with respect to the input image is smaller than the objects of interest, the network is unable to “see” the whole object. Figure 23 and Figure 24 illustrate the concept.






Figure 23: Receptive field with a 5×5 kernel (single layer).









Figure 24: Receptive field with a 5×5 kernel and two layers. The output activation at the center (right) aggregates values over the union of all blue boxes in the left figure and has thus a receptive field of \(9 \times 9\) with respect to the input activations.



The receptive field \(r_0\) of a CNN can be calculated with the following closed-form solution:
\[
r_0 = \sum_{l=1}^L \left( (k_l - 1) \prod_{i=1}^{l-1} s_i \right) + 1
\]
where \(L\) is the total number of layers, \(k_l\) is the kernel size at layer \(l\), and \(s_i\) is the stride at layer \(i\). See Araujo et al. (2019) for more details on the notation and derivation.
The following demo illustrates how the receptive field grows through a stack of layers. Choose kernel size and stride of each layer and select an activation in the last layer: the demo marks all activations in the preceding maps, down to the input, on which the selected activation depends.






Tip🎮 Interactive Demo: Receptive Field




All maps are drawn with the same size, so that the marked regions line up spatially; maps with fewer activations (after a stride of 2) have larger cells. Each layer uses the padding \(p_l = \lfloor k_l / 2 \rfloor\). A dashed frame indicates that the receptive field reaches into the zero-padding. With “Shade by number of paths”, activations are shaded by how many paths connect them to the selected activation: central inputs contribute through many more paths than those at the border of the receptive field. Open the demo in a new tab or view the source code.








🤔 Think About It
Using the demo, compare four layers with \(3 \times 3\) kernels and stride 1 against the same network with stride 2 in the first two layers. How does the stride change the receptive field, and what is the price?


Key considerations

With stride 1, every layer adds \(k - 1 = 2\) to the receptive field: \(r_0 = 4 \cdot 2 + 1 = 9\). A stride multiplies the contribution of all subsequent layers: with strides \((2, 2, 1, 1)\) we get \(r_0 = 2 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 4 + 2 \cdot 4 + 1 = 23\). The price is spatial resolution: the activation maps shrink from \(32 \times 32\) to \(8 \times 8\). Strides (or pooling) are therefore the main tool to obtain large receptive fields in classification networks, while dense prediction tasks often prefer dilation to keep the resolution.










NoteQuiz: Receptive Field





Network Architecture:

Layer 1: Conv2d(kernel=3, stride=1)
Layer 2: Conv2d(kernel=3, stride=2)
Layer 3: Conv2d(kernel=5, stride=1)

Question: What is the receptive field of the final layer with respect to the input?


Click for solution

Solution using the formula: \[r_0 = \sum_{l=1}^3 \left( (k_l - 1) \prod_{i=1}^{l-1} s_i \right) + 1\]

\(r_0 = (3-1) \cdot 1 + (3-1) \cdot 1 + (5-1) \cdot (1 \cdot 2) + 1\)
\(r_0 = 2 + 2 + 8 + 1 = 13\)

Answer: \(13 \times 13\) receptive field.
Practical insight: Each output pixel “sees” a \(13 \times 13\) region of the input image.






2.8 Additional Layers and Operations
CNNs often include layers beyond convolutions, each with a specific purpose.
Pooling provides spatial downsampling. Common variants include max-pooling (takes the maximum value in each window) and average-pooling (takes the mean). Figure 25 illustrates these operations.






Figure 25: Shown are a) Sub-Sampling, b) Max Pooling, c) Average Pooling. Source: Prince (2023)



1×1 Convolutions have a kernel size of 1×1 and thus no spatial extent. They are used to change the number of channels (\(C\)) with few parameters. For example, activation maps of dimensionality (\(C \times H \times W\)) can be changed to (\(C_2 \times H \times W\)) using only \(C_2 \times (C + 1)\) parameters. This is useful to reduce dimensionality before more complex layers or to adjust the number of channels to match the number of classes in a classification head.






Figure 26: \(1 \times 1\) convolution. Source: Prince (2023)



Global Average Pooling computes the average of each activation map, reducing the tensor from \((C \times H \times W)\) to \((C \times 1 \times 1)\). This is useful for classification — if \(C\) equals the number of classes, the network can produce logits without any fully-connected layers. Global average pooling also provides translation invariance: since the spatial information is averaged away, the output does not depend on where features appear in the image. The demo in Section 3 illustrates this: a CNN with global average pooling recognizes digits at positions never seen during training, while the same convolutional layers with a fully connected head fail.






Figure 27: Global average pooling: input (left) and output (right).
