title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
TipLearning Objectives





After this lecture you should be able to:

Explain the core mechanisms of the major generative model families: autoregressive models, GANs, VAEs, diffusion models, and flow matching
Compare the tradeoffs of each family across sampling speed, output quality, coverage, and likelihood computation
Identify the key strengths and limitations of each family
Understand how conditional generation can be applied within each model family

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
1 Generative Model Families
Over the past decade, several families of generative models have emerged. They differ in how they model the data distribution, how they generate samples, and which tradeoffs they make. We introduce a few of the most important ones in the following sections. Note that this list is not exhaustive.

1.1 Training Objectives and Sampling
Maximum likelihood is an important principle (see Generative AI for Computer Vision), but it is not the only one. Generative model families differ in how they are trained and in how they produce samples. Table 1 provides a high-level overview. We discuss the most important families in detail in the following sections.



Table 1: Generative model families differ in their training principle and sampling mechanism.










Model family
Training principle
Sampling




Autoregressive (Oord, Kalchbrenner, and Kavukcuoglu 2016)
maximum likelihood (exact)
sequential: one pixel or token at a time


Variational autoencoder (VAE) (Kingma and Welling 2014)
maximize a lower bound on the likelihood (ELBO)
sample a latent vector, decode it in one pass


Normalizing flow (Dinh et al. 2017)
maximum likelihood (exact, via invertible transformations)
transform a noise sample through the invertible network


GAN (Goodfellow et al. 2014)
adversarial objective: generator vs. discriminator
one generator forward pass


Diffusion (Ho et al. 2020; Song et al. 2021)
learn to denoise (denoising score matching)
iterative denoising, starting from pure noise


Flow matching (Lipman et al. 2023)
regress a velocity field that transports noise to data
integrate the learned velocity field, starting from noise






All of these families aim at the same goal, \(p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \approx p_{\text{data}}(\mathbf{x})\), but only some of them directly optimize the log-likelihood. GANs never evaluate a density at all: a discriminator network judges whether samples look real. Diffusion models are related to a likelihood bound, but in practice they are trained with a simplified denoising loss that prioritizes sample quality (Ho et al. 2020).
Figure 1 illustrates how the families produce a sample: in a single network evaluation, token by token, or by gradually transforming noise into an image.






Figure 1: How different model families produce a sample. The images are computed from a real photo (masking, adding noise, interpolating with noise) and only illustrate the sampling process; they are not outputs of trained models. Modern diffusion and flow matching models usually operate in a compressed latent space rather than directly on pixels. The small sketches contrast the stochastic sampling path of many diffusion samplers with the smooth, deterministic path of flow matching.









NoteKey idea



Generative models share a common goal: \(p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) \approx p_{\text{data}}(\mathbf{x})\). They differ in what they optimize to reach it and in how they generate samples.


To compare the families on equal terms, each of the following sections contains an interactive demo (in a collapsed box) built on the same toy problem: generating samples of the one-dimensional distribution from the demo in Generative AI for Computer Vision, a mixture of two Gaussians with modes at 2 and 7. In one dimension, the complete generative process can be plotted: where a sample starts, how it is transformed, and where it ends. All demos share the same layout, with the value \(x\) on the vertical axis and the target distribution on the right. Notably, most of the models in the demos are not trained networks but exact formulas derived from the known target, so that any remaining error comes from the sampling procedure itself. Only the GAN and the VAE are small networks, trained on 1,000 samples.

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
2 Autoregressive Models
Autoregressive models generate data sequentially, predicting one element at a time conditioned on all previous elements.
For an image represented as a sequence of pixels, patches, or discrete image tokens \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n\), the joint distribution can be factorized as a product of conditionals:
\[
p(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n) = p(x_1) \cdot p(x_2|x_1) \cdot p(x_3|x_1,x_2) \cdots p(x_n|x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1})
\]
During generation, the model samples step by step:

Sample \(x_1 \sim p(x_1)\)
Sample \(x_2 \sim p(x_2|x_1)\)
Sample \(x_3 \sim p(x_3|x_1,x_2)\)
Continue until all pixels generated







NoteKey Idea



Autoregressive models turn image generation into a sequence prediction problem.


Each conditional \(p(x_i|x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1})\) is modeled by a neural network (typically a masked CNN or Transformer). This sequential factorization turns the complex problem of modeling high-dimensional distributions into a series of simpler conditional distributions.
Figure Figure 2 illustrates the autoregressive generation process. The model generates pixels one by one, conditioning on all previously generated pixels. This allows for exact likelihood computation, but the sequential nature makes sampling slow and limits parallelization.






Figure 2: Autoregressive generation. Models predict each element sequentially, conditioning on all previously generated elements. Figure from Torralba et al. (2024).









Note



Autoregressive ideas are still very important. Many modern multimodal systems use LLM-like components, visual tokens, or autoregressive reasoning, even if the final image generation is diffusion-based.


A prominent example of autoregressive models is PixelCNN (Oord, Kalchbrenner, Vinyals, et al. 2016), which uses masked convolutions to ensure the autoregressive property. More recently, transformer-based autoregressive models (e.g., Parti Yu et al. (2022)) have shown strong performance by modeling images as sequences of discrete tokens. Also, OpenAI’s GPT Image / 4o image generation is described by OpenAI as an autoregressive, natively multimodal image generation model, in contrast to DALL·E-style diffusion models. The exact image tokenization and decoder architecture are not publicly specified.






NoteInteractive Demo: Autoregressive Generation





The following demo applies the factorization above to the toy problem. In the default view, a point \((x_1, x_2)\) is generated in two steps: first \(x_1 \sim p(x_1)\), then \(x_2 \sim p(x_2 \mid x_1)\). The view Sequence generates eight values one after the other, similar to a row of pixels, and 1D: two tokens writes a single value as two discrete tokens.







NoteExplore the demo






Drag \(x_1\) from the left mode to the right one. How does \(p(x_2 \mid x_1)\) change?
Switch to Sequence and draw several sequences to the end. After how many values is the direction of a sequence decided? Why can the first value not decide it?
Switch to 1D: two tokens, open Advanced and set the temperature to 0.5. How do the generated values change?



Click for possible answers


Near the left mode, \(x_2\) is concentrated in a narrow range; near the right mode, it spreads out. Within each mode, the position of \(x_2\) also shifts with \(x_1\). The second value is drawn from a distribution that depends on the first.
Typically after three to five values, when the model is more than 85% sure about the direction. All sequences start near the same value, so \(x_1\) carries no information about the direction. Early random choices decide where a sequence goes; later values follow them.
Likely tokens become even more likely: each mode gets narrower, and values in the tails and between the modes become rare. The smaller mode does not disappear, since it is also the narrower one.





The demo illustrates the defining property of autoregressive models: every value is drawn from a distribution that depends on all previously generated values. The same principle generates a row of pixels, a sequence of image tokens, or a sentence.









NotePros and Cons of Autoregressive Models



Pros

Exact likelihood computation
Natural fit for language models
Strong for discrete tokens

Cons

Sequential generation is slow
Pixel-level image generation is expensive
High-resolution images require long sequences
Errors can accumulate during sampling

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
3 Generative Adversarial Networks
GANs, see Goodfellow et al. (2014), frame generative modeling as an adversarial game between two neural networks: a generator \(g(\mathbf{z})\) that creates fake samples, and a discriminator \(d(\mathbf{x})\) that tries to distinguish real data from generated fakes (see Figure 3). This adversarial setup drives both networks to improve: the generator learns to create increasingly realistic samples, while the discriminator becomes better at spotting fakes.






Figure 3: GAN idea: The generator creates fake samples from random noise \(z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\), while the discriminator judges whether samples are real or fake. From Link



The GAN training objective can be expressed as a minimax game:
\[
\min_{g} \max_{d} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{data}}[\log d(\mathbf{x})] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_z}[\log(1 - d(g(\mathbf{z})))]
\]
The discriminator \(d\) maximizes its ability to correctly classify real (\(d(\mathbf{x}) \approx 1\)) vs. fake (\(d(g(\mathbf{z})) \approx 0\)) samples. The generator \(G\) minimizes the discriminator’s success, trying to produce samples where \(d(g(\mathbf{z})) \approx 1\) (fooling the discriminator). See Figure 4 for an illustration.
In practice, training alternates between: 1. Discriminator step: Update \(d\) to better distinguish real from fake 2. Generator step: Update \(g\) to better fool the current discriminator






Figure 4: GAN learning process: As training progresses, the generator’s distribution (green) moves closer to the real data distribution (black dots). The discriminator’s decision boundary (blue) adapts accordingly. From Foster (2023)









NoteInteractive Demo: A GAN in 1D





In the following demo, a small GAN has been trained on 1,000 samples of the toy distribution. The generator maps a one-dimensional noise value \(z\) to a value \(x = g(z)\), so the complete generator can be plotted as a curve. The view Training dynamics (under Advanced) shows how this curve changes during training.







NoteExplore the demo






Drag \(z\) slowly through the steep part of the curve. What happens to \(x\)? Why do few samples end up between the modes?
Open Advanced, switch to Training dynamics and play the standard run. Does the generator improve steadily?
Switch to the unstable run and look at the training steps 25 to 100. Which failure from the Pros and Cons below appears?



Click for possible answers


\(x\) jumps from the left mode to the right one. The steep part maps a small range of \(z\) to a wide range of \(x\), so few samples land there. Flat parts collect many values of \(z\) into a small range of \(x\): a mode.
No. The distance to the target fluctuates between training steps; it is lower after 3,000 steps than after 6,000. The final generator finds both modes with roughly the right weights, but squeezes each mode into a few narrow spikes.
Mode collapse: at steps 25 and 50, the generator only produces the right mode. Shortly after, almost all samples have the same value, and the generator then oscillates.





Notably, a continuous generator can represent this distribution exactly: flow matching below computes such a mapping. The remaining errors are problems of the adversarial training, not limits of the architecture.









NotePros and Cons of GANs



Pros

Fast sampling: one forward pass
Can produce sharp images
Historically very important for image generation

Cons

Training can be unstable
Mode collapse: generator produces limited variety
No direct likelihood computation
Modern text-to-image systems are less commonly pure GANs

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
4 Variational Autoencoders
Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) (Kingma and Welling 2014) take a different approach to generative modeling, building on the autoencoder architecture (see Figure 5) but with a crucial probabilistic twist.






Figure 5: VAE architecture: The encoder maps inputs to latent distributions \(q(z|x)\), while the decoder reconstructs from latent samples. From Source.



A VAE learns two networks that perform (approximate) inverse operations:

Encoder \(q_{\psi}(z|x)\): Maps data \(x\) to a distribution over latent codes \(z\)
Decoder \(p_{\theta}(x|z)\): Maps latent codes \(z\) back to data \(x\)

Unlike standard autoencoders, VAEs enforce structure on the latent space through probabilistic modeling (see Figure 6), ensuring that randomly sampled latent codes produce meaningful outputs.






Figure 6: VAE computational graph: The encoder outputs mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) for each latent dimension. The reparameterization trick (\(z = \mu + \epsilon \cdot \sigma\), where \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\)) enables gradient-based optimization. From Source.



VAEs optimize the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), which consists of two terms:
\[
\text{ELBO} = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_{\psi}(z|x)}[\log p_{\theta}(x|z)]}_{\text{Reconstruction}} - \underbrace{\text{KL}(q_{\psi}(z|x) \| p(z))}_{\text{Regularization}}
\]
The reconstruction term ensures the decoder can recover the input from the latent code. The KL regularization term (typically with prior \(p(z) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)\)) prevents the latent space from developing “gaps and tendrils”—ensuring that random samples from \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\) decode to meaningful outputs.
This balance is key to VAE behavior: the reconstruction loss wants to use the latent space flexibly, while KL regularization pushes latent codes toward a standard normal distribution. The result is a structured, continuous latent space where interpolation and attribute manipulation work smoothly.






Figure 7: VAE latent space: Traversing the latent space produces smooth interpolations between faces, demonstrating the structured representation learned by the model. From Prince (2023).









NoteInteractive Demo: A VAE in 1D





The following demo shows a small VAE with a one-dimensional latent space, trained on 1,000 samples of the toy distribution. For a selected latent value \(z\), the decoder outputs a Gaussian distribution \(p_{\theta}(x \mid z) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_{\theta}(z), \sigma_{\theta}(z)^2)\), from which \(x\) is drawn.







NoteExplore the demo






Keep \(z\) fixed and press Sample x again several times. Where does the variation of \(x\) come from?
Drag \(z\) through the prior. Which values of \(z\) produce the left mode?
Open Advanced and turn off the decoder noise. Does the model still produce both modes?



Click for possible answers


From the decoder’s own distribution: \(z\) only determines the mean \(\mu_{\theta}(z)\) and the spread \(\sigma_{\theta}(z)\), and \(x\) is drawn from \(\mathcal{N}(\mu_{\theta}(z), \sigma_{\theta}(z)^2)\).
Values below about \(z = -0.3\), i.e. about 38% of the prior. This is close to the weight of the left mode (40%): the decoder splits the prior between the modes according to their weights.
Yes. The decoder mean alone already places the samples in both modes; the decoder noise only adds spread around \(\mu_{\theta}(z)\). Blurry VAE images are usually explained by the decoder mean averaging over details it cannot predict, not by this noise.





The demo illustrates the two random steps of VAE generation: drawing \(z\) from the prior and drawing \(x\) from the decoder. The encoder is only needed for training and inference; the view Inference (under Advanced) shows how it maps an observed \(x\) to a distribution \(q_{\psi}(z \mid x)\).









NotePros and Cons of VAEs



Pros

Principled probabilistic foundation
Latent space structure: can interpolate in latent space and interpret factors
Stable training
Can be used for representation learning

Cons

Blurry outputs (more complex variants can reduce this)

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
5 Diffusion Models
Diffusion models Ho et al. (2020) Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015) have emerged as the state-of-the-art approach for high-quality image generation, powering systems like Stable Diffusion. The core insight is remarkably simple: learn to reverse a gradual noising process.
Figure 8 shows the forward diffusion process, whereby Gaussian noise is gradually added to an image (from left to right).






Figure 8: Forward diffusion process. From Torralba et al. (2024).



The Gaussian noise is added to data over \(T\) steps, following a pre-specified noise schedule. The forward noising process is fixed and does not involve a neural network. However, it is stochastic because Gaussian noise is sampled.
The forward process at step \(t\) can be written as:
\[\begin{equation}
\mathbf{x}_t =
\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\mathbf{x}_{t-1}
+
\sqrt{\beta_t}\mathbf{\epsilon}_t,
\quad
\mathbf{\epsilon}_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbfit{I})
\end{equation}\]
where \(\beta_t\) controls the noise level (the noise schedule). This process gradually degrades the clean image \(\mathbf{x}_0\) into an almost pure-noise image \(\mathbf{x}_T \approx \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbfit{I})\).
Common noise schedules, such as linear or cosine schedules, start with small \(\beta_t\) values and gradually increase them. This produces a smooth transition from data to noise.
A crucial mathematical property is that we can sample \(\mathbf{x}_t\) directly from \(\mathbf{x}_0\) without iterating through all intermediate steps. This enables efficient training: we randomly sample timesteps and train the denoiser on many noise levels simultaneously.
The core idea is to train a neural network to model the reverse diffusion process, thus going in the opposite direction and denoise an image. Figure 9 shows the idea.






Figure 9: Reverse diffusion process visualization. From Torralba et al. (2024).



A neural network learns to gradually remove noise, step by step. Starting from pure noise
\[
\mathbf{x}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbfit{I}),
\]
the model denoises iteratively to produce a realistic sample \(\mathbf{x}_0\).
The neural network learns to predict the noise \(\mathbf{\epsilon}\) that was added at a given timestep. Crucially, the network is conditioned on the timestep \(t\), since the noise level varies dramatically from early timesteps, where the image is almost clean, to late timesteps, where it is almost pure noise.
A common simplified training objective is:
\[\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}
=
\mathbb{E}_{t, \mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{\epsilon}}
\left[
\left\|
\mathbf{\epsilon}
-
f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)
\right\|^2
\right]
\end{equation}\]
The model is trained to predict the noise \(\mathbf{\epsilon}\) that was used to create the noised image \(\mathbf{x}_t\) from the clean image \(\mathbf{x}_0\).






Figure 10: Training and sampling algorithms: Training samples random timesteps and noise; sampling iteratively denoises from \(T\) to 0. Guidance techniques (not shown) can further improve sample quality.



The denoising network typically uses a U-Net architecture—a convolutional encoder-decoder with skip connections. The U-Net processes noisy images at multiple resolutions, with timestep \(t\) embedded and injected throughout the network.






Figure 11: U-Net architecture for diffusion models: Downsampling path (left) captures context, upsampling path (right) enables precise localization, and skip connections (horizontal) preserve spatial details. Timestep embeddings condition the network on noise level. From Prince (2023).









NoteInteractive Demo: Diffusion in 1D





The following demo applies the reverse process to the toy problem. Instead of a trained network, it uses the exact denoiser, which can be computed because the target distribution is known. Differences between settings therefore come from the sampling procedure alone.







NoteExplore the demo






Press Play and follow the highlighted sample. When does it decide on a mode?
Open Advanced and press Re-run sampler a few times. The starting noise stays the same. Why does the end point change?
Switch to the deterministic sampler (DDIM) and reduce the number of steps to 2. What happens to the samples?



Click for possible answers


Late: for most of the process, the sample wanders around in the noise. Only in the last third of the process (from about \(t = 0.3\,T\)) do almost all samples stay on the side of their final mode.
The stochastic sampler (DDPM) adds fresh noise in every step. Even for the same starting noise \(\mathbf{x}_T\), the result is random.
About 40% of the samples end between the two modes. In the first step, the denoiser can only predict the average of the data, which lies between the modes; with only two steps, the samples cannot recover. Diffusion models need many steps for this reason.





The demo illustrates why diffusion sampling is slow: the reverse process consists of many small steps, and each step requires one evaluation of the denoising network.









NotePros and Cons of Diffusion Models



Pros

High-quality, diverse outputs
Stable and reliable training

Cons

Slow inference time
High compute (training + inference) cost









NoteInteresting Note on the Noise





While the standard diffusion framework has proven highly successful, researchers have explored numerous extensions and modifications:
Cold Diffusion (Bansal et al. 2022) demonstrates that the Gaussian noise assumption is not fundamental to diffusion models. The key insight: any degradation process that can be inverted works. Instead of adding Gaussian noise, Cold Diffusion applies transformations like blurring, pixelation, or masking—yet still learns to reverse them through the same denoising framework.






Figure 12: Cold Diffusion: Various degradation operators (blur, downsampling, masking) can replace Gaussian noise in the diffusion framework. The model learns to reverse these transformations through the same training procedure. From Bansal et al. (2022).



This generalization reveals that diffusion’s success stems from the gradual, multi-step inversion strategy rather than the specific choice of Gaussian noise. The framework adapts to diverse degradation operators, opening possibilities for task-specific degradations that may better suit particular domains or applications.

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
6 Flow-Based Models
Flow-based models take yet another perspective: they transform a simple distribution, such as a standard Gaussian, into the data distribution. The name refers to the idea that probability mass “flows” from the noise distribution to the data distribution. Two variants are important: normalizing flows, which use a sequence of invertible transformations, and flow matching, which learns a continuous transformation over time. While normalizing flows are mainly of historical and conceptual interest for image generation, flow matching powers many of today’s state-of-the-art text-to-image models.

6.1 Normalizing Flows
A normalizing flow (Rezende and Mohamed 2016; Dinh et al. 2017) is an invertible neural network \(f_\theta\) that maps a latent vector \(\mathbf{z} \sim p(\mathbf{z}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\) to an image \(\mathbf{x} = f_\theta(\mathbf{z})\). Because \(f_\theta\) is invertible, every image \(\mathbf{x}\) corresponds to exactly one latent vector \(\mathbf{z} = f_\theta^{-1}(\mathbf{x})\). In contrast to VAEs and GANs, the latent vector has the same dimensionality as the image.
Invertibility allows computing the exact likelihood with the change of variables formula:
\[
\log p_\theta(\mathbf{x}) = \log p\left(f_\theta^{-1}(\mathbf{x})\right) + \log \left| \det \frac{\partial f_\theta^{-1}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial \mathbf{x}} \right|
\tag{1}\]
The first term measures how likely the corresponding latent vector is under the Gaussian. The second term, the log-determinant of the Jacobian, accounts for how much the transformation stretches or compresses space: a region that is compressed into a small volume must receive a higher density. The model is trained by maximizing Equation 1 on the training data, i.e. by maximum likelihood.
The price is a restricted architecture. For a general neural network, computing the determinant of the \(d \times d\) Jacobian is prohibitively expensive (for a \(256 \times 256 \times 3\) image, \(d \approx 200{,}000\)). Normalizing flows therefore only use layers that are invertible and have a cheap determinant, such as the coupling layers of RealNVP (Dinh et al. 2017) and Glow (Kingma and Dhariwal 2018). Sampling requires a single pass through the network, but the sample quality of normalizing flows lags behind GANs and diffusion models.






NoteKey Idea



Normalizing flows trade architectural flexibility for exact likelihoods: every layer must be invertible and have a cheap Jacobian determinant.




6.2 Flow Matching
Instead of a fixed number of invertible layers, one can describe the transformation from noise to data as a continuous process over time \(t \in [0, 1]\). A neural network \(v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)\) predicts a velocity: in which direction, and how fast, the point \(\mathbf{x}_t\) should move at time \(t\). Starting from noise \(\mathbf{x}_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\), a sample is generated by following the velocity field until \(t = 1\), i.e. by solving an ordinary differential equation (ODE):
\[
\frac{d\mathbf{x}_t}{dt} = v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)
\]
Such models are known as continuous normalizing flows (Chen et al. 2018). For a long time, they were expensive to train, because the ODE had to be simulated during training. Flow matching (Lipman et al. 2023; Liu et al. 2022) solves this problem with a surprisingly simple training procedure. Note that, in contrast to the diffusion notation above, \(t = 0\) denotes noise and \(t = 1\) denotes data.
During training, we pair a training image \(\mathbf{x}_1\) with a random noise image \(\mathbf{x}_0 = \mathbf{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\) and connect them with a straight line:
\[
\mathbf{x}_t = (1 - t)\, \mathbf{\epsilon} + t\, \mathbf{x}_1
\]
Along this line, the velocity is constant: \(\frac{d\mathbf{x}_t}{dt} = \mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{\epsilon}\). The network is trained to predict this velocity at randomly sampled times \(t\):
\[
\mathcal{L}
=
\mathbb{E}_{t, \mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{\epsilon}}
\left[
\left\|
(\mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{\epsilon})
-
v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)
\right\|^2
\right]
\tag{2}\]
It can be shown that a network minimizing Equation 2 learns a velocity field that transports the noise distribution to the data distribution. Note the similarity to the diffusion objective: both mix an image with noise and train a network with a simple regression loss. Instead of the noise \(\mathbf{\epsilon}\), the network predicts the direction from noise to data.
To generate a sample, we start from noise and take small steps along the predicted velocity (Euler method):
\[
\mathbf{x}_{t + \Delta t} = \mathbf{x}_t + \Delta t \, v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)
\]
In contrast to many diffusion samplers, no fresh noise is injected: given the initial noise, sampling is deterministic.
Figure 13 contrasts training and sampling for 1D data. During training, noise and data points are paired at random, so the straight lines cross. The network cannot know which data point a given \(\mathbf{x}_t\) belongs to and learns the average direction of all lines passing through it. The resulting trajectories never cross, and they split the noise distribution into the two modes of the data distribution.






Figure 13: Flow matching in 1D, with time on the horizontal axis. Left: training targets are straight lines between random pairs of noise samples (orange) and data samples (blue). Right: trajectories obtained by integrating the learned velocity field, on top of the density of \(\mathbf{x}_t\) (gray). Each noise sample is deterministically transported to one data sample.









🤔 Think About It
Training uses straight lines between noise and data. Why can flow matching models often generate images with fewer steps than diffusion models?


Key considerations

If the path from noise to data were exactly straight, a single Euler step would reach the end point. The learned velocity field averages over all image-noise pairs that pass through a point, so the actual sampling paths are curved, but typically less than those of diffusion models. Rectified flow (Liu et al. 2022) straightens the paths further by re-training on noise-image pairs generated by the model itself.






Figure 14: Few-step sampling on 2D data. Top: flow matching. The trajectories are curved, so a single Euler step lands every sample near the mean of the data, which is the average direction at \(t = 0\). Bottom: rectified flow, re-trained on (noise, generated sample) pairs of the model above. The trajectories are almost straight, and a single step already produces a reasonable sample.













NoteInteractive Demo: Flow Matching in 1D





The following demo extends Figure 13 with the exact velocity field of the toy problem. In the view Training, a probe (circle) shows the training lines that pass close to a point \((x, t)\) and the average of their directions. The view Sampling integrates the velocity field.







NoteExplore the demo






In the view Training, compare the default probe at \((x, t) = (1.5, 0.3)\) with a point close to the right mode late in time, e.g. \((6, 0.8)\). How do the directions of the training lines differ?
Switch to Sampling, open Advanced and reduce the number of Euler steps to 1. Where do the samples end up? Compare with Figure 14.



Click for possible answers


At \((1.5, 0.3)\), the directions split into two groups, towards the left and towards the right mode; their average lies in between, a direction that hardly any single training line has. At \((6, 0.8)\), all lines head towards the right mode, and the average points there as well.
All samples end up at the mean of the data (\(x \approx 5\)), between the modes: at \(t = 0\), the average direction of all training lines points to the mean.








Flow matching has become the basis of many modern text-to-image models. Stable Diffusion 3 (Esser et al. 2024) trains a transformer with a rectified flow objective in the latent space of an autoencoder, and FLUX.1 Kontext (Labs et al. 2025) uses flow matching for both image generation and instruction-based editing.






NotePros and Cons of Flow Matching



Pros

High-quality, diverse outputs
Simple, stable training (regression loss, no simulation)
Deterministic sampling, often with fewer steps than diffusion

Cons

Sampling still requires multiple network evaluations
High compute (training + inference) cost
Likelihood computation possible, but expensive

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
7 Comparing the Model Families
The model families make different trade-offs with respect to the desirable properties of generative models (Properties and Trade-offs). Figure 15 summarizes them.






Figure 15: Coarse summary of the desirable properties per model family. Ratings are qualitative and simplify: modern variants narrow many gaps, e.g. distillation for diffusion sampling or large-scale autoregressive models with high fidelity. Disentanglement is omitted, since no family achieves it without additional inductive biases.









NoteInteractive Demo: Where Do the Errors Come From?





The following demo compares the final distributions of three settings from the demos above: flow matching with an accurate ODE solver, flow matching with only four Euler steps, and the trained GAN.

The three panels show three sources of error. Flow matching with an accurate solver has none, apart from sampling noise. With four steps, the same velocity field is integrated too coarsely: a numerical error. The GAN has only seen 1,000 training samples and was trained with an adversarial objective that is hard to optimize: a learning error. Note that this is not a ranking of the model families, since the exact models know the true target distribution.

title: 9 - GenAI Model Families
text:
8 Conditioning Across Model Families
So far, we have introduced the model families mostly in their unconditional form: they learn to model or sample from \(p(\mathbf{x})\).
In practice, these model families can often be extended to conditional generation, where the model learns:
\[
p_\theta(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{c})
\]
The condition \(\mathbf{c}\) can be a class label, text prompt, source image, mask, layout, depth map, or reference image.
For this lecture, the important point is simple: conditioning does not define a separate model family. It is a way to control models from different families.



Model family
How conditioning can enter




Autoregressive models
condition each prediction step on \(\mathbf{c}\)


VAEs
condition encoder and/or decoder on \(\mathbf{c}\)


GANs
condition generator and often discriminator on \(\mathbf{c}\)


Diffusion models
condition the denoising network on \(\mathbf{c}\)


Flow matching
condition the velocity network on \(\mathbf{c}\)



Modern text-to-image and image-editing systems use these ideas extensively.

title: 2 - Images as Data
text:
TipLearning Objectives





After this lecture you should be able to:

Describe how images are represented as tensors and explain the role of height, width, and channels.
Distinguish between RGB and grayscale representations and their implications for model input.
Explain the trade-offs involved in choosing image resolution for a deep learning pipeline.
Describe the purpose of train, validation, and test splits and identify common sources of data leakage.
Recognize class imbalance in a dataset and explain its effect on model training.
Identify label ambiguity, label noise, and hidden biases in image datasets.

title: 2 - Images as Data
text:
1 Motivation
Understanding the data is a critical task, before training any model. In computer vision, this means understanding how images are represented numerically, how datasets are structured, and what pitfalls to watch for. Many classification failures can be traced back not to the model architecture or training procedure, but to problems in the data itself: imbalanced classes, noisy labels, or subtle biases that the model exploits as shortcuts.
Throughout this lecture, we use camera-trap images from Snapshot Kgalagadi as a running example. The dataset contains 3,611 captures (camera trigger events, usually three frames each) from 20 cameras in the Kalahari, recorded between October 2018 and January 2019 and labelled by citizen-science volunteers on Zooniverse. It is small, but it exhibits every data problem discussed below.
Even a single class hides a lot of visual variety. Figure 1 shows eight images that all carry the same label. A model has to map all of them to gemsbok, while mapping visually similar backgrounds without an animal to empty.






Figure 1: Eight Snapshot Kgalagadi images, all labelled gemsbok: close-up, far away (circled), partly visible, night (flash), unusual pose, group, back view, and half hidden in grass.

title: 2 - Images as Data
text:
2 Image Representations

2.1 Images as Tensors
A digital image is a grid of pixels arranged in rows and columns. Each pixel holds one or more numeric values representing color intensity. This grid can be described as a three-dimensional array, a tensor, with dimensions for height, width, and channels.
Figure 2 illustrates the tensor structure of an RGB image. The height and width correspond to the spatial dimensions, while the three channels encode red, green, and blue intensity values.






Figure 2: An image is a tensor of shape H × W × C. Top: zooming into a camera-trap image (790 × 1024 × 3) until single pixels become visible. Bottom: the 6 × 6 patch split into its red, green, and blue channels — each an H × W matrix of integers in \([0, 255]\) — and stacked along the channel axis C. The highlighted pixel is described by three numbers, one per channel.



Pixel values are typically stored as 8-bit unsigned integers in the range \([0, 255]\). For model training, these are usually normalized to floats in \([0, 1]\) or standardized to zero mean and unit variance.

2.1.1 Shape Conventions
Different libraries use different axis orderings for image tensors. This is a common source of bugs when moving between frameworks:

NumPy / PIL: H × W × C (height, width, channels) -> channels last
PyTorch: C × H × W (channels, height, width) -> channels first

A PyTorch tensor representing an RGB image of size 224 × 224 has shape (3, 224, 224), while the same image in NumPy has shape (224, 224, 3).






🤔 Think About It
A batch of 32 RGB images, each 224 × 224 pixels, is loaded into PyTorch. What is the shape of the resulting tensor?


Answer

The batch tensor has shape (32, 3, 224, 224) — batch size × channels × height × width.
PyTorch always prepends the batch dimension. This convention enables efficient parallel computation on GPUs.










🤔 Think About It
How would an MRI scan be represented as a tensor? Does the standard H × W × C representation still apply, and what would the “channels” correspond to?


Key considerations

The tensor paradigm generalises naturally to medical imaging — it just adds axes.

Single 2-D slice: A single MRI slice is a grayscale intensity image: shape H × W (or H × W × 1 if an explicit channel axis is kept).
Full 3-D volume: A complete MRI acquisition is a stack of slices — shape D × H × W, where D is the number of slices (the depth axis). Alternatively written H × W × D depending on the library convention.
Multi-sequence acquisition: Clinical MRI is typically acquired in multiple sequences (T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI, …), each sensitive to different tissue properties. The sequences act as additional “channels”, yielding shape D × H × W × C — directly analogous to the channel axis in RGB, just with medically meaningful channels instead of colour primaries.
4-D time series (fMRI): Functional MRI adds a time axis, giving shape T × D × H × W.

The key insight is that the H × W × C abstraction is not specific to colour images. Any multi-channel spatial measurement — MRI sequences, satellite spectral bands, depth maps paired with RGB — fits the same tensor structure. The number of spatial axes and their physical meaning change; the framework stays the same.







2.2 Color and Channels
The number of channels depends on the color representation. The most common formats are:

RGB: 3 channels (red, green, blue). Each channel encodes the intensity of one color component. The combination of all three channels produces the perceived color at each pixel.
Grayscale: 1 channel. Each pixel holds a single luminance value.

Figure 3 illustrates the difference. The RGB image stores three separate intensity maps, while the grayscale version compresses all color information into a single channel.






Figure 3: The same image shown as RGB (three channels) and grayscale (one channel), with individual channel visualizations.









🤔 Think About It
Are 1 and 3 the only possible numbers of channels? Think of other imaging modalities you might encounter in practice.


Answer

No — the number of channels depends entirely on the sensor and task:

1 channel: grayscale photo, depth map, thermal/infrared, most medical scans (X-ray, ultrasound frames)
3 channels: RGB (or HSV, Lab — still 3 channels, different encoding)
4 channels: RGBA (adds an alpha/transparency channel), or RGB + near-infrared
N channels (tens to hundreds): multispectral and hyperspectral imaging (remote sensing, agriculture, astronomy)

The tensor shape H × W × C generalizes to all of these — only C changes.




Beyond standard photography, other imaging modalities produce images with different channel structures:

Infrared: captures thermal radiation, often used in night-vision or satellite imagery
Depth maps: encode distance-to-camera as pixel values
Multispectral / hyperspectral: tens to hundreds of channels capturing narrow wavelength bands, common in remote sensing and agriculture

The key insight is that regardless of the modality, the data structure remains the same: a tensor of shape H × W × C. The number of channels changes, but the processing paradigm does not.
RGB is also not the only way to encode color. Alternative color spaces rearrange the same information along more perceptually meaningful axes — for example, HSV (Hue-Saturation-Value) separates color identity (hue) from brightness (value), which can be useful for color-based retrieval, rule-based segmentation, or hue-preserving data augmentation.
Notably, the channels of an image are rarely independent. Figure 4 compares a day image with a night image taken with the camera’s white flash. During the day, the R, G, and B channels differ noticeably (median correlation 0.71 across all daytime images). At night, the flash washes out most color, and the three channels become almost copies of each other (median correlation 0.97). Such images are stored with three channels but carry little more information than a grayscale image.






Figure 4: Left: a day and a night (white flash) image from the same camera, shown as RGB and as separate R, G, B channels. Right: distribution of the mean pairwise correlation between the R, G, and B channels per image. Night images (3% of the dataset) have highly redundant channels.





2.3 Resolution and Resizing
Image resolution — the number of pixels along height and width — directly affects both the amount of visual detail and the computational cost. Figure 5 illustrates the same image at different resolutions.






Figure 5: Top: the same image at 224 × 224, 64 × 64, and 16 × 16 pixels — fine details are progressively lost at lower resolutions. Bottom: three ways to turn a non-square image into a 224 × 224 input — center crop (discards the image borders), aspect-preserving resize with letterbox padding (wastes pixels on padding), and stretching (distorts shapes).



Most deep learning models require a fixed input size. Since real-world image datasets contain images of varying dimensions, resizing is an unavoidable preprocessing step. This introduces practical trade-offs:

Higher resolution preserves fine-grained details (e.g., small objects, textures) but requires more memory and compute.
Lower resolution is faster and lighter but may discard information critical for the task.
Aspect ratio distortion occurs when images are resized to a square input without preserving proportions. This can deform objects and change their visual appearance.

How much information is lost depends on how large the objects of interest are. All Snapshot Kgalagadi images have a native resolution of 2592 × 2000 pixels, so resizing is a choice (memory, input size of a pretrained model) rather than a necessity. Figure 6 demonstrates its cost: after resizing to 224 × 224, 12% of all animals cover fewer than 10 × 10 pixels, and 40% fewer than 32 × 32. A distant gemsbok shrinks from 74 × 74 to 6 × 8 pixels — barely more than a few dark pixels.






Figure 6: Left: area of animal bounding boxes (detected with MegaDetector) relative to the image area, on a log scale. Boxes in red are smaller than 10 × 10 pixels after resizing to 224 × 224. Right: a distant gemsbok at native resolution and after resizing the full frame to 224 × 224.



Common strategies include resizing the shorter edge to the target size and center-cropping, or resizing with padding to preserve the aspect ratio.

title: 2 - Images as Data
text:
3 Image Datasets

3.1 Labels and Classes
In supervised learning, each image in the dataset is associated with a label(s). For multi-class classification, this is typically an integer index that maps to a class name. For example, in a camera-trap dataset the mapping might be:

Example class mapping for a camera-trap dataset


Index
Class Name




0
empty


1
deer


2
fox


3
badger


4
bird



The choice of classes is itself a design decision. Finer-grained class definitions (e.g., distinguishing between red deer and roe deer) require more training data and may introduce label ambiguity. Coarser definitions (e.g., simply “animal” vs. “empty”) are easier to annotate but less informative.
In single-label classification, each image belongs to exactly one class. In multi-label classification, an image can belong to multiple classes simultaneously, for example, a camera-trap image showing both a deer and a bird.
Whether multi-label classification is necessary is an empirical question. In Snapshot Kgalagadi, only 1.6% of the captures with an animal (15 of 939) contain more than one species, and only three species pairs occur (?@fig-iad-multi-label). A single-label formulation is a reasonable simplification here, but in datasets from areas with dense, mixed herds the situation can be very different.


3.2 Dataset Splits
A well-designed dataset is divided into three non-overlapping subsets, each serving a distinct purpose:

Training set: used to optimize the model’s parameters via gradient descent. The model sees these images repeatedly during training.
Validation set: used to tune hyperparameters (learning rate, architecture choices, augmentation strategies) and to monitor for overfitting. The model never trains on these images, but they influence decisions during development.
Test set: held out entirely until final evaluation. Provides an unbiased estimate of how the model will perform on new, unseen data.

The split strategy matters. Random splitting may not be appropriate for all datasets. Two important considerations:

Stratified splits ensure that each split has roughly the same class distribution as the full dataset. This is especially important when classes are imbalanced.
Grouped splits ensure that related images end up in the same split. For example, if a camera trap captures multiple images of the same animal within seconds, these near-duplicates should all be in the same split — otherwise the model can appear to generalize when it is actually memorizing specific individuals.

Figure 7 shows three frames captured within a few seconds of each other by the same camera trap. Although each frame is technically a distinct image file, they depict the same individual in the same scene. A grouped split keeps all three in the same set (train, validation, or test) so that the model cannot see one frame during training and be evaluated on a near-duplicate.






Figure 7: Three frames from a single camera-trap trigger event. Because the images are near-duplicates, they must all be assigned to the same split.



Figure 8 illustrates the difference on a larger scale, using two weeks of images from four cameras. With a random split per image, the frames of a single capture are scattered across train, validation, and test: in this time window, 66% of the multi-frame captures end up in more than one split. Splitting by camera site keeps not only the frames of a capture together, but also all images that share the same background.






Figure 8: Images from four camera sites over two weeks; each tick is one image, and the three frames of a capture are stacked vertically. Top: random split per image — the three frames of the highlighted capture land in train, test, and validation. Bottom: split by site — each camera is assigned to one split as a whole.





3.3 Data Leakage
Data leakage occurs when information from the validation or test set inadvertently influences the training process. A concrete camera-trap example makes this easy to see: the three frames in Figure 7 come from a single trigger event. If we shuffle all images and split randomly, frame 1 may land in the training set while frames 2 and 3 land in validation. The model never has to generalize — at evaluation time it is effectively being shown images it has already seen. Accuracy on the validation set looks excellent, but performance on a truly new event collapses.
In image datasets, common sources of leakage include:

Near-duplicate images across splits (e.g., consecutive frames from a video or a camera-trap burst)
Images from the same location or subject appearing in both train and test sets
Preprocessing statistics (mean, standard deviation) computed on the entire dataset rather than on the training set alone

Leakage leads to overly optimistic evaluation metrics that do not reflect real-world performance.
How large is the effect in practice? Figure 9 shows the result of a simple experiment: frozen DINOv3 features and a logistic-regression classifier, trained on six Snapshot Kgalagadi classes (1,199 images). The only thing that changes is how the images are split. With a random image-level split, the classifier reaches a macro-F1 of 0.87. Keeping the frames of a capture together drops the score to 0.76 — those 11 points were never real. Interestingly, with the random split, the most similar training image of a validation image is a frame of the same capture in 83% of cases.
Holding out entire cameras drops the score further to 0.42. This gap is not leakage in the strict sense: it measures how well the model generalizes to a new location — which is usually exactly what matters when a model is deployed on new cameras. The split strategy therefore defines which generalization is being measured.






Figure 9: Validation macro-F1 of the same model (frozen DINOv3 ViT-S/16 features + logistic regression) under three split strategies, mean ± standard deviation over 5 seeds.









🤔 Think About It
A dataset of dermoscopy images (skin lesion photographs) is collected from 500 patients, with some patients having multiple images taken at different visits. The images are randomly shuffled and split 80/10/10 into train/validation/test. What could go wrong?


Key considerations

Multiple images from the same patient may end up in different splits. Since images from the same patient often share visual characteristics (skin color, mole patterns, lighting conditions from the same clinic), the model may learn to recognize patients rather than lesions. Evaluation metrics will be inflated because the model has effectively seen “similar” images during training.
The correct approach is to split at the patient level: all images from a given patient go into the same split.






3.4 Class Imbalance
Real-world image datasets are rarely balanced. Some classes naturally occur much more frequently than others. Figure 10 illustrates this for Snapshot Kgalagadi: 74% of all captures are empty, gemsbok accounts for 502 captures, and nine species were recorded exactly once.






Figure 10: Number of captures per class in Snapshot Kgalagadi (log scale). The “empty” class dominates, while many species have only a handful of examples.



Class imbalance has direct consequences for training:

A model trained on an imbalanced dataset tends to predict the majority class more often, since this minimizes the overall loss.
Rare classes receive fewer gradient updates, making it harder for the model to learn their distinguishing features.
Standard accuracy can be misleading — a model that always predicts “empty” achieves 74% accuracy on Snapshot Kgalagadi while being completely useless for the actual task of species identification.

Common mitigation strategies include:

Oversampling minority classes or undersampling majority classes
Weighted loss functions that assign higher penalties to errors on underrepresented classes
Evaluation metrics beyond accuracy, such as per-class precision, recall, and F1 score



3.5 Label Quality and Ambiguity
Labels in real-world datasets are created by human annotators — and humans make mistakes. Label noise refers to incorrect annotations in the training data. Even small rates of label noise can affect model performance, particularly for classes that are visually similar.
Figure 11 illustrates cases where the correct label is genuinely debatable.






Figure 11: Two camera-trap frames that are hard to label. Left: only a horn and a blurred patch of fur are visible — which species is it, and should the frame count as “empty”? Right: a buffalo in the foreground and elephants in the background — a single-label scheme cannot describe this image.



Sources of label noise include:

Inter-annotator disagreement: different annotators assign different labels to the same image, particularly for borderline cases
Systematic errors: an annotator consistently confuses two similar-looking classes
Ambiguous category boundaries: the class definitions themselves are unclear or overlapping

When several annotators label the same image, ambiguity becomes measurable. In Snapshot Kgalagadi, each capture was classified by multiple volunteers, and the share of volunteers who agree with the final label is part of the dataset. Figure 12 shows that most captures are unambiguous (median agreement 100%), but 4.2% of the captures with an animal have less than 60% agreement. Notably, the most disputed images are not hard because two species look alike — they are overexposed night images, animals cut off at the image border, or tiny animals in the distance. Low agreement often signals poor image quality rather than difficult classes.






Figure 12: Left: share of volunteers who chose the final (consensus) species, per capture with an animal (log scale). Right: the six captures with the lowest agreement, with the consensus label and its vote share.



Notably, models trained on noisy labels tend to first learn the “clean” patterns and then gradually memorize the noisy examples (Arpit et al. 2017). This means that early stopping can partially mitigate the effects of label noise.
The practical takeaway: always inspect the data before training. Visualize samples from each class, check for obvious mislabels, and examine the boundary cases.


3.6 Hidden Biases in Image Datasets
Perhaps the most subtle data quality issue is hidden bias — systematic patterns in the dataset that correlate with the target labels but are not causally related to the concept being learned. A model that exploits such shortcuts will perform well on the training distribution but fail when deployed in a different context.
A well-known example is illustrated in Figure 13: a classifier trained to distinguish cows from camels may instead learn to distinguish green backgrounds (grass, pastures) from sandy backgrounds (desert). The model performs well on the test set — which shares the same background correlations — but fails on images of cows on a beach or camels in a zoo.






Figure 13: Top-5 predictions of an ImageNet-trained classifier on three cow images. (A) Cow on a pasture — confidently labelled “cow”. (B) The same type of animal on a beach — the model no longer recognises it as a cow and instead predicts water, beach, seashore. (C) A cow in a coastal setting — again labelled “mammal” but not “cow”. The background, not the animal, is driving the prediction. Example adapted from Beery et al. (2018).



The same effect can arise within a single dataset. Camera traps are mounted at fixed locations, so each camera records the same background over and over. If a species is seen mostly at one camera, the background becomes a predictive feature. Figure 14 demonstrates this for Snapshot Kgalagadi: 83% of all ostrich captures come from a single camera (A01), which records only 15% of all animal captures. Similarly, 85% of blue wildebeest captures come from camera A06. A model can reach high accuracy by learning “background of A01 → ostrich” — and it will fail as soon as an ostrich walks past a different camera. This contributes to the drop for the site-level split in Figure 9.






Figure 14: Left: share of each species’ captures recorded at each camera site (white: never recorded there). Right: ostriches at four different sites, with the number of ostrich captures per site.



Other forms of dataset bias include:

Geographic bias: datasets collected primarily in certain regions may not represent the visual diversity of other regions (e.g., different building styles, vegetation, clothing)
Selection bias: images sourced from the internet tend to overrepresent certain demographics, settings, and photographic styles
Watermark and source artifacts: images from specific sources may carry consistent visual artifacts that correlate with certain labels

Hidden biases are difficult to detect from aggregate metrics alone. They often only become apparent through careful inspection of model errors and failure patterns.

title: Training Guide
text:
TipLearning Objectives





After reading this guide you should be able to:

Apply a systematic recipe for training deep learning models from data inspection through regularization.
Identify common issues in image datasets: corrupted images, class imbalance, ambiguous labels, and resolution requirements.
Set up a debugging pipeline using input-independent baselines, batch overfitting, and input visualization.
Select appropriate regularization techniques — data augmentation, early stopping, weight decay, transfer learning — for a given scenario.
Choose a modern pretrained backbone (DINOv2/v3, SigLIP, ConvNeXt-V2, SAM, EVA) and decide on a fine-tuning strategy given dataset size and domain.

title: Training Guide
section: 1 A Recipe for Training Neural Networks
text:
1 A Recipe for Training Neural Networks
How does one successfully train a deep learning model? Modern ML frameworks make training appear straightforward, but Karpathy observed that these abstractions are leaky: without a solid understanding of what happens inside, backpropagation, gradient descent, loss dynamics, mistakes creep in undetected. A model with a learning rate that is too high may converge to a poor solution without raising any error. A data preprocessing bug may silently corrupt every batch. Training neural networks fails silently.

your_data = # plug your awesome dataset here
model = SuperCrossValidator(SuperDuper.fit, your_data, ResNet50, SGDOptimizer)

The recipe below, based on Karpathy’s approach A Recipe for Training Neural Networks, structures the process into four phases and helps avoid the most significant pitfalls. Steps 5 (hyperparameter search) and 6 (final squeezing techniques such as ensembling and Mixup) exist but are beyond the scope of this guide.

title: Training Guide
text:
2 Step 1: Know the Data
Before fitting any model, inspect the dataset thoroughly. For images in particular, one can examine sample data points, their distribution, label quality, and potential anomalies. Corrupted images, skewed class distributions, duplicates, and ambiguous labels can all be found at this stage. Addressing them early is far cheaper than debugging a trained model.
Figure 1 illustrates that even technically usable images may be severely distorted. Detecting these early informs preprocessing decisions.






Figure 1: Examples of images from camera traps distorted by heat. They may still be usable, but their quality must be assessed.



Figure 2 shows typical challenging cases in modeling images from camera traps. For example, small regions of interest (e.g. a small or distant animal) suggest that aggressive downscaling (e.g., to 224×224) may removes the relevant patterns entirely.






Figure 2: Examples of challenging cases in camera trap images. Small ROIs suggest that resolution requirements should be assessed carefully. Source: Beery et al. (2018).



Figure 3 shows that class imbalance, for camera trap datasets, is the norm rather than the exception. In this camera trap dataset, a single species (“Deer”) comprises approximately 65% of images. A model trained on such a distribution might be biased to predict the majority class.






Figure 3: Species distribution in a typical camera trap dataset. Heavy imbalance toward a few dominant species is common.



Sometimes, one may also encounter certain limitations, such as images that are ambiguous or belong to multiple classes. Figure 4 shows an example with a herd of animals containing multiple species (Thomson’s and Grant’s Gazelle). Here, image classification does not work well and object detection is a more natural choice.






Figure 4: An image from a camera trap containing multiple species simultaneously. Standard multi-class classification cannot handle this without modification.



A practical data inspection checklist:

Sample and examine images across all classes
Check class distribution; flag severe imbalances
Look for corrupted, blurry, or ambiguous images
Assess whether the default image resolution is sufficient for the task
Evaluate label quality: Can a domain expert reliably label each image?

title: Training Guide
text:
3 Step 2: Build a Baseline Pipeline
With a clear picture of the dataset, the next step is to establish a training / evaluation pipeline (see Figure 5) before fitting any serious model. Define the performance metric, create train/validation/test splits, and implement logging. Starting with a simple, well-understood model reduces the chance of undetected bugs.






Figure 5: The components of a typical machine learning process. Source: Raschka and Mirjalili (2020).



Debugging tips for the baseline phase:

Fix the random seed. Results must be reproducible before any meaningful comparison can be made.
Train an input-independent baseline. Set all input pixels to zero and train. Since the model receives no signal from the image, it will learn to predict the class distribution of the training set. Any model that performs worse than this has a fundamental pipeline error.
Overfit a single batch. Feed the same small batch repeatedly. If training loss does not reach near-zero, there is a bug in the forward pass or loss computation.
Visualize inputs just before the forward pass. Inspect what the model actually receives — augmentation bugs and preprocessing errors are often invisible until rendered.
Track fixed validation samples throughout training. Watching the same examples evolve over epochs reveals how the model’s behavior changes.







NoteQuiz: Input-Independent Baseline





What output would you expect from a model trained on zeroed-out inputs?


Click for result

Since the model receives no information from the image, it cannot distinguish between individual samples. To minimize average cross-entropy loss, the optimal strategy is to output the class distribution of the training set. For example, if 65% of images are deer, the model will predict approximately \(P(\text{deer}) \approx 0.65\) for every input.
This serves as a sanity check: if the actual model performs worse than this baseline, something is fundamentally wrong with the training pipeline.




A human baseline is also worth establishing where possible. For certain tasks, labels are subjective — annotators may disagree — which implies an upper bound on achievable performance. In the Snapshot Serengeti camera trap dataset, amateur annotators achieved 96.6% agreement with expert labels, setting a concrete ceiling for automated classification.






Figure 6: A challenging image from a camera trap dataset. Establishing how reliably humans can label such images sets a meaningful performance ceiling.

title: Training Guide
text:
4 Step 3: Overfit First
At this point the dataset is understood and the evaluation pipeline is verified. The focus now shifts to achieving strong training performance, deliberately setting aside generalization for the moment.
For model selection, follow the principle: don’t be a hero. Use an established architecture such as ResNet-50 rather than designing a custom one. For the optimizer, Adam is a conservative and generally effective choice — it is less sensitive to the learning rate than SGD, which reduces the chance of a poor hyperparameter choice masking a real problem.
If the model cannot overfit the training set at this stage, the problem is in the architecture or training setup — not in regularization. Only move to Step 4 once training performance is strong.

title: Training Guide
text:
5 Step 4: Regularize
With strong training performance established, the goal is now to improve performance on the validation set. Regularization techniques reduce the gap between training and validation by limiting overfitting.

5.1 More Training Data
The most effective regularizer is simply more labeled data. If collecting additional data is feasible, a learning curve — training models on subsets of increasing size and observing validation performance — estimates how much additional data would help.






Figure 7: Example of a learning curve. As training set size increases, validation performance improves. Source: Raschka and Mirjalili (2020).





5.2 Data Augmentation
When additional data cannot be collected, augmentation generates new training examples by applying random transformations to existing images on-the-fly. Each epoch the model sees slightly different versions of the same images, which reduces memorization.
Common augmentation families:

Geometric: random horizontal flips, crops, rotations, scaling
Photometric: brightness, contrast, saturation, grayscale
Advanced: Mixup (blending two images), CutMix (swapping patches between images), RandAugment (automated policy search)

Libraries such as AugLy (Figure 8), Albumentations (Figure 9), and Kornia (Figure 10) extend PyTorch’s built-in transforms with more complex augmentation pipelines.






Figure 8: AugLy augmentation library.









Figure 9: Albumentations augmentation library.









Figure 10: Kornia augmentation library.



Figure 11 illustrates augmentations applied to a single image: color changes, cropping, and rotations all produce new training examples from the same source.






Figure 11: Data augmentation applied to a single image. Each transformed copy becomes a distinct training example.



A practical guideline: when fine-tuning a pre-trained model, use minimal augmentation (random crops and horizontal flips). When training from scratch, heavier augmentation is typically beneficial.
Synthetic data is another option. Figure 12 shows an example where 3D animal models were composited into real and synthetic backgrounds, effectively expanding the camera trap training set.






Figure 12: Synthetic and semi-synthetic camera trap images generated using 3D animal models. Source: Beery et al. (2020).





5.3 Early Stopping
Early stopping monitors validation performance in regular intervals (e.g. after each epoch) and halts training when no improvement is observed for a set number of cycles. This prevents the model from continuing to memorize training data after the point of best generalization.






Figure 13: Early stopping halts training at the point of best validation performance. Source





5.4 Weight Decay
Weight decay penalizes large parameter values at each gradient update, encouraging simpler models. The modified update step is:
\[
\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t (1 - \lambda) - \eta \nabla J(\theta)
\]
where \(\lambda\) is the decay factor, \(\eta\) is the learning rate, and \(\theta\) are the model parameters. Implementations are available directly in PyTorch optimizers via the weight_decay argument.


5.5 Transfer Learning
Transfer learning is the practical default for image classification: start from a model pre-trained on a large dataset such as ImageNet and adapt it to the target task. Pre-trained features — edges, textures, shapes — generalize broadly across vision domains, making fine-tuning far more data-efficient than training from scratch.






Figure 14: Transfer learning: adapt a pre-trained backbone to a new task by replacing and training the final classification head. Source: Johnson and Fouhey (2021).



Adaptation strategies range from freezing the backbone entirely (feature extraction) to fine-tuning all layers. The appropriate strategy depends on dataset size and domain similarity. More strategies are covered in the Downstream Adaptation lecture.

title: Training Guide
text:
6 Modern Pretrained Backbones
ImageNet-pretrained ResNets remain solid baselines, but a new generation of foundation-model backbones trained on orders-of-magnitude more data consistently outperforms them, often with less fine-tuning data required. The table below summarizes some practical options:









Model
Pretraining
Strengths
Good for




DINOv3
Self-supervised (images)
Strong general-purpose features; no labels needed
Feature extraction, k-NN, linear probe


CLIP and variants
Vision–language (image–text)
Zero-shot and few-shot transfer; multilingual
Open-vocabulary classification, retrieval


ConvNeXt-V2
Self-supervised (FCMAE)
Pure CNN; no attention; fast inference
When ViT overhead is a concern


SAM3
Large-scale segmentation
Powerful spatial features; click-based prompting
Segmentation, detection pre-training



Choosing a backbone:

Default choice: DINOv3 is a strong all-round starting point for feature extraction and fine-tuning on domain-specific data.

All of these backbones are available via timm (pip install timm) with a consistent API:
import timm

model = timm.create_model("vit_base_patch14_dinov2", pretrained=True, num_classes=0)
features = model(images)  # (B, 768) feature vectors, no head
How to adapt a chosen backbone to a target task, k-NN, linear probe, LoRA, partial or full fine-tuning, and how to choose between them based on dataset size and domain similarity, is covered in Adapting Models.

title: Training Guide
text:
7 Monitoring Training Progress
Beyond loss and accuracy curves, it is valuable to track model behaviour on a fixed set of validation images throughout training. For each checkpoint, run inference on the same small set of examples (e.g., 16–32 images spanning all classes) and log the top predictions alongside the images. This reveals qualitative changes, the model gaining confidence on easy examples, reducing confusion between similar classes, that aggregate metrics can obscure.
A complementary view is a prediction-confidence plot over epochs: for the same fixed samples, track how the predicted probability for the correct class evolves. An ideal trajectory rises steadily; oscillation or sudden drops signal instability or learning-rate issues.






NoteTip: Track fixed samples in Weights & Biases / MLflow



Both W&B and MLflow support logging images with annotations per step. Log the fixed validation grid at the end of each epoch with predicted class and confidence overlaid. Reviewing this timeline at the end of training is one of the fastest ways to diagnose where the model still fails.
