Stride (\(s\)): Step size when moving the kernel
Dilation (\(d\)): Spacing between kernel elements

title: 3 - Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
Receptive Field: Formula
The receptive field of a CNN \(r_0\):
\[\begin{equation}
r_0 = \sum_{l=1}^L \left( (k_l - 1) \prod_{i=1}^{l-1} s_i \right) + 1
\end{equation}\]

\(L\): Total number of layers
\(k_l\): Kernel size at layer \(l\)
\(s_i\): Stride at layer \(i\), from layer 1 up to \(l-1\)

title: 3 - Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
Quiz: Receptive Field
Three layers, each \(k = 3\), \(s = 1\). What is the receptive field \(r_0\)?

\[r_0 = (3-1) + (3-1) + (3-1) + 1 = 7\]


Three \(3\times3\) convs see \(7\times7\), with \(3 \times 9 = 27\) weights instead of \(49\) for one \(7\times7\) (per channel pair).

Downsampling
Spatial downsampling reduces resolution (H×W → H’×W’): stride \(> 1\) (learned) or pooling (fixed).

a) Sub-Sampling, b) Max Pooling, c) Average Pooling. Source: Prince (2023)

title: 3 - Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
Upsampling
Needed when the output must have pixel resolution, e.g. segmentation.

a) Duplicate, b) Max-Unpooling, c) Bilinear Interpolation. Source: Prince (2023)
Also: transposed convolutions (learnable upsampling).

title: 3 - Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
1×1 Convolutions
\((C_{in} \times H \times W) \rightarrow (C_{out} \times H \times W)\): change the number of channels, no spatial mixing.

Source: Prince (2023)

title: 3 - Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
Global Average Pooling
Averages each activation map: \((C \times H \times W) \rightarrow (C \times 1 \times 1)\). Often used right before the classifier.

Global Average pooling, input (left) and output (right).

title: 3 - Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
Quiz: MLP vs CNN Efficiency
CIFAR-10 Images: \(32 \times 32 \times 3\)

MLP: 2 hidden layers (256, 128 neurons)
How many parameters in first layer?


CNN: 2 conv layers (16 filters, \(3\times3\), then 32 filters, \(3\times3\))
How many parameters in first layer?

title: 3 - Convolutional Neural Networks
text:
Quiz: Solutions

MLP first layer:
\((32 \times 32 \times 3) \times 256 = 3{,}072 \times 256 = 786{,}432\) parameters


CNN first layer:
\((3 \times 3 \times 3 \times 16) + 16 = 432 + 16 = 448\) parameters


CNN uses 1,755× fewer parameters! 🚀


Why? Local connectivity + parameter sharing = massive efficiency!

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision

Classification: \(f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{y}\)


Many-to-one: many elephant images → one label.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Generation: \(g(\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x}\)


One-to-many: one label → many possible elephant images.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Quiz: The Problem

If the input is just the label “elephant”, how can the model generate different elephants?


Answer: Neural networks are deterministic. We need stochasticity.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
The Diversity Challenge


A specific label should produce a diverse set of outputs.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Solution: Latent Variables

Add stochastic input \(\mathbf{z} \sim p(\mathbf{z})\):
\[\hat{\mathbf{x}} = g_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z}), \qquad \mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\]


Latent variable \(\mathbf{z}\) — unobserved factors:

pose, size, number of individuals
time of day, surroundings, lighting




\(\mathbf{y}\) → what to generate (control)
\(\mathbf{z}\) → how it varies (diversity)

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Quiz: Latent Variables

Reproduced from Foster (2023).
What could the latent variables be for this dataset?


Answer: Width and height — 2 unobserved latent variables.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Latent Space → Outputs


Plausible 2D latent space and the mapping \(g\) to samples. Reproduced from Foster (2023).

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Unconditional Generation

The model receives only stochastic input:
\[\mathbf{z} \sim p(\mathbf{z}), \quad \hat{\mathbf{x}} = g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})\]



\(\mathbf{z}\) provides diversity
different \(\mathbf{z}\) → different plausible outputs
e.g. “any face”, “any room”, “any product”

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Conditional Generation

The model also receives conditioning information \(\mathbf{c}\):
\[\hat{\mathbf{x}} = g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{c})\]


\(\mathbf{c}\) specifies what should be generated, preserved, completed, enhanced, or changed.



Key idea: \(\mathbf{z}\) provides diversity, \(\mathbf{c}\) provides control.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Creative vs. Faithful


Creative: unconditional, text-to-image — diversity, plausibility
Faithful: inpainting, super-res, translation, editing — identity, geometry, layout
Most real systems need both







Prompt: Create an image where this object is shown dancing in the jungle with a banana in one hand and a shampoo in the other hand.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
The Objective


Generated \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) should have high probability under the real data distribution \(p_{\text{data}}(\mathbf{x})\).

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Fidelity and Coverage


Fidelity: samples look like real data
Coverage: samples show the full variety of real data, in the right proportions

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Two Approaches

1. Direct (Implicit)
Learn a function that generates samples directly: \[g(\mathbf{z}) = \mathbf{x}\]


2. Indirect (Density)
Learn a probability density \(p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\), then sample from it.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Density Models

Learn \(p_{\theta}: \mathbf{x} \to [0, \infty)\) with normalization:
\[\int_{\mathbf{x}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\, d\mathbf{x} = 1\]


Goal: \(p_{\theta} \approx p_{\text{data}}\).


Maximum likelihood objective:
\[\underset{\theta}{\arg\max} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})\]


Examples: VAEs, normalizing flows, autoregressive models.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Learning a Density Model






Initial







Improved






The model adapts to place high probability where training data lies.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Demo: Learning a 1D Distribution


Can a single Gaussian reach high fidelity and high coverage? Open in new tab

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Density ≠ Generation

A density model evaluates \(p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\) — useful for outlier detection.


To generate, we additionally need a sampling mechanism.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Efficient Sampling


GANs and VAEs: one forward pass. Diffusion and flow matching: tens of steps. Autoregressive: one step per token.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Fidelity and Coverage



samples between the modes. (d) Mode collapse: realistic samples, but only of a few modes, a well-known problem of GANs.



Techniques that increase fidelity often reduce coverage, e.g. guidance in diffusion models (Ho and Salimans 2022) moves a model from (c) towards (d).

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Smooth Latent Space

VAE with a 2D latent space, trained on MNIST.
Similar \(\mathbf{z}\) → similar outputs: interpolation morphs one digit into another.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Disentangled Latent Space


Not required for control: modern models are controlled through conditioning (text, masks, reference images).

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Likelihood Computation


Exact: autoregressive, normalizing flows. Bound or expensive: VAEs, diffusion, flow matching. None: GANs.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Why Evaluation Is Hard

Usually no single correct output. Many outputs may be valid for one input.


Better question than “is it correct?”:

Are the generated images realistic and varied, do they follow the condition, and are they useful?

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Likelihood

\[\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})\]


High likelihood → model assigns high probability to real data.


Not available for GANs (no explicit density)
Likelihood and sample quality are largely independent (Theis et al. 2016)

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Human Evaluation

Which image looks more realistic?
Which better matches the prompt?
Which has fewer artifacts?
Which would you prefer to use?


Most meaningful for visual quality — but slow, subjective, expensive.


Preference leaderboards: blind pairwise comparisons, aggregated into a ranking.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Distribution-Level Metrics: FID


FID (Heusel et al. 2018): Fréchet distance between Gaussians fitted to Inception features of real and generated images. Lower is better.

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Demo: FID, Precision and Recall


Compare Shifted and Mode collapse: which metric tells them apart? Open in new tab

title: 8 - Generative AI for Computer Vision
text:
Limitations of Distribution Metrics

One FID value does not say whether fidelity or coverage is the problem: precision and recall (Kynkäänniemi et al. 2019) separate them
FID depends on the number of samples and on ImageNet features
Don’t evaluate prompt adherence or input fidelity
Can hide failures on rare classes, spatial relations, text rendering

title: 7 - Modern Vision Backbones
text:
Transformers in Vision

Transformers dominate language — long-range dependencies, scale.


Can the same architecture work for images?



CNNs: strong inductive biases (locality, translation equivariance)
Transformers: minimal assumptions, treat input as a generic sequence



ViT (2020, Dosovitskiy et al. (2020)): yes, with enough pretraining data.

title: 7 - Modern Vision Backbones
section: The Trick: Treat Images as Patches
text:
The Trick: Treat Images as Patches

A 2-D image grid → a sequence of patches.

title: 7 - Modern Vision Backbones
text:
The Patch Embedding Pipeline

Divide image into a grid of patches
Flatten each patch (\(16 \times 16 \times 3 = 768\))
Project through a learnable linear layer → embedding of dim \(D\)
Add positional embeddings — encode spatial position
Prepend [CLS] token — image-level representation (à la BERT)


Result: a sequence of \(N + 1\) embeddings → standard transformer encoder.

title: 7 - Modern Vision Backbones
text:
ViT Architecture

Source: Dosovitskiy et al. (2020)

title: 7 - Modern Vision Backbones
text:
Quiz: Patch Size 32 × 32
A \(224 \times 224\) image with \(16 \times 16\) patches gives 196 patches. What changes if patch size goes from 16 to 32?


Number of patches: \((224/32)^2 = 7^2 = \mathbf{49}\) — 4× fewer




Faster — self-attention is quadratic in sequence length
Less detail — each patch covers a larger area
Trade-off — same as resolution choice in CNNs

title: 7 - Modern Vision Backbones
text:
Receptive Field — The Big Difference

CNN — local kernel → grows gradually with depth


ViT — every patch attends to every other patch from layer 1


ViT receptive field is global from the start.

title: 7 - Modern Vision Backbones
text:
Strength and Weakness

✅ Long-range dependencies for free
❌ No locality prior — must be learned from data
❌ Needs far more training examples

title: 7 - Modern Vision Backbones
text:
Quiz: Receptive Fields
A CNN with three 3×3 conv layers (stride 1) has a 7×7 receptive field.
A ViT with the same depth has a receptive field that covers…?

7×7 pixels
The entire patch
The entire image


The entire image.


After even one transformer layer, every output has aggregated information from all patches.

title: 7 - Modern Vision Backbones
text:
Inductive Biases — Help or Hindrance?

CNNs build in locality and translation equivariance.


These assumptions are often useful for natural images, especially with limited data.


ViTs have weaker image-specific priors and rely more on data and pretraining.



Small data: strong priors can help
Massive pretraining: weaker priors can become an advantage

title: 7 - Modern Vision Backbones
text:
Inductive Biases in Practice


A trained ViT learns some locality from data: wide in layer 1, more local in middle layers, then increasingly global.

title: 7 - Modern Vision Backbones
text:
Quiz: When Can Locality Hurt?
Where might a strong local bias become limiting?


Global layout: distinguishing scenes may require the arrangement of many regions, not just local patches




Long-range relations: e.g. person, leash, and dog may be far apart in the image




Repeated / non-local patterns: the relevant structure may be defined by relationships between distant regions



CNNs can capture these with enough depth and pooling, but global interactions are indirect.


ViTs model long-range interactions more directly through self-attention.

title: 7 - Modern Vision Backbones
text:
Decision Guide

Limited data / limited compute: start with a pretrained CNN or compact hybrid
Large-scale pretraining available: ViT-style models are strong defaults
Need early global context: ViT or hybrid architecture
Edge deployment / fast inference: efficient CNN or efficient hybrid
In practice: pretraining data, training recipe, and adaptation strategy often matter as much as the backbone

title: 7 - Modern Vision Backbones
text:
Hybrid Architectures

Convs early (efficient local features) + Transformers late (global reasoning).


Examples: FastViT (Vasu et al. (2023)), EfficientViT.


Conversely: ConvNeXt modernizes ResNet with ViT-style training and design.

title: 7 - Modern Vision Backbones
text:
Beyond Classification — Multimodal ViTs

BLIP-2 (Li et al. (2023)) — frozen ViT + LLM via Q-Former → visual QA
Flamingo (Alayrac et al. (2022)) — few-shot multimodal across image-text sequences


The patch-embedding approach has become a universal interface between visual and language representations.
